level.commodus.hint: Only he who has already been proclaimed co-ruler during his lifetime will receive the purple on his deathbed; a son-in-law general nearby is a temptation history rejected. And the new emperor will first pay off the Germans and depart for Rome.
level.commodus.intro: For a hundred years, power in Rome was transferred not by blood, but by merit: each princeps adopted the best. For the first time in a century, this emperor has a natural son.
level.commodus.title: The Philosopher and the Son
level.conclave.fact: In 1492, Rodrigo Borgia secured his election as Pope Alexander VI through lavish bribes to the cardinals. His pontificate became a symbol of the venality and corruption of the Renaissance Church.
level.conclave.goal: Rodrigo Borgia buys the papal throne
level.conclave.hint: Let Rodrigo first buy the cardinals' votes — and only a paid conclave will raise him to the throne. della Rovere cannot outbid the Borgia's coffers.
level.conclave.intro: 1492. The Throne of Peter is vacant. Cardinal Rodrigo Borgia and his old enemy della Rovere vie for the tiara. Rodrigo has gold.
level.conclave.title: Alexander VI
level.concordat.fact: The Concordat of 1801 returned the Catholic Church to France under state control: bishops were appointed by the First Consul, priests were paid by the treasury, and confiscated church property was not returned. Pius VII came to Paris to crown Napoleon on December 2, 1804 — and watched as Napoleon took the crown from his hands and placed it on his own head, then crowned Josephine. Five years later, Napoleon would arrest the Pope and hold him captive until 1814; the Pope would outlive him and pray for his soul on Saint Helena.
level.concordat.goal: The Consul reconciles with the Pope — and the Pope travels to watch him take the crown himself
level.concordat.hint: The Cult of Reason and the Pope's arrest are not the way. The Consul negotiates with leverage: the Pope will yield. And the yielding Pope will come to Notre Dame — for the coronation, where the crown will be taken without him.
level.concordat.intro: The Revolution closed churches and established the Cult of Reason; half of France attended mass in secret. The First Consul understands: the people need a priest, and he needs legitimacy. Pope Pius VII is ready to negotiate.
level.concordat.source: Thiers, 'History of the Consulate and the Empire'; text of the Concordat of 1801
level.concordat.title: The Concordat
level.constantine.fact: On October 28, 312, at the Milvian Bridge, Constantine defeated Maxentius, who had led his army out from behind the walls, believing a prophecy, and drowned in the Tiber during the retreat across a pontoon bridge. Eusebius recounts the cross in the sky with the inscription 'In hoc signo vinces' (By this sign you shall conquer), a quarter-century later, from the emperor's own words; Lactantius writes more simply—of a dream the night before. In 313, the Edict of Milan granted Christians freedom of worship, and several decades later, their faith became the state religion. Constantine himself was baptized only on his deathbed.
level.constantine.goal: The Empire changes its god—and does so by decree
level.constantine.hint: The omen comes only to one who has not bound himself by oath to the old gods — and grants strength for battle. And an era is made not by the sword, but by a signature on an edict — with a man in ecclesiastical robes nearby.
level.constantine.intro: The Tetrarchy crumbled, there are four Augusti once more, and each marches against the other. Outside Rome, the rival has twice as many troops and walls that have not been breached in two hundred years.
level.constantine.title: By This, Conquer
level.cook.fact: James Cook completed three circumnavigations, was the first to map New Zealand and the eastern coast of Australia (Botany Bay, 1770), crossed the Antarctic Circle, and defeated scurvy with sauerkraut. On February 14, 1779, in Kealakekua Bay, Hawaii, while attempting to take Chief Kalaniʻōpuʻu hostage for a stolen longboat, he was killed on shore; his body was divided according to Hawaiian custom for chiefs, and some bones were returned to the crew for burial at sea. The Hawaiians apparently greeted him as the god Lono — and killed him when he returned out of season.
level.cook.goal: A navigator maps half the world — and perishes where he was taken for a god.
level.cook.hint: A converted collier — preparation, strength of voyage. Then Botany Bay and a flag over new land — he will be loved. But in Hawaii, he will try to take the chief hostage — and the chief will kill him. Negotiation will fail: the chief is stronger.
level.cook.intro: The son of a Yorkshire farm labourer became the Royal Navy's best navigator. The Admiralty gives him the collier 'Endeavour' and orders to find the Southern Continent. He will find the eastern coast of Australia — and ten years later, die on a Hawaiian beach.
level.cook.source: James Cook, 'Journals'; John Beaglehole, 'The Life of Captain James Cook'
level.cook.title: Captain Cook
level.coriolanus_v.fact: Around 491 BC, Coriolanus was exiled for his speeches against the plebeians, and he went to the Volscians, to his old adversary Attius Tullius. At the head of the Volscian army, he reached the fifth milestone from Rome; he sent away envoys and priests empty-handed. Then his mother Veturia and wife Volumnia came to his camp with their children. His mother asked: 'Have you come as an enemy or as a son?' — and he withdrew his army. According to one version, the Volscians killed him for this; according to another, he lived in exile into old age, repeating that exile was the bitterest fate for an old man. Shakespeare made a tragedy out of this, and Plutarch — a lesson that immoderate anger destroys both enemies and one's own.
level.coriolanus_v.goal: An exile leads enemies against Rome — and turns back at its very walls
level.coriolanus_v.hint: First, trial and exile, then friendship with yesterday's enemy. At the walls, no army will stop him — only his mother. He must not storm the city: if he wins, there will be no one left to stop.
level.coriolanus_v.intro: Gnaeus Marcius, surnamed Coriolanus for the city he captured, is Rome's best general and its worst politician: he demanded that no grain be given to the plebeians until they renounced their tribunes. Tribune Sicinius summons him to trial.
level.coriolanus_v.title: A Mother at the Walls
level.coronation.fact: On January 16, 1547, Grand Prince Ivan IV was crowned Tsar in the Dormition Cathedral of the Kremlin, being the first to adopt the title "Tsar of All Rus'." Thus, the Tsardom of Russia was born.
level.coronation.goal: The Sovereign of All Rus' receives the Tsar's crown
level.coronation.hint: Let Ivan besiege boyar Shuisky in the Duma and become an autocrat — only then will he be crowned tsar. The boyar will not wear the crown.
level.coronation.intro: Young Ivan grew up under wayward boyar-regents. To become tsar, he must first break their power.
level.coronation.source: The Rite of Coronation of Ivan IV, 1547
level.coronation.title: Coronation as Tsar
level.corvus.fact: In 260 BC, at Mylae, Gaius Duilius for the first time defeated the Carthaginian fleet. The Romans were unskilled in ramming tactics and placed «crows» on their prows — a gangplank with a spike: it would drop onto the enemy deck, turning a naval battle into an infantry engagement, where the legionary was unmatched. In honor of the victory, a column adorned with the prows of captured ships (columna rostrata) was erected in the Forum. The «crow» had a price: it made ships unstable, and in the storm of 255 BC, Rome lost almost its entire fleet with it.
level.corvus.goal: Land-based Rome sinks the Carthaginian fleet at Mylae
level.corvus.hint: At sea, the Carthaginians are stronger – if you engage them as is. Strength is forged in the shipyard.
level.corvus.intro: Rome has been at war with Carthage for six years and can achieve nothing: the Carthaginians have the best fleet in the world, while the Romans drown as soon as they leave the shore. The fleet is commanded by Consul Gaius Duilius — a man of the land who does not trust the sea.
level.corvus.title: The Boarding Raven
level.cosimo.fact: In September 1433, under pressure from Rinaldo degli Albizzi, the Signoria arrested Cosimo de' Medici and imprisoned him in the tower of Palazzo Vecchio; he feared poison and bribed his jailer, and the death sentence was commuted to ten years of exile. In Venice, he was received like a sovereign, while the Florentine treasury, without the Medici bank, became empty. A year later, a new Signoria revoked the sentence; on October 6, 1434, Cosimo returned, and now Albizzi and seventy families of their supporters were sent into ten years of exile. For thirty years he ruled without holding office — «he governed the republic like a father governs his family»; after his death in 1464, the Signoria ordered «Pater Patriae» to be inscribed on his tomb. His grandson was Lorenzo the Magnificent.
level.cosimo.goal: The banker is exiled — and without his money, the city itself calls him back a year later, and then exiles his enemies instead.
level.cosimo.hint: First, the influential oligarch accuses the banker — condemned. The condemned goes to Venice. Florence, without money, calls him back — returned, with influence. The returned one exiles the oligarch. There's no need to buy the Signoria — a bought oligarch cannot be exiled.
level.cosimo.intro: Cosimo de' Medici is the wealthiest banker in Europe and the unofficial head of the popular party. The old oligarchy, led by Rinaldo degli Albizzi, accuses him of aspiring to tyranny and achieves his exile. But the exiled man holds all the city's money.
level.cosimo.source: N. Machiavelli, «History of Florence»; C. Hibbert, «The Medici»
level.cosimo.title: Father of the Fatherland
level.coup.fact: On June 28, 1762, the Guards enthroned Catherine, deposing her husband Peter III. A week later, the former emperor died in Ropsha. Thus began 34 years of the 'Golden Age' of the nobility.
level.coup.goal: The Guards depose Peter III — Catherine takes the throne
level.coup.hint: Let Orlov first raise the guard for Catherine — and only supported by bayonets will she depose and ruin Peter III. Without the guard, the coup will fail.
level.coup.intro: Peter III is unpopular and weak. His wife Catherine and guardsman Orlov are preparing a coup.
level.coup.title: The Coup of 1762
level.court_reform.fact: The Judicial Statutes of 20 November 1864 gave Russia an open and adversarial court, irremovable judges, a bar, and trial by jury — twelve 'judges of fact' drawn from every estate. On 24 January 1878 Vera Zasulich came to the public reception of the St Petersburg governor Fyodor Trepov and shot him with a revolver, wounding him gravely: the cause was his order to flog the political prisoner Bogolyubov, who had failed to take off his cap before him. On 31 March 1878 the case was heard in the district court under the presidency of Anatoly Koni; the jury answered 'no, not guilty' on every count, the hall exploded in ovation, and out in the street the crowd took her away from the police. Alexander II was furious; Koni refused to resign and was shunted for years into the civil department. Already in the summer of 1878 cases of attacks on officials were taken away from juries and handed to military courts. Zasulich managed to get abroad, lived until 1919 and saw the revolution, which she did not accept.
level.court_reform.goal: The jury acquits a woman who fired and does not deny firing — and the presiding judge will never be forgiven for it
level.court_reform.hint: The new court first: the sovereign introduces trial by jury, and a young lawyer enters that court. Then the governor's reception room: the shot makes her a defendant. And only the jury bench lifts the charge — at the cost of the presiding judge's career. The Senate's Special Tribunal is the trap: there a defendant is not acquitted but finished off.
level.court_reform.intro: On 20 November 1864 Alexander II introduced trial by jury: public, adversarial, with counsel for the defence and twelve elected judges of fact. Fourteen years later this court would try Vera Zasulich, who had shot the governor of St Petersburg, Trepov, presided over by Anatoly Koni, whose whole career had been made in the new courts.
level.court_reform.source: A. Koni, 'Recollections of the Vera Zasulich Case'; the Judicial Statutes of 1864
level.court_reform.title: Twelve Judges of Fact
level.cranmer_hand.fact: Under pressure, Thomas Cranmer signed six recantations of Protestantism — by law, a repentant heretic was to be pardoned, but Mary I wanted his death regardless. On March 21, 1556, at St Mary's Church in Oxford, where he was to publicly repent, he instead renounced his recantations: 'And as my hand hath offended, writing contrary to my heart, my hand shall first be punished.' At the stake, he stretched his right hand into the flames and held it there until it burned. Two and a half years later, Mary died, and his Book of Common Prayer returned to every English church.
level.cranmer_hand.goal: The recanter renounces his recantation — and thrusts the hand that signed into the fire.
level.cranmer_hand.hint: A cardinal with influence will persuade him to recant — he will yield. But on the pulpit on the day of execution, he will renounce his recantation — and be unyielding again. The queen will burn the condemned; there will be no pardon.
level.cranmer_hand.intro: Thomas Cranmer, the Archbishop who annulled Henry's marriage to Catherine and authored the English Book of Common Prayer, has been imprisoned in Oxford for two years. Cardinal Pole secured his recantation of heresy. The Queen still orders him to be burned.
level.cranmer_hand.source: John Foxe, 'Book of Martyrs', Vol. VIII; Diarmaid MacCulloch, 'Thomas Cranmer: A Life'
level.cranmer_hand.title: The Hand That Signed
level.crecy.fact: On August 26, 1346, at Crécy, English archers – up to five thousand, firing ten arrows per minute – decimated Genoese crossbowmen and fifteen charges of French knightly cavalry; France lost thousands of knights and the blind King John of Bohemia, whose motto 'Ich dien' the Black Prince adopted. When the earls asked Edward III to aid his hard-pressed son, he, according to Froissart, replied: «Let the boy win his spurs.» Thus began the Hundred Years' War in earnest – and an era ended when a knight on horseback was worth hundreds of foot soldiers.
level.crecy.goal: Archers break knightly France, and the King refuses aid to his son – so that he may win on his own.
level.crecy.hint: England's strength — archers on the hill; prepare them before battle. In battle, three positions: the third — for the prince, who is hard-pressed; the father will not send aid, and the son will earn his spurs himself. If you rescue him — there will be no glory.
level.crecy.intro: Edward III landed in France with archers recruited from yeomen and occupied a hill near Crécy. Philip VI leads a knightly army twice its size. The sixteen-year-old Black Prince commands the first line – and he is hard-pressed.
level.crecy.source: Jean Froissart, 'Chronicles', I; Geoffrey le Baker
level.crecy.title: Let the boy win his spurs
level.crimea.fact: On April 8 (19), 1783, Catherine II signed a manifesto on the annexation of Crimea 'for all time'; the last Khan Sahin Giray abdicated, received a pension of two hundred thousand rubles, and left for Russia, and later for Turkey, where he was strangled. Potemkin, who received the title of Tauride, built Sevastopol and the Black Sea Fleet in four years. In the winter of 1787, the Empress, with foreign ambassadors, traveled along the Dnieper to Crimea; the Saxon diplomat Helbig later wrote about 'Potemkin villages' — villages painted on canvas and the same herds driven along the shore. Historians consider this an exaggeration by the enemies of the Most Serene Prince — but the expression stuck.
level.crimea.goal: The Khan is bought with a pension, Crimea is taken by manifesto — and the Empress is shown happy villages
level.crimea.hint: First, a pension for the Khan — bought, an ally. The Empress with a manifesto over the bought Khan — Crimea is annexed. Then the Tauride journey: the sovereign and the Most Serene Prince — villages. No need to fight the Khan — he is not an enemy, but a purchase.
level.crimea.intro: The Crimean Khanate has broken away from the Turks and is held by Russian bayonets; Khan Sahin Giray is a protégé of St. Petersburg, hated by his own people. Potemkin suggests not fighting, but buying.
level.crimea.source: 'Manifesto on the Acceptance of Crimea', 1783; S. Montefiore, 'Potemkin'
level.crimea.title: Crimea
level.cromwell_fall.fact: In July 1540, Thomas Cromwell was condemned by an Act of Attainder — without trial, by the very method he himself introduced. Formally for heresy and treason, in essence for the marriage to Anne of Cleves, which the king disliked, and because enemies at court exploited this. From the Tower, he wrote to the king: 'Mercy, mercy, mercy.' The executioner was inexperienced and struck several times. It is said that Henry later regretted his loss and called him 'the most faithful servant I ever had.' On the same day, the king married Catherine Howard.
level.cromwell_fall.goal: The minister who arranged the king's marriage loses his head for it.
level.cromwell_fall.hint: First, the counselor must present the bride — this is both his service and his undoing. Then the king condemns the minister with a speech in Parliament, and the condemned is executed. A conversation with the king will not save Cromwell.
level.cromwell_fall.intro: Thomas Cromwell did everything for the king: severed ties with Rome, executed Anne, dissolved the monasteries. His last service was a bride from Cleves, whom he presented to the king based on Holbein's portrait. The king saw her in person and declared: 'I do not like her.'
level.cromwell_fall.title: Cromwell
level.culloden.fact: On April 16, 1746, on Culloden Moor, Charles Edward Stuart's Jacobites were annihilated in an hour: the Highlanders charged into grapeshot. Cumberland finished off the wounded and earned the nickname 'The Butcher'. The Prince hid in the mountains for five months with a £30,000 bounty on his head – no one betrayed him; Flora MacDonald smuggled him to the Isle of Skye disguised as an Irish maid, Betty Burke, for which she spent a year in the Tower. The kilt and bagpipes were banned for thirty-six years. The Prince died a drunkard in Rome; the 'Skye Boat Song' outlived him by two centuries.
level.culloden.goal: The last Stuart uprising perishes on the moor, and the Prince is spirited away disguised as a maid.
level.culloden.hint: The banner in Glenfinnan gathers the Highlanders — a force, but not against Cumberland's cannons: the prince will be defeated at Culloden. Marching on London is not an option. A lady will save the defeated, disguising him as a maidservant.
level.culloden.intro: The grandson of the deposed James II landed in Scotland with seven companions to reclaim the Stuart throne. The Highlanders followed him; he reached Derby, two hundred kilometers from London, — and turned back. Following him is the Duke of Cumberland with cannons.
level.culloden.source: J. Boswell, 'A Journey to the Hebrides'; J. Prebble, 'Culloden'
level.culloden.title: Bonnie Prince Charlie
level.cyril_methodius.fact: In 862 the Moravian prince Rastislav asked the emperor Michael III for teachers who knew Slavic speech. Constantine the Philosopher, the future Cyril, and his brother Methodius, both from Thessalonica, where Slavic was heard in the streets, took up the task. Around 863 Constantine devised the Glagolitic script — an alphabet invented for the sounds of the Slavic language rather than adapted from Greek — and translated the Gospel: 'In the beginning was the Word.' At Venice in 867 he was set upon by adherents of the 'trilingual heresy', the doctrine that only Hebrew, Greek and Latin are sacred, because the inscription on the Cross was in those languages. He answered with the apostle Paul and with a psalm: 'Let everything that has breath praise the Lord.' At Rome Pope Adrian II approved the Slavonic liturgy. Constantine died there on 14 February 869, having taken monastic vows fifty days before his death under the name Cyril. The Cyrillic alphabet — the one written today — was composed later by their disciples in Bulgaria and named in his honour.
level.cyril_methodius.goal: A philosopher invents letters to fit Slavic speech — and fights off those who hold only three languages holy
level.cyril_methodius.hint: First the letter: both brothers take on the mission. It is the philosopher sent on the mission who then puts the alphabet together. With that alphabet in hand he wins the dispute over the three languages. The library of Hagia Sophia is preparation: sitting over books, you will not begin a mission.
level.cyril_methodius.intro: A letter comes to Constantinople from Moravia: the prince is asking for teachers who could explain the faith in a language his people understand. In the capital there is a man nicknamed the Philosopher — a master of Hebrew, Arabic and Gothic, who has already travelled to dispute about faith with the Saracens and the Khazars. He has a brother who is a monk.
level.cyril_methodius.source: 'The Life of Constantine-Cyril the Philosopher'; 'The Life of Methodius'
level.cyril_methodius.title: Everything That Has Breath
level.dante.fact: In November 1301, Charles of Valois, sent by Boniface VIII, allowed the Black Guelphs of Corso Donati into Florence; the city was plundered for six days. On January 27, 1302, Dante, a former prior, was condemned in absentia for bribery and «hostility to the Pope» — a fine and exile, and on March 10, he was sentenced to be burned if caught. He never returned; in 1315, he was offered to return by admitting guilt and paying, but he refused: «Can I not gaze upon the sun and stars everywhere?» He wrote «The Divine Comedy» in exile for twenty years, placing Boniface in the eighth circle of hell while the Pope was still alive. He died in Ravenna in 1321; Florence begged for centuries to return his remains — Ravenna has not yielded them to this day.
level.dante.goal: The Pope lets the Black Guelphs into the city, the poet is condemned to the stake in absentia — and he writes a book that will outlive everyone.
level.dante.hint: First, the Pope with the Black Guelph lets Valois in — the Black Guelphs are powerful and against the poet. The influential Black Guelph accuses the poet — condemned. The condemned goes into exile — «The Comedy». To ask for pardon means to admit guilt; he did not do that.
level.dante.intro: Florence is split between White and Black Guelphs. The poet Dante is a prior of the republic and a White Guelph. Pope Boniface VIII wants the city for himself and sends the «peacemaker» Charles of Valois. While Dante is on an embassy in Rome, the French enter the city.
level.dante.source: G. Boccaccio, «Life of Dante»; Dino Compagni, «Chronicle»
level.dante.title: Dante's Exile
level.danton.fact: On April 5, 1794, Georges Danton, one of the Revolution's leaders who advocated for tempering the Terror, was executed at Robespierre's behest. 'You will show my head to the people: it is worth it,' he declared to the executioner.
level.danton.goal: Robespierre sends his former comrade to the guillotine
level.danton.hint: First, two leaders' friendship on the tribune. Then the Incorruptible condemns his former friend with a speech — and becomes a tyrant. The condemned is executed with weight.
level.danton.title: Danton on the Scaffold
level.decembrists.fact: On December 14 (26), 1825, about three thousand soldiers, commanded by officers of secret societies, marched onto Senate Square, refusing to swear allegiance to Nicholas; they stood in a square formation until dusk — the chosen dictator, Prince Trubetskoy, never appeared, and Kakhovsky shot Governor-General Miloradovich, who had come to persuade them. Around five o'clock, Nicholas ordered grapeshot to be fired; the square formation dispersed, and those fleeing were beaten on the ice of the Neva. Of the six hundred under investigation, five — Pestel, Ryleyev, Muravyov-Apostol, Bestuzhev-Ryumin, and Kakhovsky — were hanged on July 13, 1826, at the Kronwerk of the Peter and Paul Fortress; for three, the ropes broke, and they were hanged a second time. One hundred and twenty were exiled to Siberia; some were followed by their wives. Nicholas ruled for thirty years, remembering that day.
level.decembrists.goal: The new emperor receives the oath, rebellious regiments stand in the square until dark — and receive grapeshot and the gallows.
level.decembrists.hint: Re-oath — Nicholas is crowned and strong. Ryleyev leads regiments to the square — rebellion is raised. The strong emperor fires grapeshot — the defeated rebel is outlawed. The emperor, with authority, executes the condemned in the Peter and Paul Fortress. Swearing allegiance to Constantine — giving up the throne.
level.decembrists.intro: Alexander I died in Taganrog, heir Constantine abdicated, but no one knows this — the country swore allegiance to him. Interregnum. Conspirator officers decide to lead regiments to the square on the day of Nicholas's re-oath and prevent it from taking place. The dictator of the uprising, Prince Trubetskoy, will not come to the square.
level.decembrists.title: Senate Square
level.decius.fact: In 340 BC, at Veseris, Consul Publius Decius Mus performed a devotio: a pontiff dictated to him the formula by which he consecrated himself and the enemy army to the chthonic gods, and he rode into the ranks of the Latins, where he perished. Livy writes that the Latins faltered as if they had seen a celestial sign. His son repeated the vow at Sentinum in 295 BC, and his grandson, according to tradition, at Asculum against Pyrrhus. Three generations of Decii became a formula for Rome: victory costs the life of the commander, and he pays first.
level.decius.goal: The consul sacrifices himself — and buys victory.
level.decius.hint: Equal forces yield a draw — strength comes only with a vow. The doomed one must win and perish in the ranks; he cannot leave the field alive.
level.decius.intro: The Latins stand against the Romans at Veseris — identical weapons, identical formation, neither is stronger. Both consuls dreamt the same dream: the army whose commander consecrates himself to the gods will be victorious.
level.decius.title: Decius' Vow
level.delenda.fact: Cato the Elder, returning from an embassy and seeing a flourishing Carthage, concluded every speech in the Senate with the words «Ceterum censeo Carthaginem esse delendam». Scipio Nasica countered him: Carthage must be preserved, otherwise Rome would lose its fear and rot from within. Cato prevailed. In 146 BC, Scipio Aemilianus took the city after six days of street fighting; the last defenders, led by Hasdrubal, barricaded themselves in the Temple of Eshmun. Hasdrubal himself came out pleading and was pardoned, while his wife cursed him and threw herself into the fire with their children. Polybius wrote that Scipio, watching the fire, wept and quoted Homer — about how one day Troy, and Rome, would also fall. No one, contrary to popular legend, sowed salt into the furrows.
level.delenda.goal: A phrase, repeated in the Curia, wipes a city from the earth
level.delenda.hint: War will be demanded by him who has seen the rival's wealth firsthand. He who will later march to the walls himself must vote with him – do not let a peacemaker into the curia.
level.delenda.intro: Carthage is defeated, stripped of its fleet, and pays tribute — yet is rich again. In the Senate, they argue what to do about this, while one old man ends every speech, no matter the topic, with the same phrase.
level.delenda.title: Carthage Must Be Destroyed
level.deulino.fact: Prince Władysław, elected tsar of Moscow in 1610, marched on the capital for his throne in 1617. On the night of 1 October 1618 Poles and Zaporozhian Cossacks under Hetman Sahaidachny stormed the Arbat and Tver gates and were beaten off. On 1 December 1618, in the village of Deulino by the Trinity–Sergius monastery, a truce was signed for fourteen and a half years: Russia gave up Smolensk, Chernigov and Novgorod-Seversky, and Władysław never renounced the title of tsar. The real gain was the exchange of prisoners: on 1 June 1619, on the river Polyanovka, Filaret came home from eight years of captivity — in the world Fyodor Nikitich Romanov, father of Tsar Mikhail. On 24 June 1619 he was made patriarch and given the title of Great Sovereign: until his death in 1633 he effectively ruled the country, and charters were issued in both their names. Smolensk was recovered only in 1654, under Mikhail's son Alexei Mikhailovich.
level.deulino.goal: The night assault is beaten off, the truce is bought with cities — and out of captivity returns the father who will become a second sovereign
level.deulino.hint: First the gates: the strong prince batters himself against the walls and loses his strength. With the repulsed man a truce is struck — at the price of cities. The truce opens the exchange of prisoners. The man who returns is made patriarch. The treasury of the Zemsky Sobor is not needed here: a bought prince will sign away nothing.
level.deulino.intro: Prince Władysław had been elected to the throne of Moscow back in 1610, and in 1617 he came for his crown in person. The young Tsar Mikhail has nothing to pay his army with and nothing to fight with. But his father has been sitting in Polish captivity for eight years.
level.deulino.source: 'The New Chronicler'; the Truce of Deulino, 1618 (text of the treaty)
level.deulino.title: Deulino
level.diane.fact: Diane de Poitiers was twenty years older than Henry II; in 1547 he gave her Chenonceau, and his monogram was interlaced with her initial so that it read 'HD'. On 30 June 1559, at a tournament in the Rue Saint-Antoine held for the peace of Cateau-Cambrésis and the weddings of the king's daughter and sister, the lance of Gabriel de Montgomery, captain of the Scots Guard, splintered, and the fragment went in under the king's visor above his right eye. For ten days Ambroise Paré and Andreas Vesalius treated him, opening the heads of executed criminals for study; on 10 July Henry died. Catherine de' Medici demanded the crown jewels back and traded Chenonceau for Chaumont; Diane withdrew to her own château of Anet, where she died in 1566. As early as 1555 the astrologer Nostradamus had printed a quatrain about a 'young lion' who would overcome the old one 'on the field of battle in single combat' and deal him 'two wounds in one' — in France it was read after the event as a prophecy.
level.diane.goal: The king dies at the tournament in her colors — and the widow's very first act is to take the château from the favorite
level.diane.hint: First the deed of gift: the château and the monogram — the king belongs to her. The lover rides out into the lists, and the queen watches it happen — and is left a widow. The widow takes the château from the favorite. The château of Anet is a trap: once she has withdrawn there, she can no longer be driven out.
level.diane.intro: The king is forty, his favourite is nearing sixty, and for twenty years the whole court has worn her colours — black and white. The Florentine queen keeps silent, bears children and waits. In the summer of 1559 Paris celebrates a peace and two weddings — and the king rides into the lists to break one more lance.
level.diane.source: Brantôme, 'Lives of Gallant Ladies'; I. Cloulas, 'Catherine de Medici'
level.diane.title: Black and White
level.diocletian.fact: Diocletian divided the empire: the East for himself, the West for Maximian, and in 293, he added two Caesars to the two Augusti — Galerius and Constantius Chlorus. Four ruled four parts, and civil wars ceased for twenty years. In 305, he did what no Roman emperor had ever done: he voluntarily abdicated and retired to grow vegetables in Salona. When he was called to return to power, he reportedly replied: 'If you could see the cabbages I have grown, you would not ask me to return.'
level.diocletian.goal: Power is divided among four, and the elder departs alive.
level.diocletian.hint: First, an equal co-ruler, then two juniors — only then can you depart yourself. The temptation to keep everything is understandable, but it was precisely this temptation that caused the empire to die for half a century.
level.diocletian.intro: Over fifty years, two dozen emperors came and went, and almost every one was killed by his own. There are four borders, but only one emperor — and he cannot physically be everywhere.
level.diocletian.source: Lactantius, 'On the Deaths of the Persecutors'; Aurelius Victor
level.diocletian.title: The Four
level.discord.fact: In 34 BC, Antony held a ceremony in Alexandria where he distributed the eastern provinces to Cleopatra and her children, and declared Caesarion to be Caesar's son — thus a rival to the heir. In 32 BC, Octavian forcibly seized Antony's will from the Temple of Vesta and read it in the Senate: it contained both the recognition of Caesarion and a request to be buried in Alexandria next to the queen. Rome declared war — formally on Cleopatra, so as not to call it a civil war.
level.discord.goal: Rome declares its own triumvir an enemy
level.discord.hint: Rome will forgive a romance, but not the distribution of Roman lands to foreign children. And for this to become a matter of state, a document announced in the Senate is needed — his own will, obtained by a rival.
level.discord.intro: Antony rules the East and lives in Alexandria. In Rome, his rival heir awaits an opportunity — and the opportunity presents itself.
level.discord.title: The Rift
level.disgrace.fact: Fearing Belisarius's excessive fame and popularity, Justinian repeatedly recalled him, stripped him of his troops, and held him in disfavor. Legend even depicted the great general as a blind beggar — a symbol of the ingratitude of power.
level.disgrace.goal: The jealous emperor sidelines a too-glorious hero
level.disgrace.hint: Let Narses first slander the hero with an accusation — and only then will a suspicious Justinian strip the disgraced Belisarius of his honors. Mundus is not so renowned as to be feared.
level.disgrace.intro: Belisarius's glory eclipses the throne. His rival, Narses, is ready to whisper the right words to the emperor.
level.disgrace.title: The Disgrace of Belisarius
level.downfall.fact: Deprived of his father, the Pope, Cesare Borgia was arrested by Julius II, lost all his possessions, and fled to Spain, where he died in a minor skirmish in 1507. Thus, the dominion admired by Machiavelli collapsed overnight.
level.downfall.goal: Cesare, having lost his patron, is overthrown
level.downfall.hint: Let Julius first seize the duke who has lost his father — and only the captive will be stripped of all lands and power. The uncaptured cannot be deposed.
level.downfall.intro: The Warrior Pope Julius II hates the Borgia. With his father's death, Cesare lost his protector — and the hour of reckoning has come.
level.downfall.title: Cesare's Downfall
level.drake_knight.fact: In 1580, Drake returned from his circumnavigation with plunder twice the annual income of the English treasury; the Queen's share repaid all her foreign debts. Philip II demanded the pirate's execution — but in April 1581, Elizabeth boarded the 'Golden Hind' in Deptford and knighted Drake, handing the sword, as a jest, to the French ambassador: let France share the blame with her. In 1587, Drake entered Cadiz harbor and burned three dozen ships preparing for the Armada — 'singeing the King of Spain's beard.' The Armada sailed a year later.
level.drake_knight.goal: The pirate, whose execution Spain demands, is knighted by the Queen on his own deck.
level.drake_knight.hint: First, let him defeat the Spanish at Cadiz. An influential ally can knight him — on his own ship. The Queen does not yield to the Spaniard demanding his head — Drake will not go to the Tower.
level.drake_knight.intro: Francis Drake plunders Spanish ships and ports, calling it a war England has not declared. Philip demands the pirate be handed over and the gold returned. The Queen has received her share of the plunder — and must decide Drake's fate.
level.drake_knight.title: Deck of the 'Golden Hind'
level.dudley_courtship.fact: Elizabeth never married — neither Robert Dudley, whom she loved all her life, nor any of the dozen and a half princes who sought her hand. Dudley was hindered by the death of his wife Amy Robsart, found in 1560 with a broken neck at the bottom of a staircase — a marriage after this would have looked like an admission of murder. She refused Philip of Spain in 1559. To Parliament, she replied that she was already married — to England, and showed her coronation ring. The nickname 'Virgin Queen' became policy: an unmarried queen is subservient to no one and can promise any marriage indefinitely.
level.dudley_courtship.goal: The Queen loves one, refuses another — and marries no one.
level.dudley_courtship.hint: Love at Kenilworth — yes; a favorite as an ally — yes; marriage — no, neither with him nor with the Spaniard: the Queen refuses Philip herself.
level.dudley_courtship.intro: Robert Dudley — the Queen's childhood friend, her Master of the Horse, and, as the whole court whispers, her lover. King Philip of Spain, widower of her sister, sends suitors. The Council demands that the Queen finally marry someone.
level.dudley_courtship.source: W. Camden, 'Annals'; letters of the Spanish ambassador de Quadra
level.dudley_courtship.title: Married to England
level.duguesclin.fact: Charles V made Bertrand du Guesclin Constable of France in October 1370, although he was a minor Breton nobleman who had twice been taken prisoner. The strategy was chosen deliberately: accept no pitched battles, hold garrisons in fortified towns, drive off the cattle and burn the stores ahead of the English chevauchées, and then take the strongholds one at a time. John of Gaunt's chevauchée of 1373 went from Calais to Bordeaux and lost more than half its men and almost all its horses without meeting a single battle. By 1375 the English held only Calais, Bordeaux, Bayonne and a few ports in France. Du Guesclin died at the siege of Châteauneuf-de-Randon on 13 July 1380; the king ordered him buried at Saint-Denis at his own feet — an honour granted to no one who was not of royal blood. Charles V himself died two months later.
level.duguesclin.goal: The Constable starves the chevauchée and takes the fortresses one at a time — until four ports are all that is left of English France
level.duguesclin.hint: First the constable's sword: the king, who is his ally, gives him authority and an army. Then the scorched fields — and the enemy's knightly host goes hungry. Only when they are worn down are the fortresses taken one after another. The open field near Calais is a trap: in a pitched battle they cannot be beaten.
level.duguesclin.intro: After Poitiers France gave the English a third of the kingdom and three million écus in ransom. The new king is weak in body, does not take the saddle and does not lead armies. But he knows what must not be done: one must not go out into the open field against English archers. He gives the constable's sword to a Breton whom the world of chivalry takes for a boor.
level.duguesclin.source: J. Froissart, 'Chronicles'; Cuvelier, 'The Song of Bertrand du Guesclin'
level.duguesclin.title: The Constable Who Gave No Battle
level.egypt.fact: On July 21, 1798, at the Pyramids, Bonaparte, in a square formation, defeated Murad Bey's Mamluks — 'Soldiers, forty centuries look down upon you from the height of these pyramids.' Ten days later, Nelson destroyed the French fleet in Aboukir Bay: the army was cut off. A year later, in August 1799, Napoleon secretly sailed for France, leaving the army to Kléber (who was soon assassinated in Cairo) — and three months later, he staged the Coup of 18 Brumaire. The expedition gave Europe Egyptology: the Rosetta Stone, found by a French captain, was taken by the British upon capitulation and is held in the British Museum.
level.egypt.goal: The General wins at the Pyramids, loses the fleet — and abandons the army to become First Consul
level.egypt.hint: At the Pyramids, strong infantry defeats cavalry. But Nelson burns the fleet in the roadstead — the army is trapped. Then the general leaves alone, abandoning his troops: this is the path to power. The Rosetta Stone will be found without him.
level.egypt.intro: The Directory is glad to send the overly popular general far away — to Egypt, to cut off the English route to India. Against him are Murad Bey's Mamluks, the best cavalry of the East. And Nelson follows him at sea.
level.egypt.title: Forty Centuries Look Down Upon You
level.elba.fact: On February 26, 1815, Napoleon escaped from Elba with a thousand men. At Laffrey, near Grenoble, he alone approached the battalion sent to arrest him: 'Soldiers, if there is one among you who wishes to kill his Emperor, here I am'; the battalion cried 'Vive l'Empereur!'. Ney, who had promised Louis XVIII an iron cage, defected to him with his troops. On March 20, twenty days after landing, Napoleon entered the Tuileries, from which the king had fled the previous night. Newspapers wrote: 'The Monster has escaped… The Usurper is in Grenoble… Bonaparte in Lyon… The Emperor has arrived in his loyal Paris.' Ahead lay the Hundred Days and Waterloo.
level.elba.goal: The Emperor returns with a thousand soldiers — and takes Paris without a shot in three weeks
level.elba.hint: First, escape from the island — departure. At Grenoble, he offers his chest to the muskets — and they love him. The Marshal sent for him embraces him — the army is with the Emperor. And the King flees the Tuileries.
level.elba.intro: Exiled to Elba, the Emperor rules an island of twenty thousand inhabitants and reads newspapers. The Bourbons in Paris have tired everyone in ten months. Marshal Ney promises the king to bring him back 'in an iron cage'.
level.elba.source: Memorial of Saint Helena; A. Houssaye, '1815'
level.elba.title: The Flight of the Eagle
level.elizabeth.fact: Elizabeth I (1558–1603) was crowned and, through the "Elizabethan Religious Settlement," reconciled Protestants and Catholics. She rejected suitors — including Philip II and her favorite Robert Dudley — throughout her life, remaining the "Virgin Queen": an unmarried monarch is her own mistress.
level.elizabeth.goal: The Queen is crowned, her favorite by her side — and she does not marry Spain.
level.elizabeth.hint: Coronation grants authority. The court favorite becomes an ally, but there must be no wedding with the Spaniard.
level.elizabeth.intro: Elizabeth I is crowned Queen. Suitors besiege her: both Philip of Spain and her beloved Robert Dudley — but the crown is dearer.
level.elizabeth.title: The Virgin Queen
level.elizabeth_coup.fact: On the night of November 25 (December 6), 1741, Elizabeth Petrovna arrived at the barracks of the Preobrazhensky Regiment: 'Lads! You know whose daughter I am, follow me!' — and with three hundred grenadiers, she entered the Winter Palace; Regent Anna Leopoldovna and her husband were taken in bed, and the one-year-old Emperor Ivan VI was carried out in arms. Before the coup, Elizabeth made a vow: if she ascended the throne, she would not sign a single death sentence; during twenty years of her reign, no one was executed in Russia — Lestocq and the Lopukhins, sentenced to death, were pardoned on the scaffold. Ivan VI spent twenty-three years in solitary confinement and was killed by guards during an attempted rescue already under Catherine II. The grenadier conspirators became the 'Leib-Company' and received nobility.
level.elizabeth_coup.goal: 'Lads, you know whose daughter I am?' — three hundred grenadiers make her empress in one night, and she vows to execute no one
level.elizabeth_coup.hint: First, the barracks: the Tsarevna raises the grenadiers — strength and sway. At night, the regent and the infant are taken in the palace — overthrown, the Tsarevna is crowned. The crowned one vows to execute no one. Do not go to talk to the regent — the grenadiers will not rally behind a yielding Tsarevna.
level.elizabeth_coup.intro: On the throne is the infant Ivan VI, his mother Anna Leopoldovna rules, everything at court is German. Peter's daughter Elizabeth, cheerful and in debt, is loved by the guard. On the night of November 25, 1741, she puts on a cuirass over her dress and rides to the barracks of the Preobrazhensky Regiment.
level.elizabeth_coup.source: E. Anisimov, 'Elizabeth Petrovna'; dispatches of Marquis de La Chétardie
level.elizabeth_coup.title: Peter's Daughter
level.elizabeth_tower.fact: In March 1554, after Wyatt's Rebellion against the Spanish marriage, twenty-year-old Elizabeth was brought to the Tower through Traitors' Gate; according to legend, she sat on the wet steps and refused to enter. Her involvement could not be proven. Strangely, Philip of Spain intervened on her behalf: Elizabeth's death would make the Catholic Mary, Queen of Scots, fiancée of the French Dauphin, the heir — and France was an enemy of Spain. Two months later, Elizabeth was moved to house arrest in Woodstock. Four years later, she became queen — and Philip himself proposed to her.
level.elizabeth_tower.goal: The condemned sister is saved not by her sister's mercy, but by her husband's calculation.
level.elizabeth_tower.hint: The accusation will be made — she is on trial. She will not save herself, but an influential Spaniard: he will persuade the Queen. She cannot be executed in the Tower.
level.elizabeth_tower.intro: After Wyatt's Rebellion, Queen Mary imprisoned her half-sister Elizabeth in the Tower: there is no evidence, but the councilors demand her head. The Queen's husband, Philip, looks further — if Elizabeth dies, the throne will pass to Mary, Queen of Scots, and France.
level.elizabeth_tower.source: J. Foxe, 'Book of Martyrs'; D. Starkey, 'Elizabeth: Apprenticeship'
level.elizabeth_tower.title: Sister in the Tower
level.emancipation.fact: On March 30, 1856, Alexander II told the leaders of the Moscow nobility: 'It is better to abolish serfdom from above than to wait for the time when it begins to abolish itself from below'. The project was drafted by the Editorial Commissions under the leadership of Nikolai Milyutin — 'the Red', as the landowners called him; the nobility ensured that the peasants received land for redemption and remained 'temporarily obligated'. The Manifesto was signed on February 19 (March 3), 1861, on the sixth anniversary of his ascension, and proclaimed in churches on Forgiveness Sunday; about twenty-three million people gained freedom. Milyutin was immediately dismissed. For his reforms, the emperor was dubbed the Liberator — and was killed by those for whom freedom seemed insufficient.
level.emancipation.goal: The Emperor declares his will to the nobles, officials write the law — and twenty-three million people are no longer property
level.emancipation.hint: First, 'better from above' — the Emperor decided, with authority. Milyutin writes the draft — power. The Emperor, with authority, responds to the landowners — their protest is rejected. The Emperor, with the strong Milyutin, signs the manifesto. Do not accept gifts from landowners — a bought man will not sign.
level.emancipation.intro: After Crimea, it's clear: a country with serfs cannot wage war with Europe. The new emperor tells the Moscow nobility that it's better to abolish serfdom from above than to wait for it to be abolished from below. The landowners are against it, but all the work is done by the official Milyutin.
level.emancipation.source: L. Zakharova, 'Autocracy and the Abolition of Serfdom'; Manifesto of February 19, 1861
level.emancipation.title: Emancipation
level.embassy.fact: The Grand Embassy left Moscow in March 1697: some 250 people, the great ambassadors Lefort, Golovin and Voznitsyn, and on the list of volunteers 'Sergeant Pyotr Mikhailov'. In August the tsar worked for a week as a carpenter at a private yard in Zaandam, but was recognized by the crowd and moved to Amsterdam, where Burgomaster Nicolaas Witsen arranged for a new frigate, the Peter and Paul, to be laid down for the guests at the East India Company yard. For four months he worked on the stocks on equal terms with the carpenters and received a written certificate from the master shipwright Gerrit Claes Pool. Then came England and the yards of Deptford, where Peter studied the theory of ship draughting, which the Dutch did not know. The embassy hired some seven hundred foreigners into Russian service and bought mountains of weapons. The journey home had to be hurried: in July 1698 word came from Moscow of the Streltsy revolt.
level.embassy.goal: The tsar travels to Europe as an apprentice — and brings home not presents but a shipwright's certificate
level.embassy.hint: First the list of volunteers: the tsar signs on as Pyotr Mikhailov, his orderly with him. The burgomaster lays down a frigate for the man hidden under another's name. Four months on the stocks earn the certificate. The tsar's regalia are a trap: a man who has been recognized will not be let near an axe.
level.embassy.intro: In March 1697 the Grand Embassy set out from Moscow: two hundred and fifty people, three great ambassadors, and among the volunteers a sergeant of the Preobrazhensky Regiment more than two metres tall. The sergeant's name was Pyotr Mikhailov. Everyone knew his real name, but one was expected not to recognize him.
level.embassy.source: The 'Journal' of the Grand Embassy; N. Pavlenko, 'Peter the First'
level.embassy.title: Pyotr Mikhailov
level.emperor.fact: On October 22, 1721, after the victory in the Great Northern War, the Senate bestowed upon Peter I the title 'Emperor of All Russia, Father of the Fatherland, the Great'. The Russian Tsardom became the Russian Empire.
level.emperor.goal: The Senate proclaims the victor over the Swedes as Emperor
level.emperor.hint: First, victory over Charles; then, the imperial title in the Senate.
level.emperor.title: Emperor of All Russia
level.empress.fact: At the same ceremony on December 2, 1804, Napoleon crowned his wife, Joséphine de Beauharnais, Empress, placing the crown upon her head himself. Their marriage, however, was annulled in 1809 due to the lack of an heir.
level.empress.hint: Let Napoleon first seize the crown and crown himself — and only then shall the crowned emperor place the diadem on Josephine. The order cannot be broken.
level.empress.intro: Notre Dame, 1804. The Pope is ready to bestow the crown — but Napoleon has conceived an unprecedented audacity.
level.empress.title: Empress Joséphine
level.ermak.fact: On September 1, 1582, Yermak left the Stroganov lands on riverboats beyond the Urals; on October 26, at Chuvash Cape on the Irtysh, his arquebuses dispersed Kuchum's army, and the Cossacks occupied the capital of the Khanate, Qashliq. The Ataman sent sables to Moscow and news of the 'Siberian Tsardom' — Ivan the Terrible forgave the Cossacks their past, sent reinforcements, and, according to legend, two armors. On the night of August 6, 1585, Kuchum attacked the sleeping camp on the Irtysh; Yermak, according to legend, jumped towards a riverboat and drowned under the weight of the Tsar's chainmail. His body, found by the Tatars, was raised onto a platform and shot at for a week. A year later, the Russians returned and founded Tyumen, and a hundred years later — reached the Pacific Ocean.
level.ermak.goal: The Ataman takes the Khan's capital, sends Siberia to the Tsar — and drowns in the armor gifted by the Tsar
level.ermak.hint: First, the riverboats — the Ataman is strong. Battle at Chuvash Cape: the strong Ataman defeats the Khan. The victor sends sables to the Tsar — forgiven and receives armor. And then the night on the Irtysh: Kuchum drowns the sleeping man in armor. To retreat to the Volga — that's not the point.
level.ermak.intro: Volga brigand Yermak, with a detachment of eight hundred Cossacks, is hired by the Stroganov merchants to guard their Ural towns. Instead of guarding, he goes beyond the Stone (Urals) — into Kuchum's Siberian Khanate. The Tsar has long had a noose ready for him.
level.ermak.source: Stroganov and Remezov Chronicles; R. Skrynnikov, 'Yermak'
level.ermak.title: Yermak
level.essex.fact: Robert Devereux, Earl of Essex, in 1599, at the head of the largest army sent to Ireland, achieved nothing against Hugh O'Neill, concluded a truce without permission, and returned without authorization, bursting into Elizabeth's chambers. Deprived of income and favor, in February 1601, he attempted to raise London — two hundred men followed him, but none of the townspeople. Convicted of treason, he was beheaded in the Tower courtyard on February 25, 1601, at the age of thirty-four. The legend of the ring, which the queen had once given him as a pledge of forgiveness and which never reached her, appeared later. Elizabeth outlived him by two years and, it is said, never recovered.
level.essex.goal: The Queen's favorite loses Ireland, raises London — and lays his head on the block.
level.essex.hint: In Ireland, powerful Tyrone defeats him. A rebellion in the streets — and the queen condemns her favorite with a speech; she yields neither to the ring nor to pleas. She herself executes the condemned.
level.essex.intro: The Earl of Essex — favorite of the aging queen, a handsome man and hero of Cadiz. She sent him to quell Ireland — he returned without victory and without permission, bursting into her bedroom when she was without her wig.
level.essex.title: The Last Favorite
level.excommunicate.fact: The Florentine monk Girolamo Savonarola fiercely denounced the corruption of the Borgias and the entire Church, organizing 'bonfires of the vanities.' In 1497, Alexander VI excommunicated him.
level.excommunicate.goal: The Pope excommunicates the audacious preacher
level.excommunicate.hint: Let Savonarola first boldly denounce the Pope from the pulpit — and only the rebel will the Pope anathematize. Until the monk issues a challenge, there is no anathema.
level.excommunicate.intro: The monk Savonarola burns 'bonfires of the vanities' and from the pulpit denounces the corrupt Pope. Rome is divided.
level.excommunicate.title: Excommunication
level.execution.fact: On January 10, 1775, Yemelyan Pugachev was executed in Bolotnaya Square in Moscow. The rebellion was drowned in blood; Catherine II renamed the Yaik River to the Ural to erase the memory of the revolt.
level.execution.goal: The captured impostor is executed in Bolotnaya Square
level.execution.hint: First — capture by Suvorov, then — the block by the sovereign's will.
level.execution.intro: The Empress reigns; the captured impostor awaits judgment.
level.execution.title: The Execution of Pugachev
level.fabius.fact: After Lake Trasimene (217 BC), Dictator Quintus Fabius Maximus followed Hannibal along mountain ridges, avoiding battle and burning supplies. Rome nicknamed him Cunctator, «The Delayer», — and it was a mockery. The Master of Horse, Minucius, obtained equal powers with him, immediately engaged in open battle, and was surrounded; Fabius led him out of the encirclement, and Minucius publicly called him father. Once, Hannibal escaped a trap by sending a herd of oxen with burning faggots on their horns at night. A year later, Rome abandoned «delaying tactics» — and suffered Cannae.
level.fabius.goal: Hannibal is exhausted by hunger, and the hothead acknowledges the delayer's wisdom
level.fabius.hint: Hannibal is not defeated in battle – he is worn down. A hothead will learn this only through his own skin, and only he who has not been defeated can pull him out.
level.fabius.intro: Hannibal is in Italy; he has already destroyed two Roman armies. Fabius Maximus, appointed dictator, refuses battle — for this, he is called the Delayer in Rome, while the master of horse yearns to show how to fight.
level.fabius.title: The Delayer
level.falerii.fact: In 394 BC, during the siege of Falerii, a local teacher brought boys from noble families to Camillus, offering them as hostages. Camillus ordered the traitor stripped, gave the children rods, and had him driven back into the city. The Falisci, seeing this, sent word to the Senate: 'We prefer to live under Roman rule than under our own laws — so just is your general.' Livy recounts the episode as a lesson in Roman fides — faithfulness to one's word even with an enemy. It is worth remembering that a few years earlier, the same Camillus had plundered Veii and sold its inhabitants into slavery.
level.falerii.goal: A city surrenders to an enemy who refused to take it by treachery
level.falerii.hint: First, attrition — otherwise, the city has no reason to surrender. The traitor with the children must be sent home, not accepted: only an honorable general has the authority for the city to open its gates itself.
level.falerii.intro: Camillus besieges Falerii, and the siege drags on. The city teacher, whose class includes the sons of all the best families, takes the children 'for a walk' — directly into the Roman camp.
level.falerii.source: Livy, 'The History of Rome', V, 27; Plutarch, 'Camillus', 10
level.falerii.title: The Teacher of Falerii
level.fall_1453.fact: On April 6, 1453, Mehmed II besieged Constantinople; Urban's bombard, eight meters long, fired half-ton cannonballs and took three hours to load. On the night of April 22, the Ottomans dragged seventy ships over greased logs across the hill of Galata into the Golden Horn, bypassing the chain. At dawn on May 29, after a night assault, the Genoese Giovanni Giustiniani, who commanded the defense, was wounded — he ordered himself to be carried to a ship, and his men followed him; at the same time, the Kerkoporta gate was opened. Emperor Constantine XI, according to legend, tore off his insignia and rushed into battle; his body was not identified. Mehmed entered Hagia Sophia and ordered it converted into a mosque. He was twenty-one years old. Historians often mark this day as the end of the Middle Ages.
level.fall_1453.goal: The Sultan batters the walls with cannons, drags his fleet overland, the defense commander is wounded — and the last emperor tears off his purple and rushes into battle.
level.fall_1453.hint: First, the bombard — the Sultan is powerful. The powerful Sultan drags ships overland — the Emperor is besieged. Wounded Giustiniani leaves — the Emperor is no longer powerful. Then May 29: the powerful Sultan defeats the besieged and weakened Emperor — the last Emperor. To sail to Morea — he refused.
level.fall_1453.intro: Only one city remained of the empire, with seven thousand defenders; Sultan Mehmed had eighty thousand men and the cannon of the Hungarian Urban, firing half-ton cannonballs. The Genoese Giustiniani holds the defense. The Emperor is offered to flee — he stays.
level.fall_1453.source: George Sphrantzes, «Chronicle»; S. Runciman, «The Fall of Constantinople 1453»
level.fall_1453.title: May 29, 1453
level.false_dmitry.fact: In October 1604, False Dmitry crossed the Dnieper with four thousand men; cities surrendered to him without a fight, but on January 21, 1605, at Dobrynichi, the Tsar's voivodes utterly defeated him — he fled to Putivl and intended to retreat to Poland. He was saved by the death of Boris Godunov: on April 13, the Tsar rose from the table, blood gushed from his nose and ears, and two hours later he died. The army near Kromy defected to the impostor, the sixteen-year-old Tsar Fyodor Godunov and his mother were strangled, and on June 20, 'Dmitry' entered Moscow; the Tsarevich's mother, Nun Marfa, publicly recognized him as her son. He reigned for eleven months.
level.false_dmitry.goal: The impostor raises the banner — and the Tsar suddenly dies, and the entire army defects to 'Dmitry'.
level.false_dmitry.hint: First, the Tsarevich's banner — people gather under it. Do not rush into battle: a strong Tsar will defeat you. Await Boris's sudden death — the army will defect to the impostor, and he will gain the right to the crown. Then the coronation.
level.false_dmitry.intro: Fugitive monk Grigory Otrepyev declares in Poland that he is Tsarevich Dmitry, miraculously saved. With a handful of Poles and Cossacks, he marches on Moscow. Godunov is ten times stronger, but the country has been starving for three years, and everyone awaits a 'true Tsar'.
level.false_dmitry.source: R. Skrynnikov, 'Impostors in Russia in the Early 17th Century'
level.false_dmitry.title: The Impostor
level.february.fact: On February 23 (March 8), 1917, women in Petrograd took to the streets shouting 'Bread!'; four days later, the Volynsky, Litovsky, and Preobrazhensky regiments joined the crowd. Rodzianko telegraphed the Tsar at Stavka: 'The situation is serious. Anarchy in the capital'; Nicholas said: 'That fat Rodzianko has written me nonsense again.' The Tsar's train was not allowed into Tsarskoye Selo; he was stranded in Pskov; on March 2 (15), General Ruzsky and Guchkov and Shulgin, sent by the Duma, presented him with telegrams from the front commanders — all but one advised him to abdicate. Nicholas signed the abdication with a pencil — first for himself, then, 'not wishing to part with his son,' also for Alexei — in favor of his brother Mikhail, who also refused the next day. That same evening in his diary: 'Around me is treason, and cowardice, and deceit.'
level.february.goal: The capital revolts, the Duma demands, generals advise — and in the Tsar's carriage near Pskov, three hundred years of the dynasty end with a pencil signature
level.february.hint: First, bread riots: Rodzianko telegraphs the Tsar — the capital is hungry, the Duma is against the Tsar and has authority. The Duma, with authority, denounces the Tsar — he is condemned. In Pskov, a general presents the condemned Tsar with the abdication. Bribing the Duma and shooting the crowd — neither move will save him.
level.february.intro: Third year of war, bread queues in Petrograd. Women take to the streets, followed by workers, then soldiers of reserve regiments shoot officers. The Tsar is at Stavka, and the Chairman of the Duma, Rodzianko, sends him telegrams, which he calls 'nonsense.'
level.february.source: 'Diaries of Emperor Nicholas II'; V. Shulgin, 'Days'; G. Katkov, 'The February Revolution'
level.february.title: Abdication
level.fili.fact: On September 1 (13), 1812, in peasant Frolov's hut in Fili, Kutuzov listened to the generals and cut short the debate: 'With the loss of Moscow, Russia is not yet lost. I order a retreat.' The next day, the army marched through Moscow, and Napoleon entered the city after them; that same night, fires began, and three-quarters of the houses burned down in six days. For five weeks, Napoleon awaited Alexander's reply — 'I will not conclude peace as long as a single armed enemy remains in my realm' — and on October 7 (19), he left Moscow. On October 12 (24), at Maloyaroslavets, the town changed hands eight times; Kutuzov blocked the path south, and the Grande Armée had to retreat along the devastated Smolensk road, in freezing weather, towards the Berezina. The hut in Fili burned down in 1868 and was rebuilt — it is now a museum.
level.fili.goal: A draw at Borodino, Moscow is surrendered and burns — and the conqueror's starving army is defeated on its way home.
level.fili.hint: Borodino — a draw between two forces, both at war. Then the council at Fili: Kutuzov surrenders Moscow, it burns — Napoleon is hungry and no longer strong. Maloyaroslavets: a strong Kutuzov defeats him. Do not answer Napoleon's letter — a yielding Napoleon is not defeated.
level.fili.intro: The Grande Armée reached Borodino. Kutuzov gave battle — the bloodiest in history — and did not lose it. Now, in a peasant's hut in Fili, the generals decide: another battle beneath the walls of Moscow or surrender the capital without a fight. The Tsar does not answer Napoleon's letters.
level.fili.source: 'Memoirs' of A. Yermolov; E. Tarle, 'Napoleon's Invasion of Russia'
level.fili.title: Council at Fili
level.flight.fact: When Justinian was preparing to flee, Theodora stopped the council with the words: «Imperial purple makes the best shroud», preferring death on the throne to flight. Her resolve saved the throne.
level.flight.goal: Theodora restrains the emperor ready to flee
level.flight.hint: Who will stay the wavering emperor? Not the advisors who urge flight — only Theodora with the words, 'Purple makes the noblest shroud.'
level.flight.intro: The rebellion rages, the ship stands ready. The council — Narses the eunuch, Belisarius the general — whispers to flee. Only one voice commands them to stay.
level.flight.title: Purple Makes the Best Shroud
level.fontainebleau.fact: From 10 to 14 February 1814, in the Six Days' Campaign, Napoleon beat the allies at Champaubert, Montmirail, Château-Thierry and Vauchamps, but on 31 March the allied armies entered Paris. On 4 April at Fontainebleau the marshals Ney, Lefebvre, Oudinot and Moncey refused to lead the army against the capital: to the words 'the army will follow me' Ney replied that the army would follow its own commanders. That same day Napoleon abdicated in favour of his son, and on 6 April signed an unconditional abdication; the terms were discussed in Paris with Alexander I by his envoy Caulaincourt. On the night of 13 April he took the poison he had carried with him since the Russian campaign — the mixture had lost its strength, and he vomited it up. By the Treaty of Fontainebleau of 11 April he was left the title of emperor, the island of Elba and two million francs of annuity. On 20 April, in the Courtyard of the White Horse, he took leave of the Old Guard, embraced General Petit and kissed the standard; ever since, the courtyard has been called the Courtyard of Farewells.
level.fontainebleau.goal: After six days of victories the marshals refuse to march on Paris — and the emperor abdicates, to take his leave of the Guard
level.fontainebleau.hint: First the six days of victories: he is a force once more. And then a marshal tells him to his face that the army will not march — the force drains away and he is left alone. The abandoned man has nothing left but to sign an unconditional abdication before the victor. The man who has abdicated goes out into the courtyard to his Guard. The vial in the amulet is a trap: that night the poison did not work.
level.fontainebleau.intro: February 1814: with forty-five thousand raw recruits he beats the allies four times in six days — and on the map it looks like a miracle. But the allies go round him and enter Paris. At Fontainebleau he spreads out the maps and announces to his marshals that tomorrow they march to retake the capital.
level.fontainebleau.title: The Courtyard of the White Horse
level.fouquet.fact: On August 17, 1661, Fouquet hosted the King at Vaux-le-Vicomte: dinner on gold, a Molière premiere, fireworks over Le Nôtre's gardens. Three weeks later, d'Artagnan — yes, that one — arrested him in Nantes. The trial lasted three years; the judges sentenced him to exile, but Louis XIV did what no other king had done — he stiffened the sentence to life imprisonment, and Fouquet died in Pignerol in 1680. The King took Vaux's architect, gardener, and artist for himself — they built Versailles. Voltaire said: 'On August 17, at six in the evening, Fouquet was King of France; at two in the morning, he was nobody.'
level.fouquet.goal: The Minister dazzles the King with luxury — and receives life imprisonment instead of the block
level.fouquet.hint: The celebration makes the minister the King's enemy. The King condemns him in a speech — the trial is rigged. But instead of execution — a fortress forever: the King neither pardons nor executes, he forgets.
level.fouquet.intro: Superintendent of Finance Nicolas Fouquet built himself the Château de Vaux-le-Vicomte — more beautiful than anything the King possessed — and invited the twenty-two-year-old Louis XIV to a celebration: fountains, Molière, fireworks. The King watched in silence.
level.fouquet.source: Voltaire, 'The Age of Louis XIV'; letters of Madame de Sévigné
level.fouquet.title: The Feast at Vaux
level.four_emperors.fact: Between 68–69 AD, Rome saw four rulers. Galba refused to pay the Praetorians what was promised ('I recruit soldiers, I don't buy them'), and they cut him down in the Forum, proclaiming Otho, who paid. Otho was defeated by Vitellius's Rhine legions, and he took his own life; Vitellius was torn apart by the mob six months later. Vespasian, raised by the legions of Judea and Egypt, emerged victorious. Tacitus drew the main lesson of the year from this: the secret of power was revealed — an emperor could be made outside of Rome.
level.four_emperors.goal: The purple goes to him whom the legions of the provinces raise
level.four_emperors.hint: The Guard kills not for an idea, but for non-payment: deny them — and another will come to pay. Then the eastern legions will raise Vespasian against the one who bought the Guard. Vitellius will approach from the Rhine, but the purple will not be his.
level.four_emperors.intro: Nero is dead, the dynasty is no more. The governor of Hispania occupied the palace, but gave no money to the Guard — and the Guard was accustomed to a new princeps paying.
level.four_emperors.title: The Year of the Four Emperors
level.francis.fact: In 1206 Francesco, son of the cloth merchant Pietro Bernardone, stripped off all his clothes on the square of Assisi before Bishop Guido and gave them back to his father: "Until now I called you father; from now on I say: Our Father, who art in heaven." In 1209 he came to Rome with eleven companions to see Innocent III, the most powerful pope of the Middle Ages. The pope first drove the ragged men away but, so the story goes, dreamed of the Lateran basilica tilting and being held up on the shoulder of that same beggar — and approved a rule made of nothing but words of the Gospel. Seventeen years later the order numbered thousands of brothers; Francis was canonised two years after his death, and in 2013 a pope took his name for the first time.
level.francis.goal: The son strips naked to renounce his father's wealth — and the pope, after a dream, hands the beggar a rule for his order
level.francis.hint: The square first: son and father — he gives back everything, his clothes included. The pope dreams of the man who renounced all and blesses him. The blessed man receives his rule. Taking over the father's shop: a man who has been bought renounces nothing.
level.francis.intro: The son of the richest cloth merchant in Assisi caroused, went to war and sat in a prison cell — and on returning began giving his father's goods away to beggars. His father hauls him before the bishop's court: let him return every thread of it.
level.francis.source: Thomas of Celano, First Life; The Little Flowers of St Francis
level.francis.title: Brother Francis
level.fratricide.fact: In June 1497, Juan Borgia was murdered, his body cast into the Tiber. Rumor accused his brother Cesare, who eliminated a rival for their father's affection and power. The murder remained unsolved.
level.fratricide.goal: Cesare secretly murders his rival brother
level.fratricide.hint: Let the fraternal feast ignite Cesare's envy — and only consumed by it will he dispose of Juan in the Tiber. Without resentment, his hand will not rise.
level.fratricide.intro: His father made Juan Gonfalonier of the Church, bypassing the capable Cesare. The younger brother's envy grows.
level.fratricide.title: Body in the Tiber
level.frederick2.fact: Gregory IX excommunicated Frederick II in September 1227 for turning his fleet back because of an epidemic. The emperor sailed anyway, and in February 1229 concluded the Treaty of Jaffa with Sultan al-Kamil: Jerusalem, Bethlehem and Nazareth passed to the Christians for ten years, the al-Aqsa mosque stayed with the Muslims, and there was no fighting at all. On 18 March he entered the Church of the Holy Sepulchre, where no one dared crown him — and set the crown on his own head. The pope declared the crusade void and laid an interdict on Jerusalem; both sides considered Frederick a traitor to his own faith. He died excommunicated in 1250, and Dante placed him in the sixth circle of hell, among the heretics.
level.frederick2.goal: The excommunicated emperor takes Jerusalem by treaty, without a single battle — and crowns himself at the Holy Sepulchre
level.frederick2.hint: The excommunication first: a pope with standing condemns the emperor. Then Jaffa: emperor and sultan — Jerusalem handed over by treaty. An excommunicate holding Jerusalem has only one way left to be crowned: himself. No need to storm the city — it was taken with words.
level.frederick2.intro: Frederick II, the Wonder of the World: raised in Palermo among Arabs and Greeks, keeping a harem and a menagerie, corresponding with sultans about mathematics. For years he put off the crusade he had promised, and Pope Gregory IX excommunicated him. Excommunicated — and off he goes on crusade.
level.frederick2.source: E. Kantorowicz, Frederick II; the chronicle of Ibn Wasil
level.frederick2.title: The Excommunicate's Crusade
level.fronde.fact: The Fronde began in August 1648 with the arrest of the parliamentary councillor Broussel: overnight Paris was covered in barricades. On the night of 6 January 1649 the court slipped away to Saint-Germain-en-Laye, where the palace had no furniture and the ten-year-old Louis XIV slept on straw. On the night of 10 February 1651 Parisians came to the Palais-Royal to check that the king had not been spirited away again; he was put to bed, and the crowd filed past in silence — he lay with his eyes closed, not asleep. Condé spent that night under arrest at Le Havre and was freed three days later. In 1652 he fought the royal army in the Faubourg Saint-Antoine, and the Grande Mademoiselle ordered the guns of the Bastille to fire on her cousin's troops; beaten, Condé went to serve the king of Spain. On 21 October 1652 Louis returned to Paris. After Mazarin's death on 9 March 1661 he told his ministers that from now on he would rule himself, with no first minister — and spent his life building a court far from Paris, at Versailles.
level.fronde.goal: The boy who slept on straw and played at sleeping before the crowd comes back to Paris — and never trusts it again
level.fronde.hint: First the straw: the minister carries the king off by night, and the humiliation stays with him forever. The humiliated boy lies with his eyes shut while the frondeurs file past his bed — and after that he is another man. The hardened king comes back and does not forgive the insolent one. Mazarin's cabinet is a trap: a bought prince cannot be broken.
level.fronde.intro: The king is ten years old; the country is ruled by his mother and an Italian cardinal whom everyone hates: the parlement, the princes and the Paris street. In January 1649 the court flees the city by night. In the empty Saint-Germain there is no furniture: they lay straw for the boy-king.
level.fronde.source: Cardinal de Retz, 'Memoirs'; F. Bluche, 'Louis XIV'
level.fronde.title: Straw at Saint-Germain
level.gaius_gracchus.fact: In 121 BC, the Senate for the first time issued a senatus consultum ultimum — an 'ultimate decree' granting extraordinary powers to Consul Lucius Opimius. Gracchus' supporters were crushed on the Aventine; Gaius himself fled across the Tiber to the grove of Furina and there ordered his slave Philocrates to stab him, after which the slave killed himself. Opimius promised as much gold for Gracchus' head as it weighed; a certain Septimuleius brought it, having first removed the brain and filled it with lead — and received seventeen pounds. Three thousand supporters were executed without trial. This marked the end of the attempt to change Rome through laws.
level.gaius_gracchus.goal: The Senate declares the tribune an enemy — and pays for his head its weight in gold.
level.gaius_gracchus.hint: The consul, with extraordinary powers, condemns the tribune with a speech and defeats him on the Aventine. The tribune will not flee across the Tiber — he will order his slave to kill him. His head will be brought to the consul.
level.gaius_gracchus.intro: Ten years after his brother's death, Gaius Gracchus is tribune, and he has more laws than Tiberius did. For the first time in history, the Senate grants Consul Opimius the right to 'save the state' by any means.
level.gaius_gracchus.title: A Head's Weight in Gold
level.galileo.fact: «Dialogue Concerning the Two Chief World Systems» was published in 1632 with censorship approval; but the argument that Urban VIII personally requested to be included — that God could arrange the world in any way — Galileo put into the mouth of the character Simplicio, the «simpleton». The Pope felt ridiculed. In 1633, the seventy-year-old Galileo was summoned to Rome; on June 22, in the Church of Santa Maria sopra Minerva, he knelt and read his abjuration of the «opinion that the Sun is the center of the world and motionless». The words «Eppur si muove» first appeared in print a hundred years later. He spent the rest of his life under house arrest in Arcetri, went blind, and wrote «Discourses» there — the foundation of mechanics. The Church lifted the ban on his books in 1835 and admitted its error in 1992.
level.galileo.goal: The Pope's friend writes a book where the Pope is a simpleton; the Holy Office forces the seventy-year-old man to his knees.
level.galileo.hint: First, old friendship — allies. The friend writes «Dialogue» and implicates the Pope — the book is out, the Pope is now an enemy. The influential Pope judges the astronomer — condemned. The condemned abjures on his knees — house arrest. To flee to Venice — one who has left is not judged or brought to his knees.
level.galileo.intro: Galileo and Pope Urban VIII are old friends: Cardinal Barberini wrote odes in honor of the astronomer. The Pope permits a book on the two world systems to be written — «impartially». Galileo puts the Pope's arguments into the mouth of a simpleton named Simplicio.
level.galileo.source: «Il processo di Galileo Galilei» (process documents); J. Heilbron, «Galileo»
level.galileo.title: And yet it moves
level.garibaldi.fact: On the night of May 6, 1860, 1089 volunteers on two steamers sailed from Quarto near Genoa; on May 15, at Calatafimi, Garibaldi, in his red shirt, took the hill with bayonets against Bourbon troops — «here we make Italy or die». Palermo rebelled, and by September, he entered Naples by train, outrunning the army. On October 26, at Teano, he met Victor Emmanuel: «I salute the first King of Italy» — and, having handed over all his conquests, refused rewards and left for his island of Caprera with a bag of seeds and a box of pasta. On March 17, 1861, the Kingdom of Italy was proclaimed; Rome was taken in 1870, Venice in 1866. Garibaldi was invited to be a general by Lincoln and the Paris Commune; there is no city in Italy without a street named after him.
level.garibaldi.goal: A thousand Redshirts take half a kingdom — and the general gives everything to the king, leaving with a bag of seeds.
level.garibaldi.hint: First, the Thousand set sail — the Garibaldini are raised and hold sway. Calatafimi: the raised one defeats the Bourbon — a victor. The victor at Teano shakes hands with the king — King of Italy. You cannot march on Rome — the king is not your enemy.
