level.garibaldi.intro: Italy is a patchwork quilt: Piedmont of King Victor Emmanuel, Papal Rome, Austrian Venice, the Bourbon Kingdom of Naples. Garibaldi, with a thousand red-shirted volunteers, sails to Sicily — against an army of a hundred thousand.
level.garibaldi.source: G. Garibaldi, «Memoirs»; G. Trevelyan, «Garibaldi and the Thousand»
level.garibaldi.title: The Thousand
level.girondins.fact: On June 2, 1793, eighty thousand sans-culottes with cannons surrounded the Convention and would not release the deputies until they voted for the arrest of twenty-nine Girondins. Brissot and twenty of his comrades were guillotined on October 31 — all in thirty-eight minutes; on the night before their execution, they sang in prison, and one, Valazé, stabbed himself upon the reading of the verdict, and his body was taken to the execution alongside the living. Thus began the dictatorship of the Mountain — and the Terror, which eight months later would consume Danton, and a year later, Robespierre.
level.girondins.goal: Sans-culottes with cannons resolve the dispute in the Convention — and the eloquent are taken to the square
level.girondins.hint: Debating in the Convention is useless. Sans-culottes at the doors with cannons — the power of the Mountain. Then Robespierre's speech condemns Brissot, and the condemned is executed with gravity.
level.girondins.intro: In the Convention, there are two camps: Brissot's Girondins, moderate and eloquent, and Robespierre's Mountain, with the sans-culottes at their back. Debating with the Girondins is useless — there are more of them, and they speak better.
level.girondins.source: Lamartine, 'History of the Girondins'; records of the Revolutionary Tribunal
level.girondins.title: The Expulsion of the Girondins
level.giulia.fact: Giulia Farnese, the young mistress of Alexander VI, was sardonically dubbed 'Bride of Christ' by the Romans. Through her, her brother achieved a meteoric career and himself became Pope Paul III.
level.giulia.goal: A young beauty becomes the Pope's favorite
level.giulia.hint: Let Giulia first captivate the Pope during a rendezvous — and only enamored will he shower her with favors. Lucrezia is his daughter, not a mistress.
level.giulia.intro: Young Giulia Farnese captivated the old Pope. The key to papal favors lies through the pontiff's heart.
level.giulia.title: Bride of Christ
level.globe.fact: On December 28, 1598, the Lord Chamberlain's Men, with carpenter Peter Street, dismantled 'The Theatre' in Shoreditch and transported the timbers across the frozen Thames to Southwark; from these, 'The Globe' was built, opening in 1599 — likely with 'Julius Caesar'. Shakespeare owned a tenth share. In February 1601, Essex's supporters paid the troupe to stage 'Richard II' — a play about the deposition of a king — on the eve of their rebellion; the actors were interrogated and released, and the evening after Essex's execution, they performed before the Queen. The Globe burned down in 1613 from a theatrical cannon during 'Henry VIII'; only someone's breeches, which were doused with ale, were damaged.
level.globe.goal: The Theatre is moved across the Thames on timbers — and the best theatre in England opens.
level.globe.hint: First, dismantle 'The Theatre' — the timbers are the troupe's strength. Then the playwright and actor will open 'The Globe'. And playing 'Richard II' for Essex on the eve of a rebellion means facing an interrogation: don't befriend the Earl.
level.globe.intro: Burbage's troupe was denied a lease for the land under 'The Theatre'. The landowner considers the building his own. On the night after Christmas 1598, the actors dismantle it, timber by timber.
level.globe.source: Testimony of Augustine Phillips, 1601; J. Shapiro, '1599'
level.globe.title: The Globe
level.glorious.fact: On November 5, 1688, William of Orange landed in Torbay. James II's army disintegrated without a fight — commander John Churchill (the future Marlborough) defected to the Dutch. In December, James fled, on the way throwing the Great Seal of the Realm into the Thames to paralyze governance; he was caught by fishermen in Kent, but William deliberately allowed him to escape to France. Parliament declared the throne vacant and in February 1689 offered it jointly to William and Mary — under the terms of the Bill of Rights. The Revolution was called Glorious because in England it was bloodless; Ireland and Scotland paid for it in full.
level.glorious.goal: The king loses his throne without fighting a single battle — and throws the Great Seal of the Realm into the river.
level.glorious.hint: The powerful Dutchman lands — and the king's army disperses, there will be no battle. The king flees and throws the seal into the Thames — this is his departure. And then his allied daughter, with authority, proclaims her husband king alongside herself.
level.glorious.intro: The Catholic James II had a son — England feared a Catholic dynasty. Seven lords secretly invited the Dutch Stadtholder William, married to James's daughter Mary, to 'save the Protestant faith.' He landed with twenty thousand men.
level.glorious.title: The Seal in the Thames
level.godunov.fact: On May 15, 1591, eight-year-old Tsarevich Dmitry died in Uglich with his throat slit; Prince Vasily Shuisky's commission ruled that the boy, playing with knives during an epileptic fit, 'stabbed himself.' The residents of Uglich who tore apart Godunov's men were executed and exiled to Siberia, and the veche bell, which raised the alarm, was 'punished' – its clapper removed and exiled to Tobolsk. When the childless Tsar Fyodor died in January 1598, Boris secluded himself in the Novodevichy Convent with his sister, Tsarina Irina; Patriarch Job, with a procession and a crowd, went three times to beg him to accept the throne, and he agreed 'with tears.' The same Shuisky, eight years later, would declare that the Tsarevich had indeed been murdered on Boris's orders.
level.godunov.goal: The ruler emerges clean from the Uglich affair — and 'reluctantly' accepts the crown from the hands of the pleading crowd.
level.godunov.hint: First, Shuisky's investigation in Uglich: an accident, the ruler is clean, and Shuisky is with him. Then Novodevichy: the clean ruler is begged three times, and he gains the right to the crown. The coronation is at the end. To renounce the crown means to leave for good.
level.godunov.intro: Tsar Fyodor is weak-minded; his brother-in-law, Boris Godunov, rules. In Uglich, under strange circumstances, Ivan the Terrible's youngest son, Tsarevich Dmitry, dies. Prince Shuisky leads the investigation. And when Fyodor dies, the throne is empty for the first time in seven hundred years.
level.godunov.title: Boris Godunov
level.gracchus.fact: In 133 BC, Tribune Tiberius Gracchus proposed returning surplus public land to the state and distributing it to the landless. His colleague Marcus Octavius vetoed it — and Gracchus secured a vote for his removal, which the Roman constitution did not recognize. The law passed. When Gracchus ran for a second consecutive term (also an unprecedented act), senators led by Scipio Nasica Serapio, wrapping their togas around their arms and armed with bench legs, beat him to death near the Capitoline — about three hundred people died with him. This was the first political assassination in Rome in 380 years of the Republic; from then on, the count would be in the thousands.
level.gracchus.goal: The agrarian law is passed — and the tribune is killed for it on the Capitoline.
level.gracchus.hint: First, remove a colleague with his veto through a speech, then the law – and only then the senator with a club.
level.gracchus.intro: The land of Italy is being bought up into vast estates, while veterans return from wars to nothing. Tribune Tiberius Gracchus wants to distribute surplus public land to them — and runs into the veto of his own colleague. A tribune is inviolable, as long as he is a tribune.
level.gracchus.source: Plutarch, 'Tiberius Gracchus'; Appian, 'The Civil Wars', I
level.gracchus.title: The Fall of the Tribune
level.great_fire.fact: The fire began on September 2, 1666, in Thomas Farriner's bakery on Pudding Lane. Lord Mayor Thomas Bloodworth, woken at night, refused to demolish houses for firebreaks — 'Pish! A woman might piss it out!' — and missed the only opportunity. In four days, 13,200 houses, 87 churches, and St. Paul's Cathedral burned; officially, six people died. Charles II and the Duke of York personally commanded the demolition of houses by explosion in the fire's path. The French and Catholics were blamed; the French watchmaker Robert Hubert, who confessed to arson, was hanged, even though he was not yet in England on the day the fire started. Wren rebuilt the cathedral in thirty-five years.
level.great_fire.goal: A spark from the oven burns London because the mayor won't demolish houses — and the king stops the fire.
level.great_fire.hint: The baker won't extinguish the oven. The mayor won't demolish houses — and the city will ignite; if he undertakes to demolish them immediately, there will be no fire, and then nothing to stop. The king will stop the fire by blowing up houses with gunpowder.
level.great_fire.intro: September 1666, a dry summer, an east wind. At two in the morning, the royal baker Farriner went to sleep without extinguishing his oven. Woken, Mayor Bloodworth looked at the fire and returned to bed.
level.great_fire.title: Pudding Lane
level.greek_fire.fact: According to Theophanes, around 672, the architect Kallinikos from Syrian Heliopolis (Baalbek) fled to Constantinople and brought «sea fire» — a petroleum-based mixture that was ejected under pressure from bronze siphons on the prows of dromons; it burned on water and could only be extinguished with sand, vinegar, or urine. In 674–678, the Arab fleet, wintering near Cyzicus, was burned, the siege was lifted, and Caliph Muawiyah paid tribute. The composition was kept in the strictest secrecy: Constantine Porphyrogennetos wrote to his son that the fire was «shown by an angel to Constantine the Great» and to reveal it was a sin; an official who tried to sell the secret was «consumed by fire from heaven». The secret is indeed lost — the exact composition is unknown to this day.
level.greek_fire.goal: A refugee brings burning water, the Caliph's fleet burns at the Golden Horn — and the recipe becomes the empire's secret for five centuries.
level.greek_fire.hint: First, a refugee brings the recipe to the Emperor — the Emperor is powerful and has fire. Battle at the Golden Horn: the powerful Emperor defeats the Caliph. The victor with fire declares the composition a secret. To sell the recipe to the Caliph — a bought engineer will not bring the fire.
level.greek_fire.intro: The Arab fleet of Caliph Muawiyah has stood before Constantinople for four years. From captured Syria, the architect Kallinikos flees to the capital — with the recipe for a liquid that burns on water and cannot be extinguished.
level.greek_fire.source: Theophanes the Confessor, «Chronographia»; Constantine Porphyrogennetos, «De Administrando Imperio», ch. 13
level.greek_fire.title: Greek Fire
level.gunpowder.fact: On October 26, 1605, the Catholic Lord Monteagle received an anonymous letter advising him not to attend the opening of Parliament; he took it to Robert Cecil. On the night of November 5, Guy Fawkes was found in the cellar beneath the House of Lords with a fuse and thirty-six barrels of gunpowder. Under torture, he betrayed the others; Catesby died during arrest, eight were hanged and quartered in January 1606 — Fawkes jumped from the gallows ladder and broke his neck before being quartered. The day of the king's salvation is still celebrated with bonfires, and Fawkes' mask became the face of protest four centuries later.
level.gunpowder.goal: An anonymous letter reveals the plot — and the gunpowder remains in the barrels.
level.gunpowder.hint: First, the plot in the tavern. Then the letter will land on the royal spy's table — and the conspirator is condemned; the spy, with authority, executes him. If no one interferes — the fuse will be lit.
level.gunpowder.intro: Catholics hoped that the Scottish James would grant them freedom of religion. He did not. Robert Catesby gathered conspirators and hired former soldier Guy Fawkes to blow up the king and Parliament. Thirty-six barrels of gunpowder are already in the cellar.
level.gunpowder.source: 'The King's Book' (protocols 1606); A. Fraser, 'The Gunpowder Plot'
level.gunpowder.title: Remember, Remember the Fifth of November
level.hagia.fact: After the Nika fire, Justinian rebuilt the Hagia Sophia (537) — for a thousand years the greatest temple of Christianity. Upon entering its colossal dome, the emperor, according to legend, exclaimed: «Solomon, I have surpassed you!».
level.hagia.goal: The emperor erects the greatest temple of Christianity
level.hagia.hint: Let the emperor himself conceive the cathedral amidst the ruins — and only then will he erect the Hagia Sophia. Courtiers do not build temples.
level.hagia.intro: The Nika riot burned the old temple to ashes. Amidst the ruins, Justinian conceives the unprecedented.
level.hagia.title: Hagia Sophia
level.hannibal_alps.fact: In the autumn of 218 BC, Hannibal led his army across the Alps in fifteen days — according to Polybius, out of 46,000, about 26,000 and a handful of elephants survived; avalanches, landslides, and mountain tribes did the rest. But he emerged into the Po Valley, where the Boii Gauls, who had just revolted against Rome, provided him with men and grain. In the spring of 217 BC, at Lake Trasimene, in the morning fog, he ambushed the entire army of Consul Flaminius: fifteen thousand Romans perished, as did the consul. It is said that an earthquake that occurred during the battle went unnoticed by any of the combatants.
level.hannibal_alps.goal: The Carthaginian arrives in Italy from an unexpected direction — and the first consul perishes in the fog
level.hannibal_alps.hint: By sea — they will be intercepted. Half the army will make it through the mountains, but that will be its strength. The Gauls, who hate Rome, must be taken as allies. And only then — the lake in the fog.
level.hannibal_alps.intro: Hannibal departed from Spain with his army and elephants. The sea is held by the Roman fleet, and there is no direct road to Italy — only mountains, where it is already snowing in October. Consul Flaminius awaits him in Etruria.
level.hannibal_alps.title: Across the Alps
level.hastings.fact: On September 25, 1066, Harold Godwinson defeated the Norwegian King Harald Hardrada at Stamford Bridge — the latter fell in battle. Three days later, William landed in Sussex. Harold marched his army three hundred miles in nine days and on October 14, engaged in battle near Hastings, tired and with depleted forces. The Normans feigned retreat, breaking the English shield wall; by evening, Harold died — according to the Bayeux Tapestry, from an arrow to the eye. William was crowned in Westminster on Christmas Day. A century later, one third of the English language would become French.
level.hastings.goal: One king defeats another — and comes to the third without strength.
level.hastings.hint: The Norwegians must be defeated first — both are strong, but there you are home. A week's march south will exhaust the army, and it will cease to be a force. Only then will the Norman prevail; wait in London — and he will not.
level.hastings.intro: In one year, three contenders emerged for the English throne: Harold, crowned in London; Harald Hardrada, who landed with the Norwegians in the north; and William of Normandy, awaiting the wind across the Channel. Harold can reach both — but not fresh.
level.hastings.source: Anglo-Saxon Chronicle, 1066; William of Poitiers; Bayeux Tapestry
level.heir.fact: Justin I, an illiterate soldier who became emperor, brought close and adopted his gifted nephew Justinian, making him co-ruler and heir to the throne.
level.heir.goal: Old Justin makes his nephew heir
level.heir.hint: First, let Justin entrust the gifted Justinian with the palace guard — and only then declare the proven man his heir. Germanus is superfluous here.
level.heir.intro: The illiterate soldier Justin became emperor — but which of his nephews should he make his heir? Ambitious Germanus also awaits his hour.
level.heir.source: History of the Eastern Roman Empire
level.heir.title: Justin's Heir
level.henry6.fact: From August 1453 to December 1454, Henry VI neither spoke nor moved; doctors offered no help. Parliament appointed Richard of York as Protector, removing Queen Margaret. Upon awakening, the King restored power to her party — and on May 22, 1455, York and Warwick attacked the royal court at St Albans: the Duke of Somerset and about sixty others died, the King was wounded by an arrow in the neck. Thus began the Wars of the Roses — thirty years of slaughter between the descendants of one king. The only things Henry VI built still stand today: Eton and King's College, Cambridge.
level.henry6.goal: While the King is silent, the Protector seizes power — and the first blood of the Wars of the Roses is shed in the streets of St Albans.
level.henry6.hint: Stupor renders the King an empty vessel — without weight or power. Then a strong duke becomes Protector to an empty king, not the queen. Upon awakening, the King will strip him of power — and St Albans: battle, the King defeated.
level.henry6.intro: Henry VI, son of the victor of Agincourt, is meek, pious, and weak. In August 1453, upon learning of the loss of Gascony, he fell into a stupor: he does not speak, does not eat on his own, and does not recognize his newborn son. Queen Margaret demands regency. The Duke of York — also.
level.henry6.source: 'The Chronicle of John Benet'; R. Griffiths, 'The Reign of Henry VI'
level.henry6.title: The Sleeping King
level.heraclius.fact: In 622, Heraclius, borrowing gold and silver from the church, for the first time in two hundred years personally led an army on campaign — deep into Armenia and Persia, leaving the capital under the protection of its walls and the patriarch; in 626, the Avars and Persians besieged Constantinople and retreated. On December 12, 627, at Nineveh, he defeated the Persians — according to legend, personally slaying three commanders; in February 628, Khosrow II was overthrown and killed by his own son. On March 21, 630, the Emperor carried the returned Cross into Jerusalem — on foot and in simple clothes, as the patriarch demanded. Six years later, he would lose that same Syria forever — at Yarmouk.
level.heraclius.goal: The Emperor, with church money, goes to Persia, defeats the King of Kings — and on his shoulders carries the Cross into Jerusalem.
level.heraclius.hint: First, church silver — the Emperor is powerful and influential. Nineveh: the powerful Emperor defeats Khosrow's army. The victor carries the Cross into Jerusalem. To move the capital to Carthage — one who has left will not be given silver.
level.heraclius.intro: The Persians took Jerusalem and carried away the True Cross, standing at Chalcedon opposite the capital; the treasury is empty. Emperor Heraclius, advised to flee to Carthage, borrows church silver and personally leads an army into the heart of Persia.
level.heraclius.source: Theophanes the Confessor, 'Chronographia'; W. Kaegi, 'Heraclius, Emperor of Byzantium'
level.heraclius.title: The True Cross
level.horatii.fact: Tullus Hostilius, the third king of Rome, waged war with Alba Longa, and by agreement, the outcome was decided by a duel between three Horatii and three Curiatii. The last Horatius feigned flight, the wounded enemies spread out — and he killed them one by one. At the gates, his sister, betrothed to one of the Curiatii, burst into tears upon recognizing her fiancé's cloak — and her brother stabbed her, saying: 'So perish every Roman woman who mourns an enemy.' He was tried for murder and acquitted at his father's plea, but was made to pass under a beam — the 'sister's beam,' which was still shown in Rome during Augustus's time.
level.horatii.goal: One defeats three — and kills his own sister for weeping over an enemy
level.horatii.hint: One against three will not stand — one must flee so that the pursuers spread out, and strike them down one by one: this is strength. And the sister at the gates is met by the victor.
level.horatii.intro: Rome and Alba Longa decided not to destroy two armies, but to pit three brothers against three. Two Horatii fell immediately; the third remained alone against three wounded Curiatii. And his sister is betrothed to one of them.
level.horatii.title: The Horatii and the Curiatii
level.hotspur.fact: On July 21, 1403, at Shrewsbury, Henry IV defeated Henry Percy, nicknamed Hotspur. Hotspur died, having raised his visor in the heat — an arrow struck him in the face. For the Prince of Wales, the future Henry V, an arrow entered his cheek six inches below his eye; he refused to leave the field, and later surgeon John Bradmore extracted the arrowhead with special forceps and washed the wound with honey and wine — the prince survived, the scar remained for life. Hotspur's body was quartered and sent to various towns. Shakespeare made Hotspur a contemporary of Hal and his mirror image; in life, he was twenty-three years older.
level.hotspur.goal: The rebel dies at Shrewsbury, and the idle prince, with an arrow in his face, becomes the future Henry V.
level.hotspur.hint: Percy's muster is the rebel's strength. At Shrewsbury, a strong king meets him, and in the third slot — the prince: while the boy holds the flank, the rebel loses strength, and with an arrow in his face, he does not leave the field — the defeated are finished off. If you lead the prince away, there will be neither victory nor a hero.
level.hotspur.intro: The Percys helped Bolingbroke take the throne — and decided he owed them. Harry Hotspur, the best knight of the North, raised a rebellion. Against him are the King and his sixteen-year-old son Hal, whom his father considers idle.
level.hotspur.source: T. Walsingham; J. Bradmore, 'Philomena' (a surgeon's treatise)
level.hotspur.title: Hotspur
level.howard.fact: Catherine Howard, the fifth wife, was very young. Her pre-marital affairs and accusations of treason with courtier Thomas Culpeper surfaced. On February 13, 1542, she was beheaded in the Tower. According to legend, the day before, she requested the block be brought so she could 'dignifiedly' rehearse her execution.
level.howard.goal: The young queen — and the block once more
level.howard.hint: Marriage, then accusation: Cranmer, with authority, condemns the Queen with a speech in the tribunal. The condemned is executed by the King.
level.howard.intro: The fifth wife, nineteen-year-old Catherine Howard, — 'a rose without thorns,' as the King called her. A year later, Archbishop Cranmer hands him a note: before the wedding, she had lovers, and after — too.
level.howard.title: Catherine Howard
level.hypatia.fact: Hypatia, daughter of the mathematician Theon, taught philosophy in Alexandria, commented on Diophantus and Ptolemy, and, according to Socrates Scholasticus, 'surpassed all the philosophers of her time.' She was an advisor to Prefect Orestes in his struggle against Bishop Cyril; a rumor spread in the city that she was hindering reconciliation. In March 415, a mob led by the lector Peter dragged her from her chariot, hauled her to the Caesareum church, stripped her clothes, and killed her with pottery shards (or oyster shells — 'ostracon' means both), then burned her body. Cyril was later canonized; Orestes was recalled; the Alexandrian school faded. Gibbon made her a symbol of the end of antiquity, and Raphael, according to tradition, included her in 'The School of Athens'.
level.hypatia.goal: A bishop preaches against a woman philosopher, friendly with the prefect, — and a mob of monks tears her apart with pottery shards.
level.hypatia.hint: First, the prefect's friendship with the philosopher — allies. The bishop preaches against her with authority — condemned. The bishop's parabolani drag the condemned woman from her chariot. Leave for Athens — the one who left will not be touched.
level.hypatia.intro: Alexandria, 415 AD. Hypatia — mathematician, astronomer, head of the Neoplatonic school; Prefect Orestes and half the city seek her counsel. The new bishop Cyril battles the prefect for power — and declares the pagan woman the cause of discord.
level.hypatia.source: Socrates Scholasticus, 'Ecclesiastical History', VII, 15; M. Dzielska, 'Hypatia of Alexandria'
level.hypatia.title: Hypatia
level.hypatius.fact: On January 10, 1775, Yemelyan Pugachev was executed on Bolotnaya Square in Moscow. The rebellion was drowned in blood; Catherine II renamed the Yaik River to the Ural to erase the memory of the revolt.
level.hypatius.goal: The captured impostor is executed on Bolotnaya Square
level.hypatius.hint: First, let Theodora reject mercy and harden the emperor's resolve — and only then will Justinian send the usurper to the block. Without her word, he would pardon him.
level.hypatius.intro: Hypatius is captured. He swears the mob raised him by force — and Justinian is ready to forgive. But Theodora holds a different view.
level.hypatius.title: Pugachev's Execution
level.irene.fact: In 787, Irene convened the Seventh Ecumenical Council in Nicaea, which restored icon veneration; for this, she is revered as a saint in Orthodoxy. Her son Constantine VI deposed her in 790, but restored her two years later; on August 15, 797, by her order, he was seized and blinded — in the Porphyra chamber of the Great Palace, where she herself had given birth to him; the chronicler Theophanes writes that the sun darkened for seventeen days. She ruled alone for five years and signed herself 'Irene, faithful basileus' — in the masculine gender: the law had no word for a woman on the throne. In the West, it was decided that the throne was vacant — and in 800, the Pope crowned Charlemagne emperor; Charlemagne proposed to Irene, but in 802 she was overthrown and exiled to Lesbos, where she spun wool.
level.irene.goal: A regent restores icons, blinds her own son in the room where she bore him, — and is the first woman to be called basileus.
level.irene.hint: First, the Council of Nicaea — the ruler restores icons, is Orthodox and influential. Porphyra chamber: Orthodox mother and son — the son is blinded, she rules alone. The sole ruler takes a masculine title. Charlemagne's proposal — one who spares her son will not be touched and will not remain alone.
level.irene.intro: Irene, an Athenian, is the emperor's widow and regent for her son Constantine VI. She restores the icons that her father-in-law and husband had burned for half a century. Her son grows up and wants to rule himself.
level.irene.source: Theophanes the Confessor, 'Chronographia', sub anno 6289; J. Herrin, 'Women in Purple'
level.irene.title: Basileus Irene
level.isabella.fact: In 1326, Isabella of France and her lover Roger Mortimer landed in Suffolk with mercenaries; Edward II's army scattered. Hugh Despenser the Younger was hanged, castrated, and quartered in Hereford on a fifty-foot gallows; the king abdicated in favor of his son. In September 1327, Edward II died in Berkeley Castle — according to a later legend, a red-hot poker was inserted into him to leave no marks; chroniclers of the time simply speak of murder, and some historians believe he fled to Italy. Three years later, the seventeen-year-old Edward III arrested Mortimer in his mother's bedroom and hanged him; Isabella was sent into honorable confinement — for twenty-eight years.
level.isabella.goal: The queen and her lover overthrow her husband — and the husband dies in Berkeley Castle.
level.isabella.hint: First, love in Paris. Then powerful Mortimer lands and defeats the king. Despenser will be hanged without your intervention — but the king in the castle needs a killer, and that is his enemy.
level.isabella.intro: Edward II gave England to his favorite Despenser, and Queen Isabella to humiliation. Sent as an envoy to Paris, she met the exiled Roger Mortimer there. She will return with him and an army.
level.isabella.title: She-Wolf of France
level.izmail.fact: Potemkin, despairing of the siege of Izmail, handed command to Suvorov in November 1790: 'My hope is in God and your bravery.' Suvorov, in a week, built a replica of the rampart and moat near the camp and trained soldiers for the assault at night. He sent an ultimatum to Commandant Aidozle-Mehmed Pasha: 'A day to reflect – freedom. My first shot – already captivity. Assault – death.' The Pasha replied that the Danube would sooner flow backward and the sky fall to earth. On December 11 (22), at half past five in the morning, nine columns advanced on the walls; by four in the afternoon, the city was taken. Only a handful of the garrison survived, and the Russians lost four thousand killed. Catherine minted a medal 'For Exceptional Bravery,' and Suvorov, who had fallen out with Potemkin, was sent to Finland to build fortifications.
level.izmail.goal: The commander trains soldiers on a replica of the walls, gives the Pasha a day — and takes the impregnable fortress in one night.
level.izmail.hint: First, Potemkin's order — Suvorov gains influence. The training rampart — Suvorov shows strength. A strong commander with influence sends an ultimatum to the Pasha — who replies defiantly. The assault on the stubborn Pasha — the fortress is taken. Lifting the siege is not an option.
level.izmail.intro: A Turkish fortress on the Danube is considered impregnable: a ten-meter rampart, a moat, a thirty-five-thousand-strong garrison. The Russian army has besieged it for months and is suffering from illness. Potemkin hands the fortress over to Suvorov — who arrives and orders a replica of the rampart to be built.
level.izmail.source: A. Petrushevsky, 'Generalissimo Prince Suvorov'; Suvorov's report to Potemkin, 1790
level.izmail.title: Izmail
level.jacobins.fact: The Jacobin Club became the engine of the Revolution. Robespierre and his young comrade Louis de Saint-Just transformed it into a stronghold of radicals, from which the Terror emanated. Saint-Just was dubbed the 'Archangel of Terror.'
level.jacobins.hint: Let Robespierre first ignite into a radical in the debate — and only then shall he infect Saint-Just with radicalism. The Girondin Corday cannot be turned into a Jacobin.
level.jacobins.intro: The Jacobin Club is seething. Robespierre inflames his comrades, while moderate Girondins try to cool him down.
level.jacobins.title: The Jacobin Club
level.jane_grey.fact: In July 1553, the Duke of Northumberland proclaimed Lady Jane Grey — his daughter-in-law — as Queen. But the people and nobility rallied behind Henry VIII's daughter, Mary; nine days later, Jane was deposed. Northumberland was executed immediately; sixteen-year-old Jane, in February 1554. Mary I ascended the throne.
level.jane_grey.goal: Northumberland's puppet is overthrown by Mary — and Jane ascends the scaffold
level.jane_grey.hint: An influential patron proclaims the girl queen. Nine days later, Mary condemns her with a speech — and the condemned is executed.
level.jane_grey.intro: Edward VI is dead. The Duke of Northumberland places his daughter-in-law, Jane Grey, on the throne — bypassing the rightful Mary.
level.jane_grey.title: The Nine Days' Queen
level.jane_seymour.fact: On May 19, 1536, Anne Boleyn was beheaded at the Tower; just 11 days later, Henry VIII married Jane Seymour. In October 1537, she gave birth to the long-awaited son — the future Edward VI — and died twelve days later of puerperal fever. Jane was the only wife Henry mourned.
level.jane_seymour.goal: After executing Boleyn, Henry marries Jane — she bears an heir and dies.
level.jane_seymour.hint: The condemned queen is executed first — otherwise the wedding will not take place. The new queen will bear an heir, and childbed fever will claim her.
level.jane_seymour.intro: Anne Boleyn is condemned. Henry already gazes upon Jane Seymour — but the path to a new wedding lies through the executioner's block.
level.jane_seymour.title: Jane Seymour
level.jena.fact: On October 14, 1806, at Jena and Auerstedt, Napoleon and Davout crushed the Prussian army — within a week, Prussia ceased to exist as a military power; Blücher was the last to surrender at Lübeck, writing in his capitulation: 'for want of bread and cartridges.' On November 21 in Berlin, Napoleon signed the decree on the Continental Blockade — prohibiting all of Europe from trading with Britain. The blockade hit France harder than England, and it was precisely because of it that he would march on Russia six years later.
level.jena.goal: The Prussian army vanishes in a day, and from Berlin, Napoleon closes Europe to England
level.jena.hint: The Grand Army — preparation. Then mighty Prussia is crushed at Jena in a day. And from conquered Berlin — a decree: the continent is forbidden to trade with the English.
level.jena.intro: Frederick the Great's Prussia declared war — with an army unchanged for half a century. Napoleon leads the Grand Army through Thuringia; Blücher, a desperate hussar, commands the Prussian rearguard.
level.jena.source: Bulletins of the Grand Army, 1806; C. Clausewitz, 'The Year 1806'
level.jena.title: Jena
level.joan_reims.fact: In May 1429, Joan of Arc lifted the Siege of Orléans in nine days, and on July 17, she stood with her banner in Reims Cathedral, where the Dauphin was anointed as Charles VII — a legitimacy no victory could bestow. In September, she marched on Paris without the king's support, was wounded by an arrow in the thigh at the Porte Saint-Honoré, and repelled; the court deemed her task complete. A year later, the Burgundians captured her near Compiègne — and Charles VII, crowned by her, paid not a sou for her. What happened next, you saw in Rouen.
level.joan_reims.goal: The Maid lifts the siege and makes the Dauphin king — and she must go no further.
level.joan_reims.hint: First, victory at Orléans — with it, the Maid gains the authority to vouch for the Dauphin. Then, the coronation in Reims. Do not march on Paris: there she will be defeated, and a defeated Maid would crown no one.
level.joan_reims.intro: Dauphin Charles sits in Chinon, doubting even his own birth. Orléans has been besieged by the English for seven months. A peasant girl is brought to the Dauphin, claiming voices have commanded her to lift the siege and crown him in Reims.
level.joan_reims.source: Rehabilitation Protocols of 1456; "Journal of the Siege of Orléans"
level.joan_reims.title: The Road to Reims
level.joan_stake.fact: In May 1429, Joan of Arc lifted the seven-month siege of Orléans in nine days. In May 1430, the Burgundians captured her near Compiègne and sold her to the English for ten thousand livres; the French King Charles VII, whom she had crowned, offered not a sou for her. An ecclesiastical court presided over by Bishop Pierre Cauchon — a scholar, Anglophile, and ambitious man — condemned her for heresy and wearing men's clothing; on May 30, 1431, she was burned at the stake in the Old Market in Rouen, at the age of nineteen. Her ashes were thrown into the Seine. Twenty-five years later, the same ecclesiastical court annulled the verdict, and five hundred years later, declared her a saint.
level.joan_stake.goal: The victor over the English is tried as a heretic — and burned by those she defeated.
level.joan_stake.hint: First, her victory at Orléans — Bedford is defeated. Then the ecclesiastical court: the bishop, with authority, condemns her with a speech. The regent executes the condemned. No one will come to ransom her.
level.joan_stake.intro: A peasant girl in armor lifted the siege of Orléans and crowned the Dauphin in Reims. A year later, the Burgundians captured her and sold her to the English. The Duke of Bedford, Regent of France, wants not an execution — he wants a trial that will declare her a witch.
level.joan_stake.source: Trial records of 1431; Rehabilitation records of 1456
level.joan_stake.title: The Pyre in Rouen
level.john_fall.fact: Theodora and her friend Antonina, Belisarius's wife, used intrigue to lure John of Cappadocia into a fabricated conspiracy against the emperor. Exposed, the all-powerful minister fell and was sent into exile.
level.john_fall.goal: Theodora and Antonina ruin the hated minister
level.john_fall.hint: Let Antonina first lull John's vigilance with false friendship — and only then lure him into a nocturnal trap. Tribonian is not her target.
level.john_fall.intro: Theodora yearns for the downfall of John the Cappadocian. Her confidante Antonina, Belisarius's wife, weaves a snare — with feigned friendship.
level.john_fall.title: Trap for John
level.juan.fact: Alexander VI openly preferred his younger son Juan, making him Gonfalonier of the Church and a Duke. This ignited a burning envy in his elder brother, Cesare.
level.juan.goal: The Pope showers Cesare's brother, Juan, with favors
level.juan.hint: The favor goes not to the cardinal, but to his brother.
level.juan.intro: Alexander VI is on the throne and showers his favorite son with favors.
level.juan.source: History of the House of Borgia
level.juan.title: The Favorite Son
level.julius.fact: In 1503, Giuliano della Rovere became Pope Julius II, a long-standing enemy of the Borgias. The 'Warrior Pope' and patron of Michelangelo, he aimed to destroy everything Cesare had created.
level.julius.goal: The sworn enemy of the Borgias ascends to the throne
level.julius.hint: Let della Rovere first unite the enemies of the Borgia — and only having risen will he take the throne as Julius II. Cesare is a Borgia; he will not see the tiara.
level.julius.intro: Alexander VI is dead. The sworn enemy of the Borgia, della Rovere, sees his hour — but Cesare is still strong in the conclave.
level.julius.source: History of the Pontificate of Julius II
level.julius.title: Julius II
level.kazan.fact: On October 2, 1552, Ivan the Terrible's troops captured Kazan, annexing the Kazan Khanate to the Russian Tsardom. This opened the way to the east and to the conquest of Astrakhan and Siberia.
level.kazan.goal: The Tsar conquers the Kazan Khanate
level.kazan.hint: First, the tsar must be crowned in the cathedral — and only the reigning Ivan will conquer Kazan. Boyar Shuisky will not lead the troops.
level.kazan.intro: The crowned tsar needs a great victory. The Kazan Khanate is a long-standing enemy at the eastern borders.
level.kazan.source: Chronicles of the Taking of Kazan
level.kazan.title: The Taking of Kazan
level.king_trial.fact: On January 21, 1793, Louis XVI, condemned by the National Convention as 'Citizen Louis Capet,' was guillotined in the Place de la Révolution. The king's execution shocked the monarchies of Europe and accelerated the war.
level.king_trial.goal: The Convention tries the king and sends him to the guillotine
level.king_trial.hint: First — a verdict in the Convention, then — the scaffold.
level.king_trial.title: Execution of Louis XVI
level.kingmaker.fact: Richard Neville, Earl of Warwick, secured the Yorkist victory at Towton in 1461 – the bloodiest battle on English soil – and placed Edward IV on the throne. The king's secret marriage to Elizabeth Woodville and the rise of her relatives alienated Warwick; in 1470, in Angers, he allied with Margaret of Anjou, wife of the deposed Henry VI, restored Henry to the throne, and Edward fled to Burgundy. Six months later, Edward returned; on April 14, 1471, at Barnet, in a thick fog, Warwick's army slaughtered its own men, mistaking an ally's emblem for the Yorkist sun; Warwick died trying to reach his horse. His nickname – the Kingmaker – is remembered in England to this day.
level.kingmaker.goal: He who made a king turns against him with yesterday's foe – and perishes in the fog
level.kingmaker.hint: First, a powerful patron makes Edward king. Then, the aggrieved Kingmaker conspires with the Lancastrian queen – a plot. And in the battle of Barnet, the now strong king defeats him.
level.kingmaker.intro: The Earl of Warwick placed Edward of York on the throne, defeating the Lancastrians at Towton. In return, he expected obedience – but the king secretly married a knight's widow and began distributing to her relatives what Warwick considered his own.
level.kingmaker.source: The Arrival of Edward IV (Historie of the Arrivall); Philippe de Commines, Memoirs
level.kingmaker.title: The Kingmaker
level.komnenos_crusade.fact: Through the winter of 1096–1097 the leaders of the crusade swore to Alexios I one by one to return to the empire every city that had once belonged to it. Bohemond of Taranto, who had fought against Alexios in 1081–1085, swore more readily than any of them and asked for a post in the imperial army; Godfrey held out until the emperor cut off the food supply, and Raymond of Toulouse never gave the full oath at all. The siege of Nicaea ran from May to 19 June 1097; on 16 May Kilij Arslan tried to relieve the city and was beaten off. The Byzantines hauled boats overland to Lake Ascanius and closed the blockade, after which the garrison surrendered in secret to the imperial commander Manuel Boutoumites. The next morning the crusaders, ready for the assault, saw imperial banners on the towers: the city went to Alexios, and the plunder went to nobody. The Latins received gifts, and a grievance they would remember in 1204.
level.komnenos_crusade.goal: The emperor takes an oath from the crusaders — and keeps the city they captured for himself, never letting them inside
level.komnenos_crusade.hint: First the oath at Blachernae: the Latin swears for every city he takes back. Then Nicaea: the strong crusader beats the sultan. And only with a victor who has sworn the oath can the emperor raise his own banners. Palace gold is a bribe: a man who has been bought will not swear, he already has what he came for.
level.komnenos_crusade.intro: Alexios Komnenos had asked the West for mercenaries, and what came to the walls of the capital was tens of thousands of armed pilgrims led by princes — among them Bohemond, a Norman who had made war on him personally ten years earlier. They have to be fed, they must not be quarrelled with, and they certainly must not be let loose. The first city on their road is Nicaea, capital of the Seljuk sultan.
level.komnenos_crusade.source: Anna Komnene, 'The Alexiad', X–XI; 'Gesta Francorum' (The Deeds of the Franks)
level.komnenos_crusade.title: The Oath and Nicaea
level.la_rochelle.fact: In 1627–1628, Richelieu besieged La Rochelle for fourteen months. A stone dike, a kilometer and a half long, was built across the bay, sealing off the harbor; the English fleet of the Duke of Buckingham, sent by Charles I, failed to break through three times. Of 27,000 inhabitants, five thousand survived — they ate leather, rats, then the dead. The city surrendered on October 28, 1628; the Huguenots retained freedom of worship but lost their fortresses and army — the "state within a state" was over. Dumas set the siege from "The Three Musketeers" here; the dike is still visible at low tide.
level.la_rochelle.goal: The Cardinal seals the harbor with a dike — and the city surrenders to hunger, not assault.
level.la_rochelle.hint: The Cardinal will not negotiate with the besieged. The dike across the bay is his strength: with it, the English fleet is defeated, and without access to the sea, the city starves. The besieged surrenders.
level.la_rochelle.intro: La Rochelle is a Huguenot stronghold with a harbor supplied by England from the sea. Cardinal Richelieu decides: as long as the Huguenots have fortresses, there are two states in France. English King Charles I sends a fleet to its rescue.
level.la_rochelle.source: Richelieu, "Memoirs"; J. Calmann, "The Siege of La Rochelle"
level.la_rochelle.title: Richelieu's Dike
level.leipzig.fact: On October 16–19, 1813, near Leipzig, the coalition defeated Napoleon in the largest battle before World War I: half a million soldiers, one hundred thousand killed and wounded. In the midst of the battle, Saxon regiments defected to the allies and turned their cannons. During the retreat, a corporal blew up the only bridge over the Elster, leaving twenty thousand French soldiers on the other side; Marshal Poniatowski drowned. Six months later, the allies entered Paris, and Napoleon abdicated — for the first time.
level.leipzig.goal: Europe finally fights together — and a single corporal blows up the bridge under the retreating army.
level.leipzig.hint: First, the coalition — Russians and Prussians are allies. In the battle, there are three: in the midst of the fight, the Saxons will defect to the Prussians, and the French will lose strength. The defeated will be finished off by the bridge, blown up prematurely.
level.leipzig.intro: After Russia, Napoleon assembled a new army of boys. Against him stood all of Europe at once: Russia, Prussia, Austria, Sweden. Near Leipzig, half a million men, and the French had only one bridge for retreat.
level.leipzig.source: Marbot, "Memoirs"; D. Chandler, "The Campaigns of Napoleon"
level.leipzig.title: Battle of the Nations
level.leo_isaurian.fact: Leo III's iconoclasm begins around 726–730; in 730 he convened a council, declared the veneration of icons to be idolatry and demanded the patriarch's signature. Germanos I refused, took off his omophorion, laid it on the altar with the words that the faith is not changed without an ecumenical council, and withdrew to his family estate; Anastasios was installed in his place. The story of the image of Christ above the Chalke Gate — how the spatharios officer sent to take it down was torn apart by a crowd of women who overturned the ladder — is told only in iconophile sources written much later: 'The Life of Stephen the Younger' and the chronicle of Theophanes. Modern historians hold that the episode is either embellished or transposed from later years; the Latin inscription on the gate cited as proof is known only from copies. The dispute over icons lasted more than a hundred years and ended with their return in 843.
level.leo_isaurian.goal: The emperor declares icons idolatry — and gets a riot at the gate and a patriarch who lays down his omophorion and walks away
level.leo_isaurian.hint: The decree first: the emperor becomes an iconoclast, the patriarch his opponent. Then the ladder at the gate: the officer taking down the image meets the crowd, and the emperor begins to be hated. And then the opponent lays down his omophorion before the hated man. The family estate is a departure: a man who has withdrawn renounces nothing in public.
level.leo_isaurian.intro: Leo III beat the Arabs back from the capital itself and saved the empire. Now he decides that its misfortunes are sent as punishment for the sin of idolatry: people kiss painted boards, bow down to them, and make them godparents to their children. Above the Chalke Gate of the palace hangs the most venerated image of Christ in the city.
level.leo_isaurian.source: Theophanes the Confessor, 'Chronographia'; 'The Life of Stephen the Younger'; L. Brubaker, 'Inventing Byzantine Iconoclasm'
level.leo_isaurian.title: The Image Above the Gate
level.leonardo.fact: Leonardo worked on the Horse from 1489: the clay model stood seven metres high in Milan and was considered a wonder. In 1494 Ludovico il Moro sent the seventy tonnes of bronze set aside for it to Ferrara to be cast into cannon — France was marching. In 1499 the French entered Milan and Gascon crossbowmen used the clay horse for target practice. Leonardo painted The Last Supper in 1495–1498 in the refectory of Santa Maria delle Grazie and, unwilling to be hurried by wet plaster, worked in tempera and oil on a dry wall. The paint began flaking in his own lifetime; the mural has been restored seven times, the last restoration taking twenty-one years. It is the most famous and the most ruined painting of the Renaissance.
level.leonardo.goal: The duke turns the horse's bronze into cannon — and instead of a statue the master leaves the world a wall that begins flaking at once
level.leonardo.hint: The clay horse first — the master is at the height of his powers. Then the duke takes his bronze away: there will be no horse. The master left without a horse paints the Supper — the patron standing beside him, hurrying him along. Leaving for Venice means leaving the commission.
level.leonardo.intro: Leonardo came to Milan to serve Ludovico il Moro as a military engineer and musician, and was given a commission for an equestrian statue of the duke's father — the largest in the world. Seven metres of clay stood on the square for three years, astonishing everyone. The bronze for the casting had already been set aside.
level.leonardo.source: G. Vasari, Lives of the Artists; W. Isaacson, Leonardo da Vinci
level.leonardo.title: The Horse and the Supper
level.lepanto.fact: On 7 October 1571 some five hundred galleys met in the Gulf of Patras — the largest battle of oared fleets in history. Don John of Austria pushed six Venetian galleasses out ahead of the line — floating batteries — and their broadsides broke the Turkish order before the fleets closed. In four hours the Ottomans lost more than two hundred ships and their admiral Ali Pasha; fifteen thousand Christian galley slaves were freed. Miguel de Cervantes, twenty-four years old, lay in a fever but demanded the most dangerous post and took three wounds: two in the chest and one in the left hand, which was maimed for life — "to the greater glory of the right", as he wrote later. The nickname "the one-handed man of Lepanto" is inexact: he kept the hand, but it never worked again. Four years later corsairs captured him and he spent five years a slave in Algiers; Don Quixote appeared twenty-six years after that.
level.lepanto.goal: Six galleasses break the Turkish line and Ali Pasha's fleet goes down — while a fevered soldier rises from his sickbed and pays for the victory with his left hand
level.lepanto.hint: Galleasses ahead of the line first — the admiral is at full strength. The Gulf of Patras: the strong admiral beats Ali Pasha. Then the soldier and the victor: the soldier leaves his sickbed and pays with his hand. The harbour of Messina is where a fleet sits out the whole war.
level.lepanto.intro: The Turkish fleet rules the Mediterranean; the pope has assembled a Holy League of Spain, Venice and Genoa. It is led by the twenty-four-year-old Don John, the emperor's illegitimate son. Somewhere in the Spanish squadron a soldier from Alcalá lies burning with fever.
level.lepanto.source: M. de Cervantes, preface to the Exemplary Novels; R. Crowley, Empires of the Sea
level.lepanto.title: Lepanto
level.light_brigade.fact: On October 25, 1854, Lord Cardigan's Light Cavalry Brigade – about 670 horsemen – attacked a Russian battery at the end of a valley under crossfire from three sides; fewer than two hundred returned in formation. The cause was Raglan's order, written from a height where the view was entirely different, and delivered by Captain Nolan with the words, 'There is your enemy, there are your guns!' A French general remarked: 'C'est magnifique, mais ce n'est pas la guerre.' Tennyson wrote 'The Charge of the Light Brigade' in a matter of minutes. Florence Nightingale at Scutari Hospital reduced mortality from 42 to 2 percent – and became the founder of modern nursing; 'cardigan' and 'raglan' remained names for clothing.
level.light_brigade.goal: A vague order sends six hundred horsemen against cannons – and a woman with a lamp saves the wounded
level.light_brigade.hint: The order will pass through an impetuous adjutant and be misunderstood — no one will question it. The Brigade will charge and be broken. And the broken in Scutari will be received by the lady with the lamp — all England will love her.
level.light_brigade.intro: At Balaklava, the Russians are carrying off captured Turkish guns. Lord Raglan, from a height, sees this and writes an order: 'attack and prevent the removal of the guns.' Below, in the valley, Cardigan sees only a Russian battery at the end of the valley – and on the flanks too.
level.light_brigade.source: W. Russell, 'The Times' reports, 1854; Cecil Woodham-Smith, 'The Reason Why'
level.light_brigade.title: The Charge of the Light Brigade
level.lionheart.fact: In December 1192, Richard the Lionheart, returning from Palestine disguised as a merchant, was recognized in an inn near Vienna – by legend, by an expensive ring – and Duke Leopold of Austria imprisoned him in Dürnstein Castle. Emperor Henry VI set a ransom of 150,000 silver marks – double England's annual income; Eleanor of Aquitaine raised it, even taxing church chalices. John, meanwhile, offered the French king money to keep Richard imprisoned longer. Returning in 1194, Richard forgave his brother: 'You are a child who has fallen into bad company.' Five years later, he died from a crossbow bolt beneath a minor castle in Limousin – and John became king.
level.lionheart.goal: The captive king is ransomed by his mother – and he forgives his conspiring brother
level.lionheart.hint: The Duke recognizes the king in an inn and imprisons him. The mother pays the ransom – the bribed Duke will release him. The king does not wage war or litigate with his brother: he speaks with him, and the brother yields.
level.lionheart.intro: Richard returns alone from the Crusade, disguised, through the lands of Duke Leopold, whom he had insulted at Acre. In England, his brother John is already negotiating with the French king, while his mother, Eleanor, raises money.
level.lionheart.source: Roger of Hoveden, 'Chronica'; Ralph of Coggeshall
level.lionheart.title: The King in the Inn
level.livingstone.fact: On November 10, 1871, after eight months of travel, Henry Morton Stanley entered Ujiji village on Lake Tanganyika and, seeing the only white man, doffed his hat: 'Dr. Livingstone, I presume?' – a phrase he may have later invented for his book (the diary pages for that day are torn out). Livingstone refused to return to England and died in Africa a year and a half later; his servants removed his heart, buried it under a tree, and carried his body to the coast for nine months. Stanley himself later became an explorer of the Congo – and one of the perpetrators of its horrors in the service of the Belgian king.
level.livingstone.goal: A reporter finds a lost missionary – and cannot bring him home
level.livingstone.hint: A newspaper assignment and a caravan – that is the preparation. Then the meeting in Ujiji and three words the world remembered. Persuading him to return is useless: the missionary has greater conviction, he will not yield.
level.livingstone.intro: Missionary David Livingstone disappeared in Africa six years ago – searching for the source of the Nile. The 'New York Herald' sends reporter Stanley to find him: not for Livingstone's sake, but for circulation.
level.livingstone.source: H. M. Stanley, 'How I Found Livingstone'; T. Jeal, 'Stanley'
level.livingstone.title: Dr. Livingstone, I Presume?
level.lomonosov.fact: In December 1730 the nineteen-year-old Mikhail Lomonosov left the country near Kholmogory with a fish convoy, and in January 1731 entered the Slavic Greek Latin Academy in Moscow, calling himself the son of a Kholmogory nobleman: the children of peasants were not taken there. He studied among schoolboys, living on three copecks a day, and was then sent to St Petersburg, to Christian Wolff at Marburg and on to Freiberg. In 1741 he came back, and in 1745 became the first Russian professor of chemistry. The Academy's chancery was run by Councillor Johann Daniel Schumacher, and in 1743, for a quarrel with the academicians, Lomonosov spent almost eight months under arrest. In 1748 he built the first chemical laboratory in Russia; in 1755, to his design and through the efforts of the empress's favorite Ivan Shuvalov, Moscow University opened — with three faculties and teaching in Russian. Pushkin later wrote that Lomonosov 'was himself our first university'.
level.lomonosov.goal: The Pomor walks all the way to the Academy, runs up against the chancery — and comes out of it through a favorite, with a university in his hands
level.lomonosov.hint: First the convoy: the Pomor becomes a schoolboy. The chancery squeezes the schoolboy — under arrest and without pay. A curator with a plan for a university pulls the squeezed man out. The ode of praise is not needed: a man who has been bought submits no plans.
level.lomonosov.intro: The nineteen-year-old son of a Pomor fisherman leaves Kholmogory with a convoy of frozen fish — seven hundred versts, to go and study. The academy will admit him only if he lies about his birth. And at the St Petersburg Academy of Sciences a chancery awaits him where a Russian name is unwelcome.
level.lomonosov.source: A. Pushkin, 'A Journey from Moscow to St Petersburg'; E. Lebedev, 'Lomonosov'
level.lomonosov.title: The Fish Convoy
level.lorenzo_naples.fact: In December 1479 Lorenzo de' Medici sailed unescorted to Naples to see Ferrante I — the pope's ally, then at war with Florence. He gambled that the king would rather have a weakened but independent Florence than a stronger pope. For three months Lorenzo lived at court, ransoming Christian captives out of his own purse and showering gifts on courtiers — and in March 1480 he left with peace. Florence greeted him as a saviour; Machiavelli later called the journey a model of political courage. A few months afterwards the Turks landed at Otranto and the pope had no time left for Florence — Lorenzo's excommunication was lifted.
level.lorenzo_naples.goal: The Florentine puts himself in his enemy's hands — and three months later sails home from Naples with peace
level.lorenzo_naples.hint: The pope moves his army first — the city is under siege. The besieged Florentine sails to Naples alone, a hostage with standing. The king keeps his guest at court for three months and gives way. Hiring condottieri is pointless: a man who has been bought sails nowhere.
level.lorenzo_naples.intro: After the Pazzi conspiracy Pope Sixtus IV excommunicated Lorenzo and marched papal and Neapolitan troops on Florence. The city is exhausted and has no allies. And so Lorenzo secretly boards a ship for Ferrante of Aragon — a king who poisoned his guests and kept the mummies of his enemies in a cellar.
level.lorenzo_naples.source: N. Machiavelli, Florentine Histories, VIII; C. Hibbert, The House of Medici
level.lorenzo_naples.title: Lorenzo Sails to Naples
level.lucretia.fact: In 509 BC, Sextus Tarquinius dishonored Lucretia, wife of Collatinus. She made her relatives swear vengeance and stabbed herself before their eyes. The oath over her body was taken by Lucius Junius Brutus, who for years had feigned idiocy to survive at court (the nickname Brutus itself means 'dullard') — he roused Rome, expelled the Tarquins, and became one of the first consuls. 465 years later, his descendant Marcus Brutus would plunge a dagger into Caesar, and the conspirators would directly invoke this example.
level.lucretia.goal: The dishonor of one matron transforms Rome into a republic.
level.lucretia.hint: The oath is sworn over the dishonored – and only by him whom the king has not bought. A speech without an oath behind it is just words.
level.lucretia.intro: The Tarquins have ruled Rome for a quarter-century, and people have learned to tolerate them. But the king has a son, accustomed to never being refused, and at court lives the king's nephew, whom everyone considers a harmless fool.
level.lucretia.title: Expulsion of the Kings
level.lucrezia.fact: Lucrezia Borgia was married off three times by her father and brother for political alliances; one husband, deemed superfluous, was strangled. Rumor attributed poisons and debauchery to her—likely slander from the family's enemies.
level.lucrezia.goal: The Pope marries off his daughter for political gain
level.lucrezia.hint: Let the Pope first negotiate a marriage alliance — and only the betrothed Lucrezia will be led to the altar. Giulia, the mistress, is not given in marriage.
level.lucrezia.intro: The Pope trades his daughter's hand like a bargaining chip. Lucrezia is a pawn in the great game of alliances.
level.lucrezia.title: Child of Politics
level.machiavelli.fact: In September 1512, the Medici returned to Florence with Spanish pikes; on November 7, Machiavelli was dismissed and forbidden to leave. In February 1513, his name was found on a list of conspirators, Boscoli and Capponi: six hoistings on the rack — he confessed nothing and, in his own words, 'endured it in such a way that I respect myself.' Giovanni de' Medici became Pope Leo X; by amnesty, Niccolò was released and exiled to the estate of Sant'Andrea in Percussina. There, as he wrote to Vettori, during the day he caught thrushes and played backgammon in the tavern, and in the evening he donned courtly robes and 'entered the ancient courts of ancient men' — thus, in a few months, 'The Prince' was born, dedicated to Lorenzo de' Medici the Younger. The book was not printed during his lifetime; the Medici never gave him a position.
level.machiavelli.goal: The Republic falls, the secretary is tortured on the rack and exiled to the countryside — where he writes a book by which men will rule for five hundred years.
level.machiavelli.hint: The Medici return first — Duke Giuliano rules, and he is against the secretary. The Medici torture the secretary on suspicion — condemned, broken, exiled. The broken exile writes The Prince at Albergaccio. Asking for a post: a man who gives in is not tortured, but there is no book either.
level.machiavelli.intro: For fourteen years, Niccolò Machiavelli is secretary of the Florentine Republic: embassies, militia, dispatches. In 1512, the Spanish sack Prato, the Republic falls, the Medici return — the city is ruled by Giuliano, brother of Cardinal Giovanni. The secretary is left without service — and without protection.
level.machiavelli.source: Machiavelli's letter to Francesco Vettori of December 10, 1513; R. Ridolfi, 'The Life of Niccolò Machiavelli'
level.machiavelli.title: The Prince
level.magna_carta.fact: On June 15, 1215, in the meadow of Runnymede by the Thames, John affixed his seal to the Magna Carta: no one can be arrested or deprived of property except by law and the judgment of their peers, taxes – with the consent of the council. Already in August, Pope Innocent III, at the king's request, declared the charter invalid as having been extorted by force – and the Barons' War began, during which John died of dysentery, losing his baggage train in The Wash. The Charter was reissued by his young son, and it outlived everyone: three of its articles are still in force in English law today.
level.magna_carta.goal: The king signs the charter – and in the same year achieves its annulment
level.magna_carta.hint: The barons must gather strength – then they will have leverage, and the king will yield in the meadow. The king will achieve nothing with a speech against the barons. And then he will ask the Pope – and the Pope will annul the charter.
level.magna_carta.intro: John lost Normandy, quarreled with the Pope, and extorted money from the barons for a war he also lost. The barons, led by Fitzwalter, took London. Archbishop Langton suggests: let the king sign the charter.
level.magna_carta.source: Roger of Wendover, 'Flores Historiarum'; text of Magna Carta, 1215
level.magna_carta.title: Runnymede
level.manzikert.fact: On 26 August 1071 Romanos IV Diogenes met Alp Arslan at Manzikert. The emperor had sent half his army to the fortress of Khliat, while the Seljuks avoided a pitched fight and struck at the flanks. Towards evening Romanos ordered a turn back to camp; the rearguard under Andronikos Doukas announced that the emperor had been killed and led the troops off the field. Romanos fought on, was wounded and taken prisoner — the only such case in the empire's history. Alp Arslan, by the accounts, set his foot on the emperor's neck, then sat him down beside him, entertained him as a guest for eight days, concluded a treaty and released him for ransom. At home he had already been deposed: Romanos lost the civil war, was blinded and died in 1072 of the infection. The battle itself was no catastrophe in casualties — the catastrophe was what followed: in ten years of turmoil the Seljuks occupied nearly all of Asia Minor, and twenty years later the empire would have to call the West for help.
level.manzikert.goal: The rearguard walks off the field announcing that the emperor is dead — and a basileus is taken prisoner by a Muslim for the first time
level.manzikert.hint: First the march — the army is assembled, the emperor is strong. While he is strong the field cannot be lost: the rearguard must first announce that he has been killed and lead its men away. Weakened, he gives battle against the strong sultan — and is beaten. The victor lets the beaten man go. The fortress of Khliat is attrition: it was the siege by half the army that ruined the campaign.
level.manzikert.intro: The empire is rich and still thinks itself the leading power in the world, but its eastern themes are being eaten away by Seljuk raids. Romanos IV is a soldier who married the widowed empress, and the Doukas clan cannot stomach him. On his third campaign he leads a huge army that is not his own; the rearguard is commanded by the late emperor's nephew.
level.manzikert.source: Michael Attaleiates, 'History'; Nikephoros Bryennios, 'Material for History'
level.manzikert.title: Manzikert
level.marat.fact: On July 13, 1793, the Girondist Charlotte Corday stabbed Jean-Paul Marat in his bath, where he was immersed due to a skin condition. Four days later, Corday was guillotined. Marat's death was immortalized by Jacques-Louis David.
level.marat.goal: Charlotte Corday kills Marat — and ascends the scaffold
level.marat.hint: The assassin is a Girondist, the victim is Marat in the bath. The captured assassin is executed by the one with weight.
level.marat.title: The Death of Marat
level.marco_polo.fact: Marco Polo left Venice in 1271 and reached Khanbaliq (Beijing) in 1275; Kublai took him into his service and for seventeen years sent him on missions across China, Burma and India. The Polos came home in 1295 with gems sewn into the linings of their clothes. In 1298 Marco was taken prisoner by the Genoese after a sea battle, and there his cellmate, the romance writer Rustichello da Pisa, wrote down his Book of the Marvels of the World. Europe did not believe it: they called him Messer Milione, for the millions in every story. On his deathbed, so the tale goes, he was asked to recant his inventions and answered: "I have not told half of what I saw." Columbus carried a copy annotated in the margins.
level.marco_polo.goal: The Venetian serves the Khan for seventeen years — and dictates the book of his wonders in a Genoese prison
level.marco_polo.hint: The Silk Road first — the journey makes him strong. The Khan takes the strong traveller into his service: now he is an envoy. In prison a scribe cellmate writes the envoy's story down. Coming home rich instead — and there is no book.
level.marco_polo.intro: A seventeen-year-old Venetian sets out east with his father and uncle — across Persia, the Pamirs and the Taklamakan desert. The road takes three and a half years. At the end of it is the court of Kublai Khan, grandson of Genghis, ruler of the largest empire on earth.
level.marco_polo.source: Marco Polo, The Travels; J. Larner, Marco Polo and the Discovery of the World
level.marco_polo.title: The Book of Wonders
level.marie_louise.fact: The divorce from Joséphine was formalized on 15 December 1809: both spouses read out prepared speeches, and Joséphine could not finish hers. On 11 March 1810 a marriage by proxy took place in Vienna with the eighteen-year-old Marie Louise, grand-niece of Marie Antoinette; on 27 March Napoleon, unable to endure the ceremonial, intercepted her carriage in the rain on the road to Compiègne. On 20 March 1811 a son was born: Paris knew that a daughter was due twenty-one guns and a son a hundred and one, and after the twenty-second shot the city cried out. The boy was titled King of Rome. On 29 March 1814 Marie Louise left Paris with her son for Blois and then for Vienna; she did not go to Elba, received the duchy of Parma from the congress and went to live with Count Neipperg. Napoleon never saw his wife and son again after January 1814. The son, Duke of Reichstadt, the 'Eaglet', died of tuberculosis at Schönbrunn on 22 July 1832, twenty-one years old.
level.marie_louise.goal: For an heir he trades his wife for an Austrian, Paris counts a hundred and one guns — and three years later the mother carries the son off to Vienna for good
level.marie_louise.hint: First the divorce: without it there will be no heir. The man left without an heir meets his Austrian bride. Married to a Habsburg, he gets his son — count the guns. And only the heir's mother can carry him off to his grandfather, leaving the emperor alone. Malmaison is a trap: a wife who has already left will not be divorced.
level.marie_louise.intro: The empire needs an heir, and his wife is forty-six and will have no more children. The divorce is staged as an act of state: both weep, both sign. Three months later the matchmakers ride to Vienna — for the grand-niece of the queen whose head France cut off.
level.marie_louise.source: The memoirs of C.-F. de Méneval; A. Castelot, 'Napoleon'
level.marie_louise.title: A Hundred and One Guns
level.marius.fact: In 107 BC, Gaius Marius, a 'new man' without consular ancestors, for the first time recruited legions from the propertyless, who were not supposed to serve. The state gave them weapons, and the general was expected to secure land for them after the war — thus, soldiers became loyal to a man, not the Republic. Jugurtha, defeated but not captured, was handed over in 105 BC by his father-in-law, Bocchus, the king of Mauretania — and negotiations with him were conducted not by Marius, but by his quaestor Sulla. Sulla later had this scene engraved on his signet ring; Marius never forgave him for it.
level.marius.goal: Jugurtha in chains, the army — personal, but the quaestor claims the glory.
level.marius.hint: Do not go to the Senate for command — they will condemn you. Raise your own army and defeat the king. His father-in-law, the king of Mauretania, will hand him over — to whoever pays; and the glory will go to the payer, not the victor.
level.marius.intro: The war in Numidia drags on for years: King Jugurtha buys off Roman commanders faster than they can be sent. And legions are recruited only from those with property — and there are fewer and fewer such men.
level.marius.title: The Army of the Destitute
level.marriage.fact: Theodora, daughter of a bear-keeper and a former actress, captivated Justinian. For the sake of marrying her, he secured the repeal of a law that forbade senators from marrying actresses. She became one of the most influential women in history.
level.marriage.goal: Justinian marries the former actress Theodora
level.marriage.hint: First, change the law, elevating Theodora to patrician status — and only then lead her to the altar. Do not mistake the bride.
level.marriage.intro: Justinian fell in love with Theodora — an actress, daughter of a bear-keeper. But ancient law forbade nobles from marrying actresses.
level.marriage.title: Actress on the Throne
level.mary_stuart.fact: Mary, Queen of Scots, the deposed Queen of Scotland, was Elizabeth's prisoner for 19 years and the focal point of Catholic conspiracies. Francis Walsingham's spy network intercepted her encrypted letters, which approved the Babington Plot against Elizabeth. The court sentenced Mary to death; she was beheaded in 1587.
level.mary_stuart.goal: Walsingham exposes Mary, Queen of Scots — trial and scaffold.
level.mary_stuart.hint: A forged postscript to a letter — and the conspiring queen is condemned by her own hand. She is executed by the one who holds authority and a crown.
level.mary_stuart.intro: Mary, Queen of Scots, prisoner and claimant, weaves a plot against Elizabeth. The spy Walsingham reads her letters.
level.mary_stuart.title: Mary Stuart
level.masaniello.fact: On 7 July 1647 Masaniello overturned a basket of fruit in the Naples market — and within hours forty thousand people were in the streets. The rebels burned the tax farmers' houses, the viceroy the Duke of Arcos fled to a castle, and a week later signed an agreement abolishing the taxes and granting an amnesty. For ten days Masaniello effectively ruled Naples: he went about in gold brocade, judged and pardoned from a balcony, ordered executions on suspicion. By 16 July he was raving and screaming at his own men; his own companions shot him, beheaded the body and threw it into a ditch. The next day, when bread went up again, the crowd found the body, sewed the head back on and buried him like a sovereign. The revolt dragged on for another year.
level.masaniello.goal: A fisherman raises the city, the viceroy gives in — and ten days later power drives the fisherman mad
level.masaniello.hint: The fruit tax first: the fisherman raises the city and becomes a force. The rising — the viceroy is beaten. The victor bargains the taxes away from the beaten man. And then ten days of power: an alliance with the viceroy ends in madness. Sheltering in the castle is not his story.
level.masaniello.intro: Spanish Naples is taxed so heavily that even fruit — the food of the poor — is dutiable. In the market a twenty-seven-year-old fish seller, Tommaso Aniello, known as Masaniello, overturns a basket of figs.
level.masaniello.source: G. Donzelli, Chronicle of the Neapolitan Revolt; P. Burke, Popular Culture
level.masaniello.title: Masaniello's Ten Days
level.massacre.fact: Belisarius and Mundus trapped the rebels in the Hippodrome and orchestrated a massacre—according to accounts, up to 30,000 people perished. The Nika Revolt was drowned in blood, and Justinian's throne was saved.
level.massacre.goal: Belisarius Drowns the Revolt in Blood
level.massacre.hint: Let Narses bribe the Blues with gold — and only then will Belisarius (or Mundus) trap and crush the divided mob. Without bribery, the rebellion cannot be broken.
level.massacre.intro: The mob proclaimed Hypatius and filled the Hippodrome. To assault them head-on is suicide. First, they must be divided.
level.massacre.title: Massacre at the Hippodrome
level.menshikov.fact: Alexander Danilovich Menshikov, according to legend, sold pies in his youth; in 1686, he became Peter's orderly, went with him to Azov, Narva, and Poltava, received the titles of Serene Prince (the only Russian to become a Prince of the Holy Roman Empire), Generalissimo, and Governor of St. Petersburg. He was also the first embezzler: the investigation of 1714–1718 counted one and a half million rubles in embezzlement — out of a country's budget of ten million. Peter beat him with a club, fined him, but did not let him go: 'He was conceived in iniquity, born in sin, and will end his life in roguery.' Menshikov was illiterate — he could only sign his own name. After Peter's death, he effectively ruled under Catherine I.
level.menshikov.goal: The Tsar elevates his pie-seller friend, catches him stealing — and, after beating him, keeps him by his side
level.menshikov.hint: First, the Tsar's friendship with the pie-seller — they are allies. The Tsar bestows a title upon his ally — Serene Prince, with authority. The Serene Prince steals — guilty. The Tsar beats his guilty friend with a club and forgives him. There's no reason to put him on trial — he is not condemned.
level.menshikov.intro: The son of a stableman, who sold pies, became the young Tsar's orderly, then — his first friend, a commander, Serene Prince, and the wealthiest man in the empire. And the most thieving.
level.menshikov.source: N. Pavlenko, 'Menshikov'; notes of Just Juel
level.menshikov.title: Half-Sovereign Lord
level.menshikov_fall.fact: In May 1727, Menshikov enthroned the eleven-year-old Peter II, betrothed him to his daughter Maria, and moved him to his residence on Vasilyevsky Island. That summer he fell ill, and the boy, set free, befriended Ivan Dolgoruky; on September 8, 1727, the Serene Prince was arrested, stripped of his ranks, and exiled — first to Ranenburg, then to Beryozov on the Ob, where he himself built a log house and a church and died in November 1729. His daughter Maria, the 'sovereign-bride,' died there as well. Peter II became engaged to Catherine Dolgorukaya — and died of smallpox in January 1730 on the day of his scheduled wedding; the Dolgorukys forged a will, were exposed, and also went to Beryozov, to Menshikov's house.
level.menshikov_fall.goal: The Serene Prince places a boy on the throne — and the boy, having played enough with the Dolgorukys, exiles him to Siberia
level.menshikov_fall.hint: First, the Serene Prince, with authority, proclaims the boy — he is crowned. The boy and Dolgoruky conspire during a hunt. Dolgoruky, with authority, denounces the Serene Prince — he is condemned. The condemned goes to Beryozov. The betrothal to Menshikov's daughter — a superfluous move.
level.menshikov_fall.intro: After Catherine I, the twelve-year-old Peter II — Peter's grandson — is on the throne. Menshikov places the boy on the throne, betroths him to his daughter, and keeps him in his palace. But the boy has new friends — the Dolgoruky princes, hunting, and a free life.
level.menshikov_fall.source: N. Pavlenko, 'Menshikov'; E. Anisimov, 'Russia Without Peter'
level.menshikov_fall.title: Beryozov
level.militia.fact: In the autumn of 1611, Kuzma Minin, the zemstvo elder of Nizhny Novgorod, called upon the people in the square 'to spare no effort' and donated a third of his property to the militia; citizens were levied with a 'fifth penny' tax. Prince Dmitry Pozharsky, recovering from wounds on his estate, was invited to be the military commander; he agreed on the condition that Minin would manage the treasury. From August 22–24, 1612, the militia fought for three days near the walls of Moscow against Hetman Chodkiewicz, who was bringing four hundred wagons of bread to the besieged Kremlin; at the decisive moment, Minin himself, with three hundred noblemen, attacked across the Moskva River. The Hetman retreated, losing his baggage train; the starving Polish garrison in the Kremlin surrendered on October 26. Both became proverbial figures and stand on the monument near the Kremlin — Moscow's first sculptural monument.
level.militia.goal: The butcher collects the treasury, the wounded prince gathers an army, and the Hetman leaves Moscow with nothing.
level.militia.hint: First, Minin's call — the treasury is collected, the elder gains influence. Pozharsky is called to be the military commander for the treasury — now the prince has an army. A strong commander with influence defeats the Hetman near the walls of Moscow. Waiting in Yaroslavl means being too late.
level.militia.intro: A Polish garrison occupies the Kremlin, there is no Tsar, and the first militia has fallen apart and dispersed. In Nizhny Novgorod, the zemstvo elder, meat merchant Kuzma Minin, addresses the square. Hetman Chodkiewicz, with a baggage train, is marching towards Moscow to relieve the Poles.
level.militia.source: 'New Chronicler'; S. Platonov, 'Essays on the History of the Time of Troubles'
level.militia.title: Minin and Pozharsky
level.minister.fact: John the Cappadocian, Justinian's all-powerful finance minister, extorted exorbitant taxes from the people. His greed and cruelty made him the most hated man in Constantinople—and one of the causes of the revolt.
