level.scipio_spain.hint: A city is taken by the might of legions. But a captive cannot be loved: an enamored victor will not give her up. Return her to her betrothed — and the betrothed will bring horsemen who will make you more than a general.
level.scipio_spain.intro: Young Scipio took New Carthage — the capital of Carthaginian Spain — in a single day. Among the captives is a girl of rare beauty, the betrothed of the Iberian chieftain Allucius. Soldiers bring her to the victor as a gift.
level.scipio_spain.source: Livy, 'The History of Rome', XXVI, 49–50; Polybius, X, 18–19
level.scipio_spain.title: The Magnanimity of Scipio
level.scipio_trial.fact: In 187 BC, at Cato's instigation, the Scipio brothers were accused of embezzling money received from King Antiochus. Africanus, according to tradition, came forth with his accounts, tore them up before the judges, and declared: 'On this day, I defeated Hannibal at Zama — let us go to the Capitol to thank the gods,' — and the people followed him, leaving the accusers alone. He never returned to Rome: he retired to his estate in Liternum and ordered himself to be buried there, not in the ungrateful city. According to Livy, he commanded to have inscribed on his tomb: 'Ungrateful homeland, you shall not have even my bones.'
level.scipio_trial.goal: The victor over Hannibal tears up his accounts — and leaves Rome forever.
level.scipio_trial.hint: The accusation will be made — and he will be on trial. A counter-speech won't save him: he will simply remind the people what day it is, and tear up the papers. And then he will leave the city and never return.
level.scipio_trial.intro: Cato and his men accuse the victor over Hannibal of appropriating money received from Antiochus. Scipio Africanus is summoned to trial — with his accounts in hand.
level.scipio_trial.title: The Trial of Scipio
level.secession.fact: In 494 BC, plebeians burdened by debt simply left Rome for the Sacred Mount beyond the Anio — without rebellion or weapons: the city was left without hands and without soldiers. The Senate sent Menenius Agrippa, who, according to Livy, told a fable about how the body's members rebelled against the 'idle stomach' and became powerless themselves. The plebeians returned, having gained tribunes of the plebs — an office with veto power and personal inviolability. This was the first instance in Roman history when power yielded to a strike.
level.secession.goal: The plebeians gain their tribunes without drawing a sword.
level.secession.hint: As long as the plebeians are in the city, they have no leverage. You cannot negotiate with every patrician – you won't negotiate with a conspirator.
level.secession.intro: Debt in Rome is paid not with money, but with oneself: if you don't pay, you go into servitude to the creditor. This is how half the city lives: plebeians toil and fight, but have no voice in the Senate. Sicinius leads them, and they have no weapons — only their hands, without which the city cannot stand.
level.secession.title: Secession to the Sacred Mount
level.sejanus.fact: From 26 AD, Tiberius lived on Capri, leaving Rome to Aelius Sejanus — the Praetorian prefect, who had secured for himself almost imperial honors. In October 31 AD, Consul Memmius Regulus read a letter from the island in the Senate: long and convoluted, it praised Sejanus for a long time and only at the end demanded his arrest. While it was being read, Macro had already replaced the guard at the building. Sejanus was led directly from the Curia and executed the same day; the senators, who had just risen to greet him, tore down his statues.
level.sejanus.goal: The all-powerful prefect falls by a single letter read aloud.
level.sejanus.hint: As long as the Guard is loyal to the prefect, no accusation will reach him. First, quietly transfer its loyalty to Macro — and let him stand in the Curia next to Consul Regulus when the latter finishes reading the letter.
level.sejanus.intro: Tiberius long ago left for Capri and rules by letters. In Rome, the prefect of the Guard, Sejanus, runs everything: he executed whom he wished and already aims to be heir. The Emperor was the last to realize this.
level.sejanus.title: Letter from Capri
level.sertorius.fact: From 80–72 BC, Sertorius, a Marian exile, established a 'second Rome' in Spain with a senate and schools for the children of Iberian nobility. He presented a white doe, gifted to him by a peasant, as a messenger from Diana and proclaimed 'prophecies' through it — thus he held sway over the superstitious Iberians. At Sucro in 75 BC, he defeated Pompey himself. In 72 BC, Perperna, a noble officer who envied the upstart leader, killed him at a banquet. Pompey, upon receiving the conspirators' papers with letters from Roman senators, burned them unread — and executed Perperna.
level.sertorius.goal: He whom Pompey could not defeat is killed at the table by his own men.
level.sertorius.hint: Sertorius' strength is not legions, but the faith of the Iberians: the doe must be accepted. Then he defeats even Pompey. But he will be killed not by an enemy, but by his own officer — at a banquet.
level.sertorius.intro: Quintus Sertorius, the last of the Marians, holds Spain against Rome for eight years at the head of the Iberians. The Iberians believe that a white doe, gifted to him, whispers to him the will of Diana. Pompey is sent against him.
level.sertorius.title: The White Doe
level.sevastopol.fact: On November 18 (30), 1853, Nakhimov's squadron burned the Turkish fleet in Sinop Bay in three hours — the last great battle of sailing ships. In London and Paris, it was called the «Sinop massacre,» and in March 1854, England and France declared war on Russia. In September, the allies landed in Crimea; Nakhimov, Kornilov, and Totleben surrounded Sevastopol with bastions in a month, and scuttled the fleet at the bay's entrance. The defense lasted 349 days; Kornilov died on Malakhov Kurgan on the first day of bombardment. Nakhimov, who walked along the bastions in admiral's epaulets, died there on June 28 (July 10), 1855, from a rifle bullet to the temple. Nicholas I died in February, not living to see the city's fall; Tolstoy described the siege in «Sevastopol Sketches.»
level.sevastopol.goal: The admiral wins — and this victory brings about a siege, in which he perishes on a bastion
level.sevastopol.hint: First, Sinop — the victorious admiral with power. Allies land — strength. Siege: a strong ally bombards the victor's bastions — the admiral is exhausted. The exhausted admiral still walks along the bastions under fire — Malakhov Kurgan. Breaking through to the sea — abandoning his city.
level.sevastopol.intro: Nicholas I decided that Turkey was the «sick man of Europe» and started a war. Nakhimov burned the Turkish fleet in Sinop — and thereby brought England and France to the Black Sea. Allies land in Crimea, the sailing fleet is scuttled at the bay's entrance, sailors went to the bastions; 349 days of siege lie ahead.
level.sevastopol.source: E. Tarle, «The Crimean War»; L. Tolstoy, «Sevastopol Sketches»
level.sevastopol.title: Sevastopol
level.shuisky_tsar.fact: In the summer of 1605, Vasily Shuisky was implicated in a conspiracy and sentenced to death; at Lobnoye Mesto, as he had already laid his head on the block, a messenger arrived with a pardon – False Dmitry replaced the execution with exile, and soon after returned him to court. On May 8, 1606, the Tsar married the Catholic Marina Mniszech, crowning her Tsarina – for the first time in Russian history; Poles in Moscow drank and rioted. At dawn on May 17, Shuisky and the boyars rang the alarm bell with the cry, «The Poles are beating the boyars!»; while the crowd cut down the Poles, the conspirators stormed the palace, the impostor jumped from a window, broke his leg, and was shot. For three days, the corpse lay on the square with a mask and a pipe, then it was burned, and its ashes were shot from a cannon towards Poland. On May 19, Shuisky was «proclaimed» Tsar on Red Square.
level.shuisky_tsar.goal: The boyar, pardoned on the block, raises Moscow in alarm – and himself ascends the impostor's throne.
level.shuisky_tsar.hint: Shuisky must be pardoned on the block – he cannot be executed, or there will be no one to rouse Moscow. The wedding with the Polish woman is the pretext. Then the alarm: a respected boyar rouses Moscow against the married impostor, who perishes, and the boyar gains the right to the crown. The coronation is at the end.
level.shuisky_tsar.intro: The impostor reigns. Prince Shuisky, implicated in a conspiracy, is sentenced to death and already stands at the block. From Poland comes the Tsar's bride – Marina Mniszech, accompanied by thousands of armed Poles.
level.shuisky_tsar.source: «Diary of Marina Mniszech»; R. Skrynnikov, «Vasily Shuisky»
level.shuisky_tsar.title: Wedding and Alarm Bell
level.simnel.fact: On May 24, 1487, in Dublin, Lambert Simnel was crowned 'Edward VI'; on June 16, at Stoke Field, Henry VII defeated the army of Yorkists and German landsknechts — the Earl of Lincoln died. This was the last battle of the Wars of the Roses. The king pardoned the boy and sent him to the palace kitchen to turn the spit; later, Simnel became a royal falconer and died a natural death around 1525. Henry even invited the Irish lords who had crowned the impostor to a feast, where Simnel himself served wine: 'My Irish lords, you will yet crown monkeys'.
level.simnel.goal: The impostor is crowned, defeated — and instead of the block, sent to turn the spit.
level.simnel.hint: A weighty guarantor crowns the boy in Dublin. At Stoke, a strong king will defeat him. And then the victor will send the defeated impostor to the kitchen: laughter is more useful than execution.
level.simnel.intro: Two years after Bosworth, a ten-year-old boy was crowned in Dublin as Edward VI — son of the Duke of Clarence. The real son of Clarence is in the Tower; the boy's name is Lambert Simnel, he is the son of a carpenter from Oxford, and behind him is the Earl of Lincoln, nephew of Richard III.
level.simnel.source: Polydore Vergil, 'Anglica Historia', XXVI; F. Bacon, 'The History of Henry VII'
level.simnel.title: The King in the Kitchen
level.sistine.fact: Michelangelo signed the contract for the ceiling fresco on May 10, 1508, considering it a trap set by Bramante — he was a sculptor and in his notes called painting 'not my craft.' He dismissed his assistants and spent four years painting the vault alone, standing on scaffolding of his own design with his head thrown back — in a sonnet, he complained that 'my beard points to heaven, my nape is on my hump, and the brush drips on my face.' Julius II impatiently climbed the scaffolding and once struck him with his staff; to the question 'when will you finish?' the artist replied: 'When I can.' On October 31, 1512, the chapel was opened: three hundred figures, 'The Creation of Adam' with two outstretched fingers. Twenty years later, he returned to paint 'The Last Judgment' on the altar wall.
level.sistine.goal: The Pope with his staff forces the sculptor to take up a brush — and four years later, five hundred meters of fresco adorn the chapel.
level.sistine.hint: First, the Pope with influence summons the artist — he yields. The artist builds scaffolding — strength. The yielding and strong artist under the ceiling with the Pope — a masterpiece. Fleeing to Florence — he already fled, the Pope brought him back.
level.sistine.intro: Warrior-Pope Julius II — Giuliano della Rovere — commissioned his tomb from the sculptor Michelangelo, then changed his mind and ordered him to paint the ceiling of the Sistine Chapel. The sculptor hates painting, suspects a plot by Bramante, and once already fled from the Pope to Florence.
level.sistine.source: G. Vasari, 'Lives of the Artists'; A. Condivi, 'The Life of Michelangelo'
level.sistine.title: The Ceiling
level.sloboda.fact: On 3 December 1564 Ivan IV rode out of Moscow with the treasury, the icons, his whole family and a picked guard; after a month of moving about he appeared at Alexandrov Sloboda. On 3 January 1565 two charters were brought to the capital. In the first, to the clergy and the boyars, the tsar listed their treasons and announced that he had 'left his realm'; in the second, to the merchants and townspeople, he wrote that he bore them no anger or disgrace whatever. Moscow came to a standstill: the chanceries stopped working, the shops shut, the crowd demanded that the sovereign be brought back and the traitors handed over. A delegation headed by Pimen, archbishop of Novgorod, set out for the Sloboda. Ivan agreed to return on two conditions: to execute traitors at his own will, and to establish the Oprichnina — a domain of his own with an army of his own. In February 1565 the Oprichnina was proclaimed. Five years later that same Pimen was accused of treason, carried off from a devastated Novgorod, and died in confinement.
level.sloboda.goal: The tsar walks out of his capital, splits wrath and mercy between two charters — and comes back stronger than he left
level.sloboda.hint: First the convoy: the tsar leaves with the treasury. From the Sloboda two charters go out at once — disgrace for the boyar, mercy for the townsfolk. Then the bishop rides out to plead with him, and the tsar, beloved of the town, returns. The Lithuanian border is Kurbsky's road, not his.
level.sloboda.intro: On 3 December 1564 the tsar carried the treasury, the icons and his whole family out of the Kremlin and went off no one knew where. For a month there was no word of him. Then two letters came from Alexandrov Sloboda — and it turned out that the country had been left without a sovereign by his own will.
level.sloboda.source: The Pskov Chronicle; R. Skrynnikov, 'Ivan the Terrible'
level.sloboda.title: Two Charters
level.south_sea.fact: In 1720, South Sea Company shares rose from 128 to 1050 pounds in six months — everyone bought, from Isaac Newton (who lost 20,000 and said he could calculate the motion of the stars, but not the madness of men) to chambermaids. By autumn, they crashed to 150. Robert Walpole, who had sold his shares in time, saved the government and the king from investigation — earning him the nickname 'The Screen' — and for twenty years became the first Prime Minister in history. The word 'bubble' in the stock market sense dates from then.
level.south_sea.goal: The first stock market bubble bursts — and England's first Prime Minister is born from its wreckage.
level.south_sea.hint: First, the bubble must inflate, then it will burst — otherwise, there's no one to save. Walpole, with a speech in Parliament, shields the guilty: he will be lauded for it. The directors will not be hanged.
level.south_sea.intro: The South Sea Company undertook to buy up England's national debt in exchange for a trade monopoly it barely possessed. Its director, John Blunt, knew one thing: how to make shares rise. Half of Parliament were already shareholders.
level.south_sea.source: J. Carswell, 'The South Sea Bubble'; C. Mackay, 'Extraordinary Popular Delusions and the Madness of Crowds'
level.south_sea.title: The South Sea Bubble
level.spartacus.fact: In 73 BC, about seventy gladiators escaped from a school in Capua, armed with kitchen knives, and for two years defeated consular armies. Marcus Crassus reinstated decimation in his troops — the execution of every tenth man by lot in a disgraced cohort, a custom forgotten for centuries. Spartacus died in battle, his body was not found; six thousand captives were crucified along the Appian Way from Capua to Rome. Pompey, returning from Spain, intercepted the surviving fugitives and wrote to the Senate that he had ended the war with the slaves — the triumph went to him, Crassus received only an ovation.
level.spartacus.goal: The rebellion is crushed – and the laurels do not go to another
level.spartacus.hint: A rebellion is a conspiracy of two in a school. An army that fled from slaves must first be strengthened by decimation. Do not let a third man near the road.
level.spartacus.intro: Seventy men with kitchen knives escaped from a gladiatorial school in Capua. Two years later, they are defeating consular armies. Crassus is tasked with suppressing them — who remembers that Pompey always manages to appear next to someone else's victory.
level.spartacus.title: Crosses Along the Road
level.speransky.fact: Mikhail Speransky, son of a priest from Vladimir Governorate, by 1809 became State Secretary and presented to Alexander I «Introduction to the Code of State Laws» — a plan for an elected Duma, an independent judiciary, and a State Council. He introduced exams for rank, which turned all officialdom against him. Karamzin presented the tsar with «A Note on Ancient and Modern Russia» against the reforms, and courtiers whispered that the reformer was a French spy. On March 17, 1812, after a two-hour audience, Speransky was taken away that same night to Nizhny Novgorod, then to Perm; the emperor said: «They have taken my right hand.» Four years later, he was returned as governor to Penza, and under Nicholas I, he compiled the Code of Laws and judged the Decembrists.
level.speransky.goal: The priest's son writes a constitution for Russia — and in one night goes into exile under the whispers of the court
level.speransky.hint: First, the emperor's friendship with the priest's son — allies. The reformer writes a plan — strength. Arakcheev with influence whispers — the reformer is condemned. The condemned goes to Nizhny. Dueling Arakcheev — not his style.
level.speransky.intro: The son of a rural priest became the emperor's right hand and wrote a plan for a constitution: State Duma, separation of powers, exams for rank. The nobility is furious, Arakcheev is jealous, and the reformer's French language is passed off as treason.
level.speransky.source: M. Korf, «The Life of Count Speransky»; N. Eidelman
level.speransky.title: Speransky's Disgrace
level.spider_king.fact: In October 1468 Louis XI came to Péronne to see Charles the Bold almost without escort — and that same day news arrived that Liège had risen, stirred up by the king's own agents. The duke shut the king in a tower, kept him there several days, made him sign a ruinous treaty and ride with him to subdue Liège — wearing the Burgundian cross on his sleeve and watching his own allies burned out. After that the king made war with money: he paid the Swiss cantons yearly subsidies and pushed Lorraine against Burgundy. In 1476 the Swiss infantry beat Charles at Grandson and Murten, and on 5 January 1477 he was killed at Nancy; the body was found two days later in a frozen pond, stripped and disfigured — he was identified by old scars and missing teeth. Louis carved up the Burgundian inheritance, and Philippe de Commynes, who had gone over from the duke to the king, called him 'the universal spider'.
level.spider_king.goal: The king gets out of the trap by way of humiliation, buys other men's pikes — and the duke is found in a ditch at Nancy
level.spider_king.hint: First Péronne: the duke locks up his guest, and the king is a prisoner. The prisoner is made to ride against Liège; he comes out of that journey slyer than he went in. The sly man pays the Swiss, and the pikes are his. Only bought pikes can reach the man who believed in his own strength. The Burgundian treasury is a trap: Swiss who have been bought away can no longer be hired.
level.spider_king.intro: The Duke of Burgundy is richer than his king, dresses in gold and dreams of a crown between France and Germany. The king wears a shabby hat hung with pewter badges, pays his spies better than his soldiers, and is called 'the universal spider'. The duke invites the king to a private meeting at Péronne — and the king goes.
level.spider_king.source: P. de Commynes, 'Memoirs'; J. Calmette, 'The Great Dukes of Burgundy'
level.spider_king.title: The Spider and the Bold
level.st_bartholomew.fact: On the night of August 24, 1572, six days after the wedding of Henry of Navarre and Margaret of Valois, at the tolling of the bell of Saint-Germain-l'Auxerrois, Huguenots began to be slaughtered in Paris: Admiral Coligny was thrown from a window, his body dragged through the streets. Within a week, five to thirty thousand were killed across France. Henry of Navarre was spared as the king's brother-in-law, forced to convert to Catholicism; four years later, he escaped and became a Huguenot again — and twenty-one years later, to take Paris, he converted to Catholicism for the third time: "Paris is worth a mass." Who exactly gave the order — Catherine, King Charles IX, or the Guises — is still debated.
level.st_bartholomew.goal: A wedding of peace ends in massacre — and the groom is forced to change his faith.
level.st_bartholomew.hint: The Queen Mother rings the tocsin — and the Admiral is the first to die. The Navarrese cannot be killed: he is the Princess's husband. He is offered mass or death — with the weight of the massacre, he will yield.
level.st_bartholomew.intro: Paris celebrates the wedding of the Huguenot Henry of Navarre to the king's sister—peace after ten years of religious war. Catherine de' Medici, the Queen Mother, fears Admiral Coligny's influence over her son. Thousands of Huguenot nobles are in the city.
level.st_bartholomew.source: Agrippa d'Aubigné, 'Histoire Universelle'; A. Jouanna, 'The St. Bartholomew's Day Massacre'
level.st_bartholomew.title: St. Bartholomew's Day Massacre
level.st_helena.fact: On St. Helena, Napoleon lived five and a half years in the damp Longwood House under the supervision of Hudson Lowe, who refused to address him as anything but 'General Bonaparte' and cut his expenses; their quarrels made Lowe a villain of European scale. Napoleon dictated 'The Memorial of Saint Helena' to Count Las Cases—a version where he was a son of the revolution and a martyr for Europe; the book became a bestseller of the century. He died on May 5, 1821—from stomach cancer, like his father, or from arsenic, as is still debated. In 1840, his remains were returned to Paris, and a million people stood in the cold as he was brought to Les Invalides.
level.st_helena.goal: The jailer turns the prisoner into a martyr, and the prisoner dictates a legend that will outlive everyone.
level.st_helena.hint: First, exile across the ocean. The governor's petty guardianship turns the exile into a martyr—this works to his advantage. Then he dictates the Memorial: legend is stronger than truth. Fleeing to America is not part of this story.
level.st_helena.intro: After Waterloo, he surrendered to the British, hoping for honorable exile in England. He is taken to a rock in the middle of the Atlantic, two thousand kilometers from shore. Governor Hudson Lowe counts wine bottles and forbids calling him emperor.
level.st_helena.source: Las Cases, 'The Memorial of Saint Helena'; F. Masson, 'Napoleon on St. Helena'
level.st_helena.title: St. Helena
level.stanley_fall.fact: Sir William Stanley, whose intervention decided the outcome of Bosworth, was executed in 1495 for his connection with Perkin Warbeck — an impostor claiming to be Richard, Duke of York, the younger of the Princes in the Tower. He was accused of saying that he would not fight against Warbeck if he was indeed the son of Edward IV. Henry VII confiscated his fortune — about 40,000 pounds, the largest in the kingdom. Warbeck, once caught, was hanged in 1499. The lesson of the first Tudor: he who once defected can defect again — and the king did not wait to find out.
level.stanley_fall.goal: He who gave the crown loses his head for a single letter to an impostor.
level.stanley_fall.hint: Friendship with an impostor — that is treason. The influential king condemns the lord with a speech and executes him. Defecting a second time, as at Bosworth, will not be possible.
level.stanley_fall.intro: William Stanley placed the crown on Henry at Bosworth and became the wealthiest man in England. Ten years later, Perkin Warbeck appeared in Flanders, claiming to be the escaped prince from the Tower — and Stanley said that if it were true, he would not go against him.
level.stanley_fall.source: Polydore Vergil, 'Anglica Historia', XXVI; F. Bacon, 'History of Henry VII'
level.stanley_fall.title: The Fall of Stanley
level.strafford.fact: In 1641, Parliament, unable to prove the treason of Thomas Wentworth, Earl of Strafford, passed a Bill of Attainder against him — condemnation without trial. Crowds besieged Whitehall, demanding the head of 'Black Tom the Tyrant'. Strafford himself wrote to the King, releasing him from his promise; Charles I signed on May 10 — and, it is said, never forgave himself for it until the scaffold: 'I deserved to have my word false'. On May 12, Strafford was beheaded on Tower Hill before two hundred thousand spectators. A year later, the Civil War began.
level.strafford.goal: The King signs a death warrant for the man to whom he promised life.
level.strafford.hint: Pym, with authority, condemns the minister with a Bill of Attainder — without trial. Then persuade the King to sign: he will yield. Parliament will execute the condemned. If the King refuses — the mob will besiege the palace, and that will be another story.
level.strafford.intro: Earl Strafford ruled for the King for eleven years without Parliament — with an 'iron hand'. Now Parliament is assembled, and John Pym demands his head. The King promised Strafford that he would suffer 'neither in estate nor in life'.
level.strafford.source: Clarendon, 'History of the Rebellion'; C. Wedgwood, 'Thomas Wentworth'
level.strafford.title: The King's Servant
level.streltsy.fact: After suppressing the Streltsy Uprising of 1698, Peter I executed over a thousand Streltsy and disbanded their corps. This reprisal freed his hands for reforms and the creation of a regular army.
level.streltsy.goal: The young Tsar brutally suppresses the Streltsy rebellion.
level.streltsy.hint: Let Sophia's rebellion enrage Peter — and only the furious tsar will become an autocrat with an iron hand. Sophia will not take the throne.
level.streltsy.intro: While Peter strives for Europe, his sister Sophia raises the streltsy behind his back. The rebellion must be drowned in blood.
level.streltsy.title: The Streltsy Uprising
level.sudebnik.fact: On 21 June 1547 Moscow burned: about 1,700 people died, the Kremlin was gutted, the powder magazines exploded. Five days later a mob tore apart the tsar's kinsman Yuri Glinsky inside the Dormition Cathedral, and the archpriest Sylvester of the Annunciation came to the sixteen-year-old Ivan — with a direct rebuke, according to Kurbsky. It was then that Alexei Adashev rose, the son of a modest Kostroma gentleman: he was given the Petitions Chancery, where complaints came in from the whole land. Kurbsky later called this circle of advisers the Chosen Council. The Sudebnik of 1550 ran to a hundred articles: the governors' fees were cut, bribes were made punishable, St George's Day was confirmed but the departure fee raised. It was followed by the Hundred Chapters council of 1551, the zemstvo and criminal-court reforms, and the abolition of "feeding". The Council ruled about ten years: in 1560 Sylvester was exiled to the Kirillo-Belozersky monastery and Adashev was sent to Livonia, where he died under arrest at Dorpat in 1561.
level.sudebnik.goal: The archpriest breaks the tsar with a rebuke, a low-born okolnichy enters the inner council — and rewrites the law
level.sudebnik.hint: First the burnt ruins: the archpriest and the tsar — the tsar is humbled. The humbled tsar draws the okolnichy into his inner council. The man admitted to the Council writes the Sudebnik. The Treasury Yard is not needed here: a man who has been bought is not taken into the Council.
level.sudebnik.intro: On 21 June 1547 Moscow burned to the ground: thousands died and the fire reached the Kremlin. The crowd decided that the Glinskys, the tsar's kin on his mother's side, had set the city alight, and tore his uncle Yuri apart. The sixteen-year-old tsar sees a riot up close for the first time — and listens to a priest telling him the fire was sent for the sins of those in power.
level.sudebnik.source: A. Kurbsky, 'History of the Grand Prince of Moscow'; the Sudebnik of 1550
level.sudebnik.title: The Chosen Council
level.suez.fact: In November 1875, Disraeli bought 44% of the Suez Canal shares from the bankrupt Khedive Isma'il for 4 million pounds overnight, borrowing the money from Lionel Rothschild on the government's word of honor — Parliament was dissolved. He wrote to the Queen: 'It is all over; it is yours, Madam.' Gladstone called it an adventure. In 1876, Disraeli passed a law making Victoria Empress of India — she, in turn, made him Earl of Beaconsfield. The rivalry between Disraeli and Gladstone spanned forty years of English politics; the Queen said that Gladstone addressed her as if she were a public meeting.
level.suez.goal: The Prime Minister buys the canal overnight with Rothschild's money and makes the Queen Empress.
level.suez.hint: The shares must be bought overnight — by himself, with the Prime Minister's authority; there's no time to consult Parliament. Then a powerful ally proclaims the Queen Empress of India. Let Gladstone denounce it — so be it.
level.suez.intro: The Khedive of Egypt is ruined and selling his shares in the Suez Canal — the road to India. The French are negotiating. Parliament is in recess, and there's no money in the treasury. Disraeli has an evening and one acquaintance, a banker.
level.suez.source: W. Monypenny and G. Buckle, 'The Life of Benjamin Disraeli'; Disraeli's letters to the Queen
level.suez.title: The Khedive Sells
level.sulla_march.fact: In 88 BC, the tribune Publius Sulpicius Rufus transferred command in the war against Mithridates from Sulla to Marius. Sulla came to his legions near Nola and led them on Rome — something no one had done in four and a half centuries of the republic. All his senior officers refused to go, except for one quaestor, Lucius Lucullus. Sulpicius was killed, Marius was outlawed, and he fled to Africa. The Pomerium — the sacred boundary of the city, which could not be entered with arms — Sulla crossed first; forty years later, Caesar would follow in his footsteps.
level.sulla_march.goal: The legions enter Rome, the tribune is killed, and the old rival is defeated and flees
level.sulla_march.hint: Senior officers will not march on their native city — only Quaestor Lucullus will remain with the commander, and without him, the legions are no force. First, a battle with the rival in the city, then the tribune.
level.sulla_march.intro: A tribune passed a law transferring command in the rich war against Mithridates from Sulla to Marius. Sulla, at this time, stands with his legions near Nola. In four hundred and fifty years of the Republic, no army has marched into Rome.
level.sulla_march.title: The March on Rome
level.tabel.fact: On 24 January 1722 Peter signed the Table of Ranks — fourteen classes on three parallel ladders: military, civil and court. Military service granted hereditary nobility from the lowest, fourteenth class, civil service from the eighth, that is from collegiate assessor. Mestnichestvo, which distributed offices by the standing of one's clan, had already been abolished in 1682, and now rank too depended on service: "count distinction by fitness". Andrei Nartov, son of a Moscow townsman, came to Peter's turnery and became his personal mechanic: he built screw-cutting lathes with a mechanical slide rest, among the first in Europe. After Peter's death Nartov worked at the Academy of Sciences and in 1746 received the rank of state councillor — fifth class, hereditary nobility. The Table lasted almost two centuries and was abolished by decree only in November 1917.
level.tabel.goal: Birth stops being a pass — and a craftsman serves his way up to hereditary nobility
level.tabel.hint: First the fourteen classes: the tsar and the high-born man — birth has been reduced to nothing. With the new Table in hand the tsar takes the turner into his service. The man given rank serves his way to the eighth class. The pedigree roll is useless: ranks are not granted to a man who has been bought.
level.tabel.intro: The high-born boyar is certain that a place beside the sovereign is granted by blood. The tsar thinks otherwise and signs a ladder of fourteen rungs that can be climbed from nothing. Beside him stands a turner, the son of a Moscow townsman.
level.tabel.source: The Table of Ranks of 1722; E. Anisimov, 'The Age of Peter's Reforms'
level.tabel.title: The Table of Ranks
level.tarpeia.fact: According to legend, Tarpeia demanded from the Sabines 'what they wore on their left arm,' referring to their golden bracelets. Upon entering the citadel, Tatius' warriors buried her under their shields — which they also carried on their left arm. The rock on the Capitoline, from which traitors were later thrown, was thus named the Tarpeian Rock by the Romans. Livy adds another version: she specifically asked for shields to disarm the enemy — meaning she was not a traitor, but a heroine. Which is true, we cannot know: Rome preserved both versions with equal care.
level.tarpeia.goal: The Sabines enter the citadel — and bury the one who let them in
level.tarpeia.hint: The girl is bought with bracelets, the bought one opens the gates to him who paid. But the Sabines pay her with what they also wear on their left arm.
level.tarpeia.intro: The Sabines have come for their abducted daughters and stand beneath the Capitoline. The citadel is held by Spurius Tarpeius, and his daughter Tarpeia goes for water every day past the enemy camp — and cannot take her eyes off the golden bracelets on the Sabines' left arms.
level.tarpeia.source: Livy, 'The History of Rome', I, 11; Propertius, IV, 4
level.tarpeia.title: The Tarpeian Rock
level.tarsus.fact: In 41 BC, Cleopatra sailed up the Cydnus to Tarsus on a ship with a gilded stern and purple sails, dressed as Aphrodite — the entire city flocked to the shore, and Antony, who awaited her on the tribunal, was left sitting alone. Regarding the feast, Pliny the Elder recounts that the queen wagered ten million sesterces that she would consume them in a single dinner, and dissolved a pearl earring in vinegar. Accusations of aiding Cassius were no longer mentioned.
level.tarsus.goal: The trial of the queen transforms into her triumph
level.tarsus.hint: You must appear in such a way that the summons is forgotten: first an entrance that draws the entire city, and only then the feast. If you allow the triumvir to begin with an accusatory speech — the condemned will no longer be loved.
level.tarsus.intro: The Triumvir Antony summoned the Queen of Egypt to Tarsus — to answer for whom she had aided in the war. Cleopatra arrived — with her servant Apollodorus and a golden barge.
level.tarsus.title: The Queen and the General
level.templars.fact: At dawn on Friday, October 13, 1307, Templars were arrested simultaneously across France; under torture, they confessed to heresy, idol worship, and sodomy. Pope Clement V, indebted to the king for his tiara, dissolved the order in 1312. On March 18, 1314, Grand Master Jacques de Molay, recanting his forced confessions, was burned on an islet in the Seine; legend has it that from the pyre he summoned the Pope and the King to God's judgment within a year—both died before the end of 1314. The king's debts to the order burned with him; the superstition about Friday the 13th also originates here, though much later.
level.templars.goal: The king destroys the order he owes—and the Master, from the pyre, curses him and the Pope.
level.templars.hint: All Templars must be seized on one day—under torture, they confess, and the Master is condemned. The Pope, swayed by the arrests, is persuaded to dissolve the order. The condemned Master is burned. The order's gold won't buy off the king—he'll take it anyway.
level.templars.intro: Philip the Fair owes the Knights Templar more than he can repay. The order is wealthy, independent, and answers only to the Pope. And Pope Clement V resides in Avignon—under the king's thumb.
level.templars.source: M. Barber, 'The Trial of the Templars'; Geoffroi de Paris, 'Chronicle'
level.templars.title: Friday the Thirteenth
level.teutoburg.fact: In September 9 AD, Arminius, chief of the Cherusci, who had served in the Roman army, led three legions of Quintilius Varus into the Teutoburg Forest and annihilated them in three days. Segestes, Arminius' father-in-law, tried to warn Varus the day before — but Varus dismissed him. Varus fell upon his sword; Augustus, according to Suetonius, for months did not cut his hair and repeatedly struck his head against doors, crying: 'Quintilius Varus, give me back my legions!' The numbers XVII, XVIII, and XIX were never again assigned to any legion. Rome no longer attempted to conquer Germania beyond the Rhine; the border held for four centuries.
level.teutoburg.goal: A trusted ally leads three legions into the forest — and Rome forever halts at the Rhine.
level.teutoburg.hint: First, friendship at the table — only an ally will be allowed to lead the army. Segestes' speech against Arminius should not be heeded: a condemned man cannot set an ambush. The defeated general will end on his sword.
level.teutoburg.intro: Germania is almost a Roman province. Governor Varus dines at the same table with Arminius, chief of the Cherusci — a Roman citizen and equestrian. Old Segestes warns: do not trust him.
level.teutoburg.title: Varus, Give Me Back My Legions
level.theodora_death.fact: Theodora died in 548 AD, likely from cancer. Justinian, who outlived her by 17 years, never recovered from the loss of his co-ruler and main support. With her death, the 'golden age' of his reign began to wane.
level.theodora_death.goal: The Empress Fades — and the Court's Light Dims
level.theodora_death.hint: Let the emperor be at the bedside of the dying empress — and only after being widowed will he plunge into unending grief. Antonina cannot replace either her or him here.
level.theodora_death.intro: 548 AD. Theodora wastes away from illness. Justinian is at her bedside — and seventeen years of widowhood lie ahead.
level.theodora_death.title: The Death of Theodora
level.theodosian_walls.fact: The earthquake of 27 January 447 brought down long stretches of the Theodosian Walls and fifty-seven towers — just as Attila's army was ravaging Thrace. The rebuilding was directed by the praetorian prefect Constantine: the circus factions, eternal enemies in the Hippodrome, turned out for the work — sixteen thousand men. In sixty days they did not merely repair the old line but added a second wall and a moat. The inscription on the Rhegium Gate records it word for word: 'In sixty days Constantine the eparch raised wall to wall.' Attila did not storm Constantinople: he beat the Romans in the field, at the river Utus, and took an enormous tribute — but he never came up to the walls. Those walls held for another thousand years, until 1453.
level.theodosian_walls.goal: The city raises its ruined walls in sixty days — and the Hun, learning of it, turns aside without ever reaching the city
level.theodosian_walls.hint: The earthquake first: the emperor loses his strength, and the fallen walls come down on the prefect. The man whose walls are down is the one who raises them in sixty days. The Hun, learning of the new walls, turns aside. Gold was indeed paid to the Huns — but a man who has been bought does not turn aside, he simply takes the money.
level.theodosian_walls.intro: The walls put up thirty years earlier under the boy Theodosius were held to be impassable. On a night in January the city is shaken so hard that towers and stretches of the main wall come down. And Attila is already moving through Thrace.
level.theodosian_walls.source: The Chronicle of Marcellinus Comes; the inscription on the Rhegium Gate; J. B. Bury, 'History of the Later Roman Empire'
level.theodosian_walls.title: Sixty Days
level.theodosius.fact: In 390, in retaliation for the murder of a military commander in Thessalonica, by order of Theodosius, citizens were locked in the hippodrome and massacred, by various estimates, up to seven thousand people. Ambrose, Bishop of Mediolanum, denied the emperor communion and refused him entry to the church until he publicly repented. Theodosius did not enter the church for several months, then removed his insignia of power and begged forgiveness before all. This was the first instance where the Church punished an emperor and he submitted — a precedent that would be cited for a thousand years.
level.theodosius.goal: Secular power bows to ecclesiastical authority for the first time.
level.theodosius.hint: First, blood must be shed, otherwise there will be nothing to forgive. Then the bishop will close the church doors — and here, one thing decides everything: will you insist on the inviolability of the purple, or will you remove it yourself?
level.theodosius.intro: In Thessalonica, a mob killed the garrison commander. The emperor is enraged, and his prefect is already ready to relay the order to the troops.
level.theodosius.source: Ambrose, Letter 51; Theodoret of Cyrrhus, V
level.theodosius.title: The Emperor on His Knees
level.thermidor.fact: On July 27, 1794 (9 Thermidor), the Convention rebelled against Robespierre; the next day, he and his associates, including Saint-Just, were guillotined without trial. Thus ended the Terror.
level.thermidor.goal: The Convention deposes the tyrant Robespierre and executes him
level.thermidor.hint: The tyrant is vulnerable: a deputy accuses him in the Convention, then — the guillotine.
level.thermidor.intro: Robespierre — the all-powerful leader of the Terror; the Convention prepares a coup.
level.thermidor.title: Thermidor
level.thomas_more.fact: Thomas More refused to swear an oath to the Act of Supremacy, which recognized Henry VIII as the head of the English Church, but he did not openly deny it: by law, silence was not treason. At his trial in 1535, Solicitor General Richard Rich testified that More, in a private conversation in the Tower, had denied the King's supremacy – almost certainly a lie. More was beheaded on July 6, 1535; on the scaffold, he asked the executioner to spare his beard, 'for it has committed no treason.' The Catholic Church canonized him as a saint, and the film 'A Man for All Seasons' hailed him as a hero of conscience. Rich lived to become Lord Chancellor.
level.thomas_more.goal: Silence does not save one from the block if a false witness is found
level.thomas_more.hint: The Chancellor will refuse to swear the oath and remain silent – that is his resolve. The silent can only be condemned by false testimony: Rich's speech. The condemned will be executed by the King. To take the oath means to live, but not in this story.
level.thomas_more.intro: Thomas More, author of 'Utopia' and Lord Chancellor, resigned when the King declared himself head of the Church. He said not a word against it – he simply remained silent. This is not enough for the King: he demands an oath.
level.thomas_more.source: W. Roper, 'The Life of Sir Thomas More'; trial records of 1535
level.thomas_more.title: A Man for All Seasons
level.tilsit.fact: On June 25, 1807, after the defeat at Friedland, Napoleon and Alexander I met on a raft in the middle of the Neman River near Tilsit; Alexander began with the words: 'Sire, I hate the English no less than you do.' In two weeks of friendship, Prussia lost half its lands, Russia joined the blockade, and Prussian Queen Louise vainly begged Napoleon for mercy. The friendship lasted five years—until the Neman of 1812, which Napoleon crossed in the opposite direction.
level.tilsit.goal: The defeated Tsar becomes the victor's friend—and together they divide Europe.
level.tilsit.hint: First, Friedland—a strong Napoleon defeats the Tsar. Continuing the war is not an option. Then, friendship on the raft, and the allies carve up Prussia.
level.tilsit.intro: After Friedland, the Russian army is defeated but not destroyed. Two emperors decide to meet in the middle of the river—on a raft, so no one steps on foreign soil. The Prussian king waits on the bank in the rain.
level.tilsit.title: The Raft on the Neman
level.titus_oates.fact: In 1678, Titus Oates under oath described a 'Popish Plot' against Charles II — entirely fabricated. A wave of panic: about twenty-two people were executed, including Edward Colman, secretary to the Duchess of York, whose letters about Catholic restoration proved to be the only 'evidence'. Oates was given an apartment in Whitehall and a pension. In 1685, under James II, Judge Jeffreys sentenced him for perjury to the pillory, a whipping from Aldgate to Newgate and from Newgate to Tyburn, and life imprisonment; he survived, and after the Glorious Revolution, he received a new pension.
level.titus_oates.goal: Lies under oath send innocents to the gallows — and six years later, the liar is whipped throughout the city.
level.titus_oates.hint: False testimony, with the weight of an oath, condemns a Catholic — he will be hanged. The King has no need for a pension. And when the wind changes, Judge Jeffreys, with authority, will put the liar in the pillory.
level.titus_oates.intro: Titus Oates — a priest expelled from everywhere, with a phenomenal memory and no conscience. He declares that Jesuits want to kill the King and place his Catholic brother on the throne. There is no proof, but there is an oath and fear.
level.titus_oates.source: J. Kenyon, 'The Popish Plot'; T. Macaulay, 'The History of England'
level.titus_oates.title: The Popish Plot
level.torquatus.fact: In 340 BC, the son of Consul Titus Manlius Torquatus accepted the challenge of the Latin horseman Geminus Maecius and killed him in single combat — contrary to orders not to leave the ranks. His father commanded the lictors to execute him before the army: 'You have violated military discipline, upon which the Roman state was founded.' From then on, 'Manlian orders' became a byword in Rome for ruthless severity. Livy writes that the youth hated Torquatus for the rest of his days — but that the army became more obedient that day, and the Latins were defeated.
level.torquatus.goal: The son wins a duel — and the father executes him for it before the ranks.
level.torquatus.hint: The son is stronger and will win — the Latin will perish in the duel. The father executes the victor: thus the army becomes disciplined. To forgive the son is to lose to the Latins in the great battle.
level.torquatus.intro: Consul Manlius Torquatus forbade engaging in battle without orders. A Latin horseman challenged his son to a duel — and the son accepted the challenge.
level.torquatus.title: The Father's Axe
level.toulon.fact: In December 1793, 24-year-old artillery captain Napoleon Bonaparte planned the capture of Toulon, occupied by the British. The success earned him the rank of brigadier general and his first widespread fame.
level.toulon.goal: Young Bonaparte gains glory at Toulon
level.toulon.hint: Let Bonaparte first propose a daring artillery plan at the council — and only by his plan shall he take the fort and become a hero. Carteaux sees no key to the city.
level.toulon.intro: 1793. Toulon has surrendered to the English. Incompetent General Carteaux dithers outside the city, while unknown Captain Bonaparte sees a weak point.
level.toulon.title: Siege of Toulon
level.trafalgar.fact: On October 21, 1805, Nelson led 27 ships in two columns perpendicular to a line of 33 Franco-Spanish vessels, cutting it in two – a risk where the lead ships endured an hour of fire without return. Before the battle, he hoisted the signal 'England expects that every man will do his duty.' A French sharpshooter from the 'Redoutable's' mast hit him in the shoulder; he died three hours later in the 'Victory's' cockpit, telling Captain Hardy: 'Kiss me, Hardy' – and 'Thank God, I have done my duty.' The allies lost 22 ships, the British none. Napoleon cancelled the invasion; Britain ruled the seas for a hundred years, and Nelson's body was brought home in a barrel of brandy.
level.trafalgar.goal: A fleet, cut into two columns, destroys the enemy – and the admiral dies upon learning of victory
level.trafalgar.hint: Line ahead formation – a stalemate: that's how they fought for a hundred years. Two columns across the enemy line – that is preparation and strength. Before the battle, the signal: 'England expects' – and the fleet loves him. The battle – and the wounded admiral will ask Hardy for a kiss.
level.trafalgar.intro: Napoleon has assembled an invasion army in Boulogne; he needs the strait for one day. Villeneuve's combined Franco-Spanish fleet has sailed from Cadiz. Nelson, one-eyed and one-armed, awaits him off Cape Trafalgar and intends to break all rules of naval combat.
level.trafalgar.source: Collingwood's dispatch, 1805; W. Beatty, 'A Narrative of the Death of Lord Nelson'
level.trafalgar.title: England Expects
level.trajan.fact: In 105–106 AD, Trajan built a stone bridge over the Danube, more than a kilometer long — the work of Apollodorus of Damascus, the largest bridge of antiquity — and took the Dacian capital Sarmizegetusa; King Decebalus stabbed himself, not awaiting capture. The gold from the Dacian mines paid for 123 days of games and a column with a forty-meter frieze of reliefs, which still stands in Rome. Under Trajan, the Empire reached its greatest extent in history — and stopped there: his campaign beyond the Tigris faltered, and his successor Hadrian immediately abandoned the conquests beyond the Euphrates.
level.trajan.goal: Dacia is taken and immortalized, and the Empire stops in time
level.trajan.hint: First, a bridge is laid across the Danube — without preparation, one cannot enter the mountains. After victory, the temptation to go even further east is great; it is there that the empire overextended itself.
level.trajan.intro: The Danube is the border; beyond it lie the Dacians of King Decebalus, who have twice defeated the Romans. Emperor Trajan decided to put an end to this once and for all. Beside him is his young relative Hadrian, who will one day return everything Trajan conquers in the East.
level.trajan.title: The Empire's Limit
level.trianon.fact: At the Petit Trianon, Marie Antoinette built the Queen's Hamlet—with a mill, a dairy farm, and real peasants; the court, excluded from it, retaliated with rumors. Swedish Count Axel von Fersen was her friend and likely lover—he also organized the flight to Varennes. She never said the phrase 'let them eat cake': Rousseau recorded it for 'a certain princess' even before Antoinette arrived in France. But pamphlets attributed everything to her—extravagance, orgies, treason to Austria—and by 1789, the Queen was hated more than the King.
level.trianon.goal: The Queen plays at a simple life—and Paris turns her into 'the Austrian woman'.
level.trianon.hint: A shepherdess at Trianon—a challenge to the court. Love for the Swede—fodder for gossip. And then the pamphlets: 'let them eat cake.' Observing etiquette is not her way.
level.trianon.intro: Marie Antoinette flees Versailles etiquette for the Petit Trianon: there's a village with a pond and cows, simple dresses, and only her inner circle is allowed. Among them is the Swedish Count Fersen. Paris reads pamphlets.
level.trianon.title: The Shepherdess Queen
level.triumph_orthodoxy.fact: Theophilos died on 20 January 842; his widow Theodora became regent for the three-year-old Michael III. Early in 843 a council deposed the patriarch John VII the Grammarian, and the throne was taken by Methodios, who had himself spent years in confinement under the iconoclasts. Theodora set one condition: the restoration of the icons must not mean the posthumous condemnation of her husband — and the council agreed. On the first Sunday of Lent, 11 March 843, the icons were carried into Hagia Sophia in procession; the Church still celebrates that day as the Triumph of Orthodoxy. So ended a dispute that had lasted more than a century. Her own son Theodora could not hold: once grown, Michael III sent his mother to a convent.
level.triumph_orthodoxy.goal: The regent removes the iconoclast patriarch, installs her own — and the icons come back into the churches in procession
level.triumph_orthodoxy.hint: First the deposition of the Grammarian: that is how the regent gains her standing. Only with that standing can she vouch for a new patriarch. It is the patriarch she raises who leads the procession. The monastery on the Bosphorus is a departure: you cannot depose a man who has already withdrawn.
level.triumph_orthodoxy.intro: The emperor Theophilos, the last iconoclast, has died, leaving a three-year-old son and his widow Theodora. Icons have been hidden away for more than a hundred years; the patriarchal throne is held by John the Grammarian, the most learned man in the empire and the chief enemy of images. The widow begins to rule, and she knows what she wants.
level.triumph_orthodoxy.source: Theophanes Continuatus, IV; 'The Synodikon of Orthodoxy'
level.triumph_orthodoxy.title: The Triumph of Orthodoxy
level.triumvirate.fact: In November 43 BC, Antony, Octavian, and Lepidus formed the Second Triumvirate—a legal alliance to wage war against Caesar's assassins. It began with proscriptions: hundreds of enemies, including Cicero, were outlawed and executed.
level.triumvirate.goal: The triumvirs avenge Caesar — and outlaw his killer
level.triumvirate.hint: First a public alliance, then a secret pact. Bound by the plot, they bring the proscription down on Caesar's killer.
level.triumvirate.intro: Caesar is dead, his assassins have fled to the east, and in Rome, two men divide the inheritance: the dictator's right-hand man and his nineteen-year-old heir.
level.triumvirate.title: The Second Triumvirate
level.tullia.fact: According to tradition, Lucius Tarquinius and his wife Tullia conspired against her father, the sixth king Servius Tullius: Tarquinius seized the throne in the Curia, while the old man, thrown down the steps, was killed in the street. Tullia, rushing to congratulate her husband, ordered her charioteer to drive over her father's body — and returned home splattered with blood. The street has since been called Sceleratus, 'The Wicked'. Thus Tarquinius Superbus ascended the throne — the last king of Rome; you already know how that ended for him.
level.tullia.goal: The daughter and son-in-law kill the king — and she drives her chariot over his body
level.tullia.hint: First, a conspiracy of two. The son-in-law will kill the king on the steps of the Curia. And after that, the daughter does not mourn her father — she drives over him.
level.tullia.intro: King Servius Tullius is old. His daughter Tullia is married to Tarquinius — and both believe that her father has overstayed his welcome on the throne.
level.tullia.title: The Street of Wickedness
level.tushino.fact: In the summer of 1608, False Dmitry II encamped in Tushino; Marina Mniszech, released from exile, «recognized» him as her husband — secretly remarrying so as not to live in sin. From Tushino, he ruled half the country — the «Tushino Thief,» as Muscovites called him. On July 17, 1610, after the defeat of the tsar's troops near Klushino, Zakhar Lyapunov of Ryazan, with a crowd, «deposed» Shuysky from the throne; the next day, he was forcibly tonsured as a monk — Prince Tyufyakin pronounced the vows for the resisting tsar. The former tsar was handed over to the Poles, and he died in captivity in Gostynin in 1612. The Tushino Thief was killed in December 1610 in Kaluga during a hunt by his own Tatar bodyguard.
level.tushino.goal: The widow recognizes her «husband,» in Moscow they shout against the tsar — and Shuysky is forcibly tonsured as a monk
level.tushino.hint: First, the Tushino camp — the thief is raised and with power. Marina «recognizes her husband» — love. The thief with power sends letters to Moscow against the tsar — Shuysky is condemned and overthrown. The condemned tsar is tonsured as a monk. No need to storm Moscow — a strong Shuysky will defeat.
level.tushino.intro: Shuysky reigns, but a new «Dmitry» appears — supposedly saved again. He sets up camp in Tushino near Moscow; nobles flock to him, Marina Mniszech is brought to him. For a year and a half, there are two tsars, two Dumas, two patriarchs in the country.
level.tushino.source: S. Platonov, «Essays on the History of the Time of Troubles»; R. Skrynnikov, «Impostors»
level.tushino.title: The Tushino Thief
level.union.fact: In 1486, Henry VII, a Lancastrian, married Elizabeth of York, uniting the Red and White Roses; their son Arthur solidified the dynasty. But Yorkist pretenders — Lambert Simnel and Perkin Warbeck — challenged the throne for years; Warbeck was executed at the Tower in 1499.
level.union.goal: Henry seals the union of roses, provides an heir, and executes the pretender.
level.union.hint: First a wedding with the Yorkist heiress, then an heir in the bedchamber. The captured impostor is executed by the king — he holds authority.
level.union.intro: Henry VII weds the Lancastrians to the Yorks — but the pretender Warbeck threatens new turmoil.
level.union.title: Union of Two Roses
level.valmy.fact: On September 20, 1792, at the Mill of Valmy, the French army of Dumouriez and Kellermann withstood the Prussian cannonade and, when the Prussian infantry advanced, responded with volleys and the cry 'Vive la Nation!'—Kellermann, according to tradition, raised his hat on the tip of his sword. The Duke of Brunswick called off the attack. Casualties—about three hundred men on each side; there was hardly a battle, but the revolution survived, and the next day a republic was proclaimed in Paris. Goethe, who was with the Prussian army, said that evening: 'From this day and from this place begins a new era in world history.' Blücher, the future victor over Napoleon, was a Rittmeister there.
level.valmy.goal: A cannonade, the cry 'Long live the Nation!'—and the Prussians turn back without attacking.
level.valmy.hint: Occupy the mill and position cannons—that's strength. Then the general raises his hat on his sword and cries 'Vive la Nation!'—and the army loves him, while the Prussians hesitate. Retreating beyond the Argonne means defeat.
level.valmy.intro: The Prussian army of the Duke of Brunswick marches on Paris to restore the king; with it is young officer Blücher. Against them is General Kellermann with an army of former soldiers and yesterday's volunteers in wooden shoes, whom Europe does not consider an army.
level.valmy.title: Valmy
level.varangians.fact: In 988, Basil II, pressed by the rebel Bardas Phokas, received six thousand Varangians from Prince Vladimir of Kyiv — they decided the outcome at Chrysopolis and Abydos and became the core of the Imperial Varangian Guard. In return, Vladimir demanded the hand of Anna Porphyrogenita — the Emperor's sister, and porphyrogenita princesses were never given to 'barbarians': Otto I was refused for his son. Basil agreed on condition of baptism; when the bride was not sent, Vladimir took Byzantine Chersonesus (Korsun) in Crimea — and Anna, weeping 'I would rather die,' was sent to him. According to the chronicle, the prince was baptized in Chersonesus, married, and upon returning, baptized Rus' in the Dnieper. Anna died in Kyiv in 1011.
level.varangians.goal: The Prince saves the Emperor with Varangians, takes Chersonesus, is baptized — and receives a bride never given to anyone else.
level.varangians.hint: First, six thousand Varangians — the Prince buys the Emperor, who is now an ally. The Emperor delays — the Prince takes Chersonesus and is baptized there: baptized, the door to the bride is open. Then the wedding with the princess. There's no need to march on Constantinople — you don't strike an ally.
level.varangians.intro: Against Basil II, the general Bardas Phokas rebelled and stands at the Bosphorus. The Emperor asks Prince Vladimir for help — he sends six thousand Varangians, but in return demands the impossible: the Emperor's sister, Princess Anna, born in the purple.
level.varangians.source: 'The Primary Chronicle'; Leo the Deacon; Psellus, 'Chronographia'
level.varangians.title: The Porphyrogenita Bride
level.varennes.fact: On the night of June 21, 1791, Louis XVI and his family secretly fled Paris but were recognized and apprehended in Varennes. The flight shattered the image of the patriot-king and hastened the fall of the monarchy.
level.varennes.goal: The King flees Paris — and is declared a traitor
level.varennes.hint: Let the King first flee disguised — and only then shall a patriot identify and arrest the fugitive in Varennes. The royalist Fersen will not betray the King.
level.varennes.intro: Night of 1791. Louis XVI secretly flees Paris, hoping to reach loyal troops. Loyal Count Fersen drives the carriage.
level.varennes.source: J. Michelet, 'History of the French Revolution'
level.varennes.title: Flight to Varennes
level.vendee.fact: In March 1793, the Vendée rebelled against conscription and persecution of the church; peasants elected the peddler Jacques Cathelineau as their leader. The Catholic Royal Army took cities—Saumur, Angers—but on June 29, near Nantes, Cathelineau was mortally wounded, and the rebellion receded. In 1794, General Turreau led twelve 'infernal columns' through the Vendée with orders to burn everything and kill everyone: an estimated one hundred to two hundred thousand people died, including women and children—sometimes called the first modern genocide. The Vendée has not forgiven the Republic for this to this day.
level.vendee.goal: The peasant army takes cities, is broken at Nantes—and the Republic burns the region.
level.vendee.hint: The Sacred Heart on his chest—peasants follow the peddler, that's his influence; negotiating with the strong Republic won't work. At the walls of Nantes, its strength defeats him. The broken are finished off by infernal columns—along with the entire region.
level.vendee.intro: The Republic announced a levy of three hundred thousand—and the peasants of the west, whose churches were closed and king executed, took up pitchforks. Their leader is the peddler Cathelineau, 'the Saint of Anjou,' with the embroidered Sacred Heart of Jesus on his chest.
level.vendee.source: R. Secher, 'A French Genocide'; memoirs of Madame de La Rochejaquelein
level.vendee.title: The Vendée
level.verdi.fact: Verdi staged Nabucco, with its chorus of Hebrew captives Va, pensiero, at La Scala in 1842; the audience demanded an encore of the chorus although encores were forbidden by the Austrian censors, who had gone through the libretto line by line. Italians heard themselves in a song about a lost homeland, and the melody became the unofficial anthem of the Risorgimento. Later, by 1859, Viva VERDI began appearing on the walls of Italian cities — the censors could not ban a composer's surname, and it read as Viva Vittorio Emanuele Re D'Italia, long live Victor Emmanuel, King of Italy. In 1861 Verdi himself, at Cavour's insistence, became a deputy in the first Italian parliament, though he disliked politics. At his funeral in 1901 eighty thousand people sang Va, pensiero in the streets of Milan.
level.verdi.goal: Censors cut the words — and the chorus of captives becomes an anthem, while the composer's name turns into a slogan
level.verdi.hint: The censor's scissors first: the words are struck out — the music remains. The censored composer gives the hall its chorus, and the hall falls in love. The beloved composer and the king — and V.E.R.D.I. appears on the walls. Writing for Vienna: a man who has been bought writes no anthem.
level.verdi.intro: Lombardy is under Austria and the word fatherland is struck out of librettos. A young composer who has just lost his wife and both children swears never to write music again — and then picks up a libretto about the Babylonian captivity.
level.verdi.source: M. Phillips-Matz, Verdi: A Biography; La Scala chronicles
level.verdi.title: Viva V.E.R.D.I.
level.verginia.fact: In 449 BC, the decemvir Appius Claudius, seeking Virginia, orchestrated a trial where his client declared the girl his runaway slave — and then Claudius himself awarded her to the plaintiff. Her father, centurion Virginius, asked to take his daughter aside, seized a knife from a butcher's stall, and stabbed her: 'Only thus, my daughter, can I make you free.' He fled to the army, the army withdrew to the Aventine, and the decemvirs fell; Appius committed suicide in prison. The story deliberately echoes Lucretia — and Livy emphasizes this: for the second time in Rome, tyrants fall because of a woman who could not be touched.
level.verginia.goal: A father kills his daughter to save her honor — and the decemvirs fall
level.verginia.hint: Dishonor is brought by a false claim. Here, the father's knife replaces a vow of vengeance: it gives weight to the accusation. And only then — a speech in the forum against the one who started it all.
level.verginia.intro: Rome is ruled by ten decemvirs, who wrote laws and refused to step down. The chief among them, Appius Claudius, set his eyes on Virginia, the daughter of a centurion — and ordered his client to declare her a slave.
level.verginia.title: The Butcher's Knife
level.vespers.fact: On March 30, 1282, Easter Monday, near the Church of the Holy Spirit in Palermo, a French sergeant, Drouet, began to search a Sicilian woman under the pretext of looking for weapons; the crowd killed him, the bells rang for vespers, and by morning no Frenchmen remained alive in the city — about two thousand. Within two weeks, the revolt engulfed the island; foreigners were identified by their accent, forced to pronounce 'ciciri' — 'chickpea.' Charles of Anjou, according to tradition, said: 'Lord, if it is Your will to cast me down, let me at least fall gradually.' In August, Peter III of Aragon, married to the daughter of Manfred of Hohenstaufen, landed in Trapani and was crowned in Palermo; the War of the Sicilian Vespers lasted twenty years. Verdi wrote an opera about it.
level.vespers.goal: At vespers in Palermo, a massacre erupts, the French are slaughtered in two weeks — and the crown of Sicily goes to Aragon.
level.vespers.hint: First, Procida's conspiracy with Aragon — they are in league. The conspirator incites Palermo at vespers — the French are defeated and expelled, the conspirator has influence. The influential conspirator proclaims the Aragonese king. Complaining to the Pope is useless — a yielding conspirator won't raise a rebellion.
level.vespers.intro: Sicily is ruled by the Frenchman Charles of Anjou, brother of Saint Louis; his officials plunder, his soldiers grow insolent. The exile Giovanni da Procida secretly travels between Constantinople, Aragon, and Palermo, preparing an uprising.
level.vespers.source: S. Runciman, 'The Sicilian Vespers'; Chronicle of Bartholomew of Neocastro
level.vespers.title: The Sicilian Vespers
level.vesuvius.fact: On August 24, 79 AD, Pliny the Elder, commanding the fleet at Misenum, was about to set sail out of scientific curiosity, but received a note from Rectina, cut off at the foot of the volcano — and turned the excursion into a rescue mission, ordering the quadriremes to be launched. He landed at Stabiae, where he died of asphyxiation on the shore. His eighteen-year-old nephew remained home with his rhetoric lessons — and later, at Tacitus's request, wrote two letters that became the most detailed description of the eruption in antiquity. Eruptions with a column of ash reaching the stratosphere are now called Plinian.
level.vesuvius.goal: The fleet sails to rescue, the admiral remains forever, and yet the chronicle is written.
level.vesuvius.hint: The ships sail not out of curiosity, but at a plea for help — first, a note. Do not take your nephew with you: he who steps onto the deck will record nothing, and it is he who must record it.
level.vesuvius.intro: Over the bay rose a cloud in the shape of a pine. Pliny, commanding the fleet at Misenum, was about to go observe — and then a note arrived from the other shore. Beside him was his nephew, also Pliny, seventeen years old.
level.vesuvius.source: Pliny the Younger, Letters, VI, 16 and VI, 20
level.vesuvius.title: Vesuvius
level.victoria_albert.fact: Lord Melbourne, premier and mentor, spent up to six hours a day with the young Queen; when in 1839 she refused to replace her Whig ladies-in-waiting with Tories, Peel's government failed to form – the 'Bedchamber Crisis.' In October 1839, Victoria, seeing Albert of Saxe-Coburg on the Windsor staircase, wrote: 'It was a painful pleasure to look at him,' – and five days later, she herself proposed to him, as etiquette required for a monarch. The wedding on February 10, 1840, introduced the fashion for white wedding dresses. Nine children, the Christmas tree, the Crystal Palace – and forty years of widow's mourning after his death in 1861.
level.victoria_albert.goal: The Queen, tutored by the old premier, proposes to the prince herself
level.victoria_albert.hint: First, friendship with Melbourne – he makes a queen out of a girl. Then love at Windsor: she makes the proposal. And the wedding in St. James's Chapel. The Bedchamber Crisis is not about this.
level.victoria_albert.intro: The eighteen-year-old Queen learns to rule from Prime Minister Melbourne – he is like a father to her. And from Coburg arrives cousin Albert, and by etiquette, only she can make the proposal.
level.victoria_albert.source: Queen Victoria's Diaries; L. Strachey, 'Queen Victoria'
level.victoria_albert.title: Victoria and Albert
level.vienna_congress.fact: The Congress of Vienna sat from September 1814 to June 1815. Talleyrand came to represent defeated France and put forward the principle of legitimacy — the inviolability of lawful dynasties: it suited every monarch and at the same time protected the Bourbons newly restored in France. Within six weeks France had joined the committee of powers deciding the fate of Europe. The quarrel over Poland and Saxony — Alexander I demanded Poland, promising Prussia the whole of Saxony — brought matters to the brink of war, and on 3 January 1815 France, Austria and Britain signed a secret defensive alliance against Russia and Prussia. Returning from Elba, Napoleon found a copy of the treaty in the Tuileries and sent it to Alexander, hoping to set the allies at each other's throats; the tsar showed the paper to Metternich and threw it into the fire, saying this was no time for quarrels. The Prince de Ligne summed the congress up: "The congress dances, but it does not move." Talleyrand outlived every regime he served: after the congress he saw two more changes of power, was ambassador in London until 1834 and died in 1838.
level.vienna_congress.goal: Defeated France walks into the circle of the victors — and six months later signs a secret alliance against two of them
level.vienna_congress.hint: First the green table: a single word wins the diplomat his seat, while the tsar shows his appetite. The tsar's appetite frightens the Austrian. The man who has taken his seat and the frightened one sign what no one expected. The ballroom is a trap: whoever is dancing is not at the table.
level.vienna_congress.intro: Vienna in the autumn of 1814: four victorious powers are dividing Europe, and the representative of a shattered France has no place at their table. He arrives without an army, without money and without a vote — but with one word that every monarch needs at once.
level.vienna_congress.source: C.-M. Talleyrand, 'Memoirs'; H. Nicolson, 'The Congress of Vienna'
level.vienna_congress.title: The Congress Dances
level.wallace.fact: On September 11, 1297, at Stirling Bridge, Wallace allowed half of the English army to cross the narrow bridge – and then annihilated it on the other bank. A year later at Falkirk, Edward I personally defeated him: Scottish schiltrons of spears could not withstand Welsh archers. Wallace hid for seven years, was betrayed in 1305, tried in Westminster as a traitor (he responded that he had never sworn allegiance to Edward) and executed in Smithfield: hanged, drawn, and quartered; his head was displayed on London Bridge. The 1995 film is true in spirit and almost nothing in detail.
level.wallace.goal: The rebel defeats the English at the bridge, loses to the king in the field – and dies on the block
level.wallace.hint: At the bridge, the rebel becomes a force through cunning – and defeats Surrey. But against the King himself with his archers, he is weak: Falkirk is a rout, and the defeated will be outlawed. The condemned will be executed by the King.
level.wallace.intro: Edward I conquered Wales and turned his attention to Scotland. Against him rose not a lord, but a minor knight, William Wallace – with peasants and spears. The English army of the Earl of Surrey marches towards Stirling, where a single narrow bridge crosses the River Forth.
level.wallace.source: 'The Chronicle of Lanercost'; Guido of Warwick; Blind Harry, 'Wallace'
level.wallace.title: Braveheart
level.wat_tyler.fact: On June 15, 1381, at a meeting in Smithfield, Lord Mayor of London William Walworth struck Wat Tyler with a dagger – for the insolence with which he spoke to the King. The crowd drew their bows; and then fourteen-year-old Richard II rode out to them alone with the words: 'I am your King, I will be your leader, follow me' – and led the rebels into the fields, where they were met by the militia. All promises – the abolition of serfdom, pardons – he later revoked: 'You were and remain villains.' But the poll tax was no longer collected, and serfdom in England quietly died out over the next hundred years.
level.wat_tyler.goal: The leader is killed during negotiations, and the crowd is led away by the boy-king
level.wat_tyler.hint: The rebels are strong – the King cannot attack them. At the meeting, the mayor will kill the leader. And then the boy has one option: ride out to the leaderless crowd and declare himself their leader.
level.wat_tyler.intro: The third poll tax in four years roused Kent and Essex. Wat Tyler's peasants entered London, burned the Duke's palace, and beheaded the Archbishop. King Richard II is fourteen years old, and he has agreed to meet them in Smithfield.
level.wat_tyler.title: I Will Be Your Leader
level.waterloo.fact: On June 18, 1815, at Waterloo, Napoleon's army was defeated by the forces of the Duke of Wellington and Prussian Field Marshal Blücher. The Emperor abdicated a second time and was exiled to the island of Saint Helena, where he died in 1821.
level.waterloo.goal: The Coalition deposes the Emperor — and he is sent into exile
level.waterloo.hint: Let the coalition first break the emperor on the field of Waterloo — and only then shall the broken one be exiled to Saint Helena. The undefeated cannot be sent overseas.
level.waterloo.intro: June 1815. Napoleon, returned from Elba, stakes everything on a single battle at Waterloo against Wellington.
level.waterloo.title: Waterloo
level.waterloo_1815.fact: On June 18, 1815, Wellington held the ridge of Mont Saint Jean all day against the attacks of Ney and the Old Guard, and by evening, Blücher, who had kept his promise to arrive, appeared on the French right flank. Wellington called it 'the nearest run thing you ever saw in your life' — 'a damned nice thing'. Napoleon abdicated four days later and died on Saint Helena. Wellington wept upon learning of the losses; Blücher suggested naming the battle 'Belle Alliance', but the victor named it after the village where he had spent the night. 'Wellington' boots, 'Waterloo' station, and the ABBA song — all from there.
level.waterloo_1815.goal: The ridge holds all day, the Prussians arrive by evening — and the Emperor loses forever.
level.waterloo_1815.hint: Occupy the ridge in advance — preparation; attack first — lose. The Prussians are allies: only with them does Wellington have strength against a strong Napoleon. And then the battle — three in one frame.
level.waterloo_1815.intro: Napoleon returned from Elba, and he has a hundred days. Wellington stands on the ridge near the village of Waterloo with an army of English, Dutch, and Germans, while Blücher's Prussians, defeated two days ago, are somewhere twenty kilometers away. It is raining.
level.waterloo_1815.source: Wellington's Dispatch of June 19, 1815; E. Creasy, 'The Fifteen Decisive Battles of the World'
level.waterloo_1815.title: Waterloo
level.wilberforce.fact: In 1787, under an oak in Holwood, William Pitt said to his friend: 'Wilberforce, why don't you take on the slave trade?' Wilberforce introduced an abolition bill almost every year from 1791; he was opposed by Liverpool MP Banastre Tarleton, a hero of the American War, and the planter lobby. On March 25, 1807, the Act for the Abolition of the Slave Trade passed by 283 votes to 16 — the House stood and applauded. Slavery itself in the colonies was abolished in 1833; Wilberforce learned of it three days before his death. The anti-slavery campaign invented the sugar boycott, petitions with hundreds of thousands of signatures, and the badge 'Am I not a Man and a Brother?' — the entire toolkit of modern activism.
level.wilberforce.goal: Twenty years of speeches — and the House rises to applaud the ban on the slave trade
level.wilberforce.hint: Friendship with the Prime Minister is a pillar. A weighty speech condemns the slave trader. And then the bill will pass — but only if the MP hasn't been bought by Liverpool money.
level.wilberforce.intro: Britain transports forty thousand slaves across the Atlantic each year, and Liverpool thrives on it. Young MP Wilberforce, under an oak on the estate of his friend — Prime Minister Pitt — decides to dedicate his life to abolishing the trade. Against him stand Tarleton and all the money of Liverpool.
level.wilberforce.source: R. and S. Wilberforce, 'The Life of William Wilberforce'; W. Hague, 'Wilberforce'
level.wilberforce.title: The Holwood Oak
level.witte.fact: Sergei Witte, minister of finance from 1892 to 1903, brought in the liquor monopoly and the gold rouble of 1897 and pressed on with the Trans-Siberian; to shorten the route he ran the Chinese Eastern Railway through Manchuria. He thought the Far Eastern adventure ruinous and argued with the Bezobrazov circle, who were pursuing timber concessions on the river Yalu; in August 1903 Nicholas II removed him from the ministry, giving him the honorary chair of the Committee of Ministers. Six months later the war with Japan began, and after Tsushima in May 1905 there was no one left to send for peace — so Witte went. The talks were held at Portsmouth in America under the mediation of President Theodore Roosevelt; on 23 August (5 September) 1905 the peace was signed: Russia gave up the southern half of Sakhalin, the Liaodong peninsula and the South Manchurian Railway, but did not pay a single rouble of indemnity. Witte received the title of count — and the nickname 'Count Half-Sakhalin'. That autumn he drew up the Manifesto of 17 October and became the first chairman of a Council of Ministers in Russian history, and in April 1906 he was dismissed; Roosevelt received the Nobel Peace Prize for the mediation.
level.witte.goal: The dismissed minister is sent to fetch a peace — and brings back a peace without indemnity, a count's title and an insulting nickname
level.witte.hint: First the rails: the minister is strong, and the sovereign is looking to the Far East. Carried away by the East, the sovereign moves the strong minister into an honorary chair. And then the dismissed man travels to Portsmouth, to the mediator. The timber concession is a trap: a man who has been bought will not be let near the peace table.
